McKennie indicates USA players could follow Pochettino to Manchester United

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that weston McKennie has noted USA players could follow Mauricio Pochettino to Manchester United, days after his national team coach took the job there.
  • Recent findings suggest that the question put to Weston McKennie was whether USA players might follow their coach to Old Trafford.
  • McKennie called the speculation inevitable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that weston McKennie has noted USA players could follow Mauricio Pochettino to Manchester United, days after his national team coach took the job there. Juventus, already without Thuram and Locatelli, now face pressure to rule out a mid-season sale.

Recent findings suggest that the question put to Weston McKennie was whether USA players might follow their coach to Old Trafford. His answer was that it could potentially happen.

McKennie called the speculation inevitable. He said many USA players are due to change clubs within the next year, calciomercato.com reported.

Sources indicate that pochettino was asked about the same subject. He remarked now was not the right time to discuss it. He added that United are among the very top clubs and a dream for many players.

Pochettino and his staff remain in charge of the USA for two games against Haiti, on 14 and 17 November. United agreed with the federation that the staff would be released once those national-team duties were over. Pochettino became USA head coach in September 2024. His record with the national team stands at 21 wins, 12 defeats and two draws from 35 matches.

The comments land awkwardly in Turin. Reports had already linked United with a January move for the American. Juventus regard him as central to Luciano Spalletti’s plans and are reluctant to let him leave mid-season, ESPN reported.

His contract, which runs until June 2030, offers the club some protection. It was signed only months before Pochettino’s switch to English football.

In a recent development, mcKennie arrived from Schalke 04 in August 2020. His value to Spalletti lies in his flexibility.

Industry observers note that the club noted in its renewal announcement that he had been used on both flanks under Spalletti. He had also recently played as a striker.

Sources indicate that the timing makes McKennie harder to replace. He is one of the few senior midfielders Spalletti still has available.

Thuram is out until 2027 after knee surgery. Captain Manuel Locatelli also faces a long absence after twisting his right knee against Milan. He had surgery in Lyon on 8 September to repair the external meniscus, and Corriere dello Sport put his lay-off at five to six months.

Losing him in January would thin the squad further at a delicate point of the season. Juventus are chasing a Champions League place. Qualification is key to the club’s finances.

That is why the club’s stance matters as much as the player’s words.

Sources indicate that mcKennie’s own answer was measured. He mentioned nobody knows which players a coach really wants.

It has been revealed that for now, the pressure falls on Juventus. A clear statement ruling out a January sale would end the debate. Silence would leave it open until the window.

The next step comes at Old Trafford. Pochettino takes charge of Manchester United from 18 November, and his first squad decisions will show whether the interest is real.

Welcome to our Live Comments section, where new comments will appear automatically.

If it’s a good fee and we can reinvest into two players to help the squad depth I would be fine with it.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 17:22 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 19:04 EST, 24 November 2026.
  • Whether through complacency, boredom, or a mixture of both, Arsenal's habit of switching off in the second half of matches is becoming a serious issue.
  • It is a flaw which could bite them hard against teams they would encounter in the later stages of the Champions League.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 17:22 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 19:04 EST, 24 November 2026.

Whether through complacency, boredom, or a mixture of both, Arsenal's habit of switching off in the second half of matches is becoming a serious issue.

It is a flaw which could bite them hard against teams they would encounter in the later stages of the Champions League.

When Kepa Arrizabalaga parried Julian Ryerson's shot into the path of Jobe Bellingham, the Arsenal script had seemingly flipped from first-half domination to second-half capitulation.

Luckily for Mikel Arteta, Bellingham's tap-in was flagged for offside to keep the north London club's unbeaten record in this competition intact, stretching back to 20 matches (excluding penalty shootouts).

Earlier in the second half, Maximilian Beier had equalised, skilfully turning Gabriel before placing a neat strike past Kepa.

In a recent development, but this match should have been sealed well before then for Arsenal - and they had enough chances to win it late on, too. Viktor Gyokeres headed wide when unmarked and Declan Rice struck the woodwork.

Arsenal were made to pay for their complacency again by drawing with Borussia Dortmund.

Arsenal were held 1-1 with Dortmund thanks to this Maximilian Beier's strike for the visitors.

By full-time, the Gunners had mustered 30 shots, but no winning goal.

Despite his team's wastefulness, Arteta said: 'The domination and threat was really impressive. The general feeling inside the dressing room is that we should reward ourselves with more. I love the courage, the fluidity and the understanding with the players with and without the ball.'.

But the recurrence of losing concentration later in matches, as the Gunners did against Slavia Prague and Newcastle in recent weeks, is an issue which Arteta must urgently address.

Recent findings suggest that it is not sustainable, and ruined an evening initially lit up by Gyokeres' stunning strike. The Sweden striker's display reflected the fierce competition for places at Arsenal. Perform well and you have a chance of a starting spot. Anything less results in a place on the bench in the winter's cold.

Gyokeres received Noni Madueke's pass outside the area on ten minutes and Dortmund's back line completely backed off, almost pleading for him to shoot.

Sources indicate that he obliged, cocking his right boot back to unleash a powerful strike which initially looked to be going over the bar before dipping into goalkeeper Gregor Kobel's net. It was a top-drawer finish from a man who cannot nail down a regular starting spot, despite 21 goals last season and a goal and assist in Arsenal's previous Champions League match against Slavia Prague.

It is the kind of luxury Arteta has worked towards since taking on this job seven years ago.

One back-up player who inspires rather less confidence is goalkeeper Kepa. No1 David Raya injured his shoulder at Newcastle and so in came his fellow Spaniard. Kepa's touches early on were cheered by the Arsenal faithful, massaging the confidence of a man who has endured the kind of calamity which is not easily erased from memory.

The dropping of Rayan Cherki's cross in March's Carabao Cup final defeat by Manchester City; his lapse to misjudge a corner and gift Real Betis a goal during pre-season - these are the sorts of errors which have Arsenal fans feeling uncomfortable whenever Raya is unavailable.

Viktor Gyokeres (left) opened the scoring with this stunning long-range strike for the Gunners.

Kepa Arrizabalaga (right) started in goal for Arsenal with first-choice David Raya out injured.

Arsenal (4-2-3-1): Arrizabalaga 6; White 6 (Timber 65, 6), Konsa 6, Gabriel 5, Hincapie 6; Lewis-Skelly 5 (Guimaraes 66, 6), Rice 7; Madueke 8, Odegaard 7, Tzolis 5 (Eze 66, 6); Gyokeres 7.

Borussia Dortmund (3-4-2-1): Kobel 6; Gadou 7, Anton 6, Schlotterbeck 6; Ryerson 6, Nmecha 6, Veerman 6, Svensson 6; Bellingham 6, Beier 7 (Guirassy 65, 6); Fabio Silva 6 (Karetsas 65, 6).

Raya is battling to return for Arsenal's huge Premier League clash against Manchester City on Sunday and the sense of panic in the days after his injury has been understandable.

Raya is so much more than just an excellent shot-stopper. His distribution is second to none: pinpoint long throws to set wingers away on counter-attacks and a highly impressive passing range, both aerially and across the floor.

Still, Kepa just about survived. There were jitters, like passing the ball straight to a yellow shirt on 52 minutes, which the opposition failed to punish. But he hung in there and that will have given his confidence a boost.

According to recent reports, arsenal started well, Madueke continuing his excellent form of late in place of the injured Bukayo Saka. Madueke crossed for Christos Tzolis, who drove his shot into the turf, before setting up Martin Odegaard to shoot wide.

It didn't take long for the winger's passing to produce results, as he fed Gyokeres for that venomous strike from distance.

Rice lashed a strike from range which dipped just over the bar as Dortmund showed a tendency to gift too much time on the ball.

It has been revealed that after the break Dortmund changed tack. Sitting back and soaking up the pressure was not working, so they got the ball forward more quickly and more often, forcing Arsenal on to the back foot.

The Gunners held on for a point - and endured another lesson in switching off.

By Darren Plant | 26 Nov 2026 12:15.

Wolverhampton Wanderers make the trip to Lincoln City on Saturday afternoon looking to strengthen their hold of a top-three position in the Championship table.

Meanwhile, Lincoln play host to one of the form teams in the division having just sacked co-managers Chris Cohen and Tom Shaw.

Positives can be taken from Lincoln - last season's League One champions - reaching this stage of the season sitting three points above the relegation zone.

Nevertheless, Tuesday's 4-0 defeat at Charlton Athletic represented their fifth successive defeat and was the final straw for Lincoln's hierarchy.

Despite Cohen and Shaw arguably performing better than anticipated in their surprise role, Lincoln had also only recorded four points from their last 10 games, losing on eight occasions.

A change in direction has, theoretically, been made at the right time, and a permanent successor is expected to be selected ahead of the trip to Cardiff City on December 5.

For now, first-team coach Shaun Pearson and fellow backroom staff members will attempt to guide Lincoln to just their second home win in nine matches, their only such success having come against struggling Burnley by a 4-1 scoreline last month.

As for Wolves, they make the trip to the ProAmpac Stadium having recorded a 3-0 win over Derby County and having had the most shots (39) in a Championship fixture in 11 years.

For all the criticism that has come Cesar Peixoto's way, Wolves remain in third spot with 31 goals and 34 points from their 17 games.

An eight-match unbeaten streak has been put together, the West Midlands outfit picking up six wins and two draws since October 16.

Sources indicate that lincoln may take belief from Wolves only prevailing from four of their eight away games. That noted, Peixoto's side have already made trips to the likes of West Ham United, Birmingham City, Sheffield United, Middlesbrough and Wrexham this season, suggesting that it is a far better record than in black and white.

Sonny Bradley, Yunus Konak, Dom Jeffries and Freddie Draper are all in contention for recalls to the team.

However, midfielder Conor McGrandles is again expected to miss out through injury.

Meanwhile, Peixoto could make a number of alterations, with Toti Gomes and Marshall Munetsi among those who could feature for Wolves.

Rodrigo Gomes may also get the nod over Rafiki Noted in the final third, while Adam Armstrong scoring on five of his last six appearances will see him keep his place ahead of Sean Neave.

Lincoln City possible starting lineup:.

Wickens; Coubis, Bradley, Elerewe, Towler; Reach, Konak, Varfolomeev, House; Street; Draper.

Wolverhampton Wanderers possible starting lineup:.

Sa; Trippier, Djiga, Krejci, T Gomes; Andre, Munetsi; R Gomes, Lopez, Mane; Armstrong.

Norway's ice hockey team notes Russia replacing it at World Juniors

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (861 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With just weeks to go until the start of the 2027 World Junior Championship, it remains unclear who will be the 10th, and final, participant.
  • The move, which has yet to be publicly revealed by the IIHF, comes in apparent response to the Court of Arbitration (CAS) ruling in late October, which ordered it to allow Russia to return to international play.
  • The IIHF barred Russia and Belarus from international play shortly after Moscow released its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With just weeks to go until the start of the 2027 World Junior Championship, it remains unclear who will be the 10th, and final, participant. This comes after the Norwegian Ice Hockey Association mentioned the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) had said it had been removed from the tournament so that Russia could take part.

The move, which has yet to be publicly revealed by the IIHF, comes in apparent response to the Court of Arbitration (CAS) ruling in late October, which ordered it to allow Russia to return to international play. The World Juniors is the first tournament affected by the CAS decision.

The IIHF barred Russia and Belarus from international play shortly after Moscow released its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

In a statement issued Saturday, the IIHF mentioned it was "taking the necessary steps required by the CAS ruling and reviewing what conditions would need to be met to safeguard our Championships, protect the organization's financial stability and secure the long-term future of international ice hockey.".

As of Monday, the IIHF website still listed Norway as one of the participants in the World Juniors, which is to be hosted by Edmonton and Red Deer, Alberta, beginning on December 26. But Swiss Ice Hockey has responded to Norway's statement, saying its team would not face Russia at the World Juniors — as would be the case if it replaces Norway in the schedule.

However, it's far from certain that Russia will actually be able to ice a team in the tournament, as just last week, the Canadian prime minister ruled out the possibility.

"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," stated Mark Carney.

"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors, the Russians will not be there.".

In a recent development, how this circle could be squared is unclear. Carney's pledge, coupled with the stated refusal by Finland, Sweden, Switzerland and others to face Russia in an international tournament, appears to have given the Norwegian Ice Hockey Association (NIHF) hope that its team could still play in the upcoming tournament. Several long-time corporate sponsors have also threatened to pull out if Russia is allowed to compete.

"This makes us hope that the last word has not been said about our participation in Canada in December," said NIHF General Secretary Petter Salsten.

"The Norwegian Ice Hockey Association is awaiting further information from the IIHF in the coming days.".

Meanwhile, the German Ice Hockey Association (DEB) is still in discussions with the government in Berlin and the IIHF about how to proceed — or not — with hosting the Men's Ice Hockey World Championship in May.

Sources indicate that "We intend to host the world championship in Germany next year, and I am very optimistic that we will succeed in doing so," DEB chairman Frank H. Lutz told German broadcaster MagentaSport on Saturday.

While he acknowledged the IIHF's CAS-ordered requirement to include Russia and reiterated the DEB's rejection of the court ruling, he provided no indication as to how this obstacle could be overcome.

Lutz, who remarked he would be in Berlin for more consultations this week, had previously said handing back Germany's hosting rights was a possibility — if only as a last resort.

On Friday, government spokesman Stefan Kornelius said Berlin supports the DEB's efforts to find a solution.

Industry observers note that "However, given the boycotts that would follow Russia's readmission, that would effectively be impossible. For this reason, we intend to explore, through dialogue, how we can still ensure the tournament takes place.".

Asked at the same press conference whether Germany could matter visas to a Russian team for the tournament, a Foreign Ministry spokesman indicated that this would be difficult under restrictions at the moment in place.

"At a time when Russia is waging a war of aggression against Ukraine, there can be no 'normalcy' — and we will certainly not pretend that there is," remarked spokesperson Martin Giese.

However, he did not categorically rule out the possibility.

It has been suggested that government officials could be choosing their words carefully out of concern for Munich's chances as it bids to host the Summer Olympics in 2036, 2040 or 2044.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) recently lifted its sanctions on Russian athletes and suspension of the Russian National Olympic Committee, opening the door for their return to competition despite the ongoing war in Ukraine.

The thinking goes that the IOC would expect national Olympic committees who are bidding to host an Olympic Games — like the German Olympic Sports Confederation (DOSB) — to follow its lead.

Asked whether the debate over Russia's possible involvement in a hockey tournament could affect Munich's chances, government spokesman Kornelius said he didn't wish to "speculate on implications.".

Still, with the IOC set to decide in the next few weeks whether Munich advances to the next stage of the process, one has to think that the glitch could hardly have come up at a more inopportune time for the DOSB.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • CRISPR-associated transposases (CASTs) achieve site-specific DNA integration by combining the RNA-guided targeting action of a nuclease-deficient CRISPR–Cas system with the assembly of a Tn7-like transpososome complex1,2.
  • It has been revealed that transposons are pervasive DNA segments capable of mobilizing within and between genomes, thus serving as potent drivers of genome evolution and horizontal gene transfer10,11,12.
  • The inherent programmability of CASTs has driven their development as genome-editing tools that enable the site-specific insertion of multi-kilobase DNA cargoes without generating double-stranded breaks in the target DNA.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CRISPR-associated transposases (CASTs) achieve site-specific DNA integration by combining the RNA-guided targeting action of a nuclease-deficient CRISPR–Cas system with the assembly of a Tn7-like transpososome complex1,2. Understanding the detailed mechanisms of this elaborate process is paramount to engineering CAST systems into programmable genetic tools3,4,5,6. Type I-F Pseudoalteromonas CAST (PseCAST) demonstrates the highest activity in mammalian cells so far7 and has been adapted extensively through directed evolution8. However, its continued rational engineering requires addressing critical gaps in our understanding of transpososome assembly and activation9. Here we perform structural analyses using cryogenic electron microscopy, validated by DNA transposition assays, to visualize the PseCAST system in a series of functional states that define the stepwise mechanism of RNA-guided DNA integration. The structures of the PseCAST targeting and transposase recruitment complexes revealed that conformational changes in the Cascade–TniQ module, induced by R-loop formation, are associated with target-DNA stabilization and TnsC heptamerization. This, in turn, results in the recruitment of the TnsAB transposase by conserved interactions with the carboxy-terminal tail of TnsB. Finally, the structure of the 1.2 MDa PseCAST transpososome holocomplex revealed allosteric coupling of TnsC–TnsB and TnsB–target-DNA interactions to the conformational remodelling of the TnsB catalytic site, activating donor-DNA integration. Together, these findings establish a unified mechanistic blueprint for RNA-guided DNA integration by type I CASTs and provide a structural framework to guide their engineering for genome-editing applications.

It has been revealed that transposons are pervasive DNA segments capable of mobilizing within and between genomes, thus serving as potent drivers of genome evolution and horizontal gene transfer10,11,12. CASTs have evolved repeatedly by exaptation of minimal, nuclease-deficient CRISPR–Cas systems to enable RNA-guided, site-specific DNA integration13,14,15. These systems operate through the concerted action of a CRISPR-based targeting module and a Tn7-like transposition machinery comprising the TnsC AAA+ ATPase, the TnsB transposase and, in some systems, the TnsA endonuclease. The CASTs characterized so far differ mainly in the organization of their DNA-targeting and transposition modules1,2,16,17,18. Type I variants typically use a multi-subunit Cascade–TniQ (QCascade) complex for target recognition guided by CRISPR RNA (crRNA) and TnsA–TnsB for cut-and-paste transposition19,20,21. By contrast, type V-K systems rely on the Cas12k–TniQ–S15 complex for crRNA-guided targeting5 and use only TnsB for copy-and-paste transposition, resulting in cointegrate products22. TnsC plays a pivotal part in all CASTs, acting as an adapter that bridges the targeting module and the transposase enzymes to define the insertion site23,24.

The inherent programmability of CASTs has driven their development as genome-editing tools that enable the site-specific insertion of multi-kilobase DNA cargoes without generating double-stranded breaks in the target DNA. CAST-based editing has been implemented in bacteria25,26,27,28 and mammalian cells7,8,29,30, offering considerable potential for research and therapeutic applications. Type V-K CASTs generally show low integration efficiencies in human cell lines29,30, limited specificity2,26,27,31 and heterogeneous insertion profiles22,30. By contrast, type I-F systems can perform precise, simple insertions with substantially higher efficiencies1,7,22,26. In particular, the type I-F system of the Pseudoalteromonas Tn7016 transposon (Fig. 1a) has emerged as a highly promising candidate for genome-engineering applications, because of its uniquely high integration activity in human cells7,9. Directed evolution and structure-guided engineering of PseCAST components in Escherichia coli have resulted in the evoCAST system. This system has markedly improved integration efficiencies, reaching up to 10–30% in human cells, yet maintains precise, cointegrate-free insertion outcomes8. Although structural studies of type V-K CAST systems have provided mechanistic insights into various stages of transpososome assembly5,6,32,33,34,35,36, structural information about type I CASTs is presently limited to sub-complexes9,19,20,21,37,38,39,40,41,42. This presents a knowledge gap in the mechanistic understanding of the RNA-guided DNA-integration pathway. Specifically, the mechanism by which the RNA-guided targeting module induces the assembly and catalytic activation of the transposase components remains unclear.

Recent findings suggest that here we report a series of structural snapshots of the PseCAST system obtained using cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM), including a previously unresolved transpososome holocomplex assembly comprising all molecular components. These snapshots reveal the molecular determinants and critical checkpoints at key stages of the RNA-guided DNA-integration pathway, including target DNA recognition, TnsC oligomerization, transposase recruitment and catalytic activation. Our findings define the molecular mechanisms that govern RNA-guided DNA integration by type I CASTs, thereby establishing a structural foundation for the further development of these systems as genome-engineering tools.

In a recent development, tnsC oligomers function as bridging modules for the assembly of the transposition machinery in both type V-K and type I-B CASTs, interacting with the RNA-guided CRISPR module through their amino-terminal face and with the transposase through their carboxy-terminal face6,20,36,41. To elucidate the structural basis of the guide-RNA-dependent assembly of TnsC in the type I-F PseCAST, our initial cryo-EM analysis yielded a reconstruction of a target-DNA-bound complex comprising PseCascade–TniQ and a heptameric TnsC ring (hereafter the targeting complex) at an overall resolution of 3.1 Å (Fig. 1b–d, Extended Data Table 1 and Extended Data Fig. 1a–c). Resembling the architecture of TnsC heptamers from the canonical Tn7 element of E. coli and other type I CAST systems20,40,42,43 (Extended Data Fig. 2), the TnsC heptamer has a near-perfect seven-fold symmetry without a helical rise or seam, fully enclosing the DNA duplex in a positively charged central channel, in which all seven TnsC ATPase sites are occupied by ATP molecules and Mg2+ ions. The enclosed DNA adopts B-form geometry and is contacted by the Glu105–Asp120 loops of TnsC.1 and TnsC.5 through nonspecific interactions.

According to recent reports, notably, the structure of the targeting complex includes a complete 32-base-pair R-loop (Fig. 1e), which was only partially formed in the previously reported intermediate PseQCascade complex structure9. In contrast to the open arrangement of the partial R-loop intermediate9, the Cas8 α-helical bundle (residues 272–421) undergoes an approximately 90° rotation into a closed or locked state (Extended Data Fig. 3a), establishing additional contacts with the protospacer-adjacent motif (PAM)-distal segment of the target DNA, both TniQ subunits and Cas7.5 (Extended Data Fig. 3b–d). Moreover, three nucleotides of the displaced non-target strand (NTGS) are bound in a pocket in the Cas8 bundle (Extended Data Fig. 3e), which likely facilitates reannealing of the NTGS with the target strand (TGS) in the PAM-distal DNA segment and its interactions with the TniQ dimer. This feature is absent from the partial R-loop and open helical-bundle states of type I-F CAST QCascade complexes published previously19,21. As the presence of a full R-loop and a closed Cas8 helical-bundle conformation have been suggested to be a prerequisite for stable target engagement21, our structural observations indicate that the formation of the locked state serves as a target fidelity checkpoint upstream of transposase recruitment.

Unexpectedly, the structure of the PseCAST targeting complex revealed that the TnsC heptamer interacts with both TniQ.1 and Cas8 through extensive interfaces spanning 947 Å2 and 818 Å2, respectively (Fig. 1d and Extended Data Fig. 3f), forming a ‘super-ring’ assembly that bridges the PAM-proximal and PAM-distal ends of the QCascade subcomplex. At the N-terminal face of the heptamer, TnsC protomers use the same surfaces for interactions with both TniQ and Cas8 (Extended Data Fig. 3f). At the PAM-distal end, the N-terminal region of TniQ.1 is wedged into the TnsC.1–TnsC.7 inter-subunit interface. An aromatic pocket in TniQ.1 comprising Phe3, Phe5, Phe29 and Phe30 interacts with a hydrophobic loop in TnsC.1 containing Leu101, Leu104, Leu106, Phe107 and Ile112 (Fig. 1f). TnsC.1 further engages TniQ.1 in a series of ionic interactions (Fig. 1g) and bridging interactions that also contact the TnsC.1–TnsC.7 interface (Fig. 1h). Individual mutations in the inserted TnsC loop (L106S or F107A) did not affect the transposition activity of PseCAST in E. coli. By contrast, a strong synergistic effect in the TnsC double mutant L106A, F107A led to a near-complete loss of transposition activity (Fig. 1i). Whereas alanine substitutions in pairs of residues in the TniQ hydrophobic pocket (either F3A and F5A, or F29A and F30A) had a mild effect on transposition efficiency (Fig. 1i), charge-reversal substitutions at these positions (either F3E and F5E, or F29E and F30E) had a substantially stronger effect (Extended Data Fig. 3g). Deletion of the seven N-terminal TniQ residues resulted in the loss of transposition activity (Fig. 1i). Moreover, cross-subunit mutant combinations involving residues in the TnsC loop and the TniQ hydrophobic pocket, either TnsC(L106S) and TniQ(F3A, F5A), or TnsC(F107A) and TniQ(F29A, F30A), resulted in a marked decrease in or the complete loss of transposition activity in vivo (Fig. 1i), confirming the importance of the TniQ–TnsC interactions for the assembly of the PseCAST transpososome.

Recent findings suggest that at the PAM-proximal end, Cas8 and TnsC.5 form a shape-complementary interface, mediated by aromatic and electrostatic interactions (Fig. 1j–l). The combination of TnsC mutations R68A, Y75A, R77A and Pheresulted in a pronounced reduction in transposition activity in vivo (Fig. 1m), indicating that the Cas8–TnsC interaction contributes to transpososome assembly. However, mutations of interacting residues in Cas8, alone or in cross-subunit combinations with TnsC, had a mild or negligible effect (Fig. 1m), suggesting that the sensitivity of the TnsC–Cas8 interface to mutational perturbations is lower than that of the TnsC–TniQ interface. Similarly, whereas the individual charge-reversal TnsC mutant Y75E alone was sufficient to decrease transposition activity substantially, single charge-reversal mutations in Cas8 (T486R, W465E or H469E) had variable effects on transposition efficiency (Extended Data Fig. 3g). Together, these structural observations define the molecular coupling between the CRISPR targeting machinery and TnsC that results in the assembly of an ATP-loaded TnsC heptamer on the target DNA.

Recent findings suggest that in the canonical Tn7 element in E. coli44, as well as in the type V-K CAST system of Scytonema hofmanni (ShCAST) and the type I-B CAST system of Peltigera membranacea cyanobiont 210A (PmcCAST), transposase recruitment is mediated by TnsC interactions with the C-terminal region of TnsB6,23,41. In the structure of the paired-end complex (PEC) of PseTnsAB, the C-terminal tail of PseTnsB (residues 574–613) is disordered45. To assess whether the unstructured tail plays a similar part in interacting with PseTnsC, we performed co-precipitation experiments using affinity-tagged PseTnsB constructs comprising either the full-length protein or the standalone C-terminal tail (TnsB(575–613)) (Fig. 2a). Both full-length TnsB and TnsB(575–613) co-precipitated target-DNA-bound QCascade and TnsC efficiently in the presence of ATP (Fig. 2b), indicating that TnsB interacts directly with the targeting complex and that its C-terminal tail is sufficient for this interaction. The amount of co-precipitated TnsC remained unchanged in the presence of the non-hydrolysable ATP analogue ATPγS (Extended Data Fig. 4a), indicating that, similar to the type I-B PmcCAST system41,42, TnsB does not stimulate ATPase-dependent depolymerization of TnsC in PseCAST. Furthermore, co-precipitation of TnsC by TnsB(575–613) decreased strongly in the absence of ATP, suggesting that the interaction requires ATP-dependent TnsC oligomerization (Extended Data Fig. 4b). This result was corroborated by the loss of TnsC co-precipitation in the absence of QCascade or after introducing mutations in the TniQ- and Cas8-interacting interfaces (Extended Data Fig. 4c). Together, these results indicate that TnsB recruitment requires QCascade-dependent assembly of TnsC on the target DNA.

In a recent development, to validate these findings structurally, we aimed to reconstitute and determine the structure of QCascade–TnsC in complex with TnsAB bound to the excised transposon ends. To this end, we performed affinity co-precipitation using a recombinant TnsAB fusion protein construct (Fig. 2a), pre-assembled with a segment of the right end of the transposon (RE), to capture the QCascade–TnsC complex assembled on the target substrate comprising a linear double-stranded DNA (Extended Data Fig. 4d). Single-particle cryo-EM analysis of the resulting sample yielded a 2.8-Å reconstruction of a PseCAST transposase recruitment complex comprising target-bound QCascade and heptamerized TnsC decorated with TnsB C-terminal segments (or TnsB hooks; residues Trp605–Glu613). The TnsB hooks are bound to all TnsC subunits at the junction between the N-terminal α/β core domain and the C-terminal α-helical bundle close to the ATP binding pocket (Fig. 2c,d, Extended Data Table 2 and Extended Data Fig. 5a–c), similar to the arrangement described for type V-K34,36 and I-B41,42 CASTs (Extended Data Fig. 6). They are anchored by hydrophobic interactions of TnsB residues Trp605, Leu609 and Phe612 and an additional hydrogen bond between the backbone carbonyl of residue Asp606 of TnsB and Arg212 of TnsC (Fig. 2e). Corroborating these observations, TnsB mutation W605A caused a substantial decrease in the transposition activity of PseCAST in E. coli. Moreover, individual TnsB mutations L609K or F612A, as well as the deletion of the entire TnsB hook (Δ604–613) resulted in a complete loss of transposition activity (Fig. 2f). These findings highlight the functional requirement of the interactions between the TnsB hook and TnsC for the transposition activity of PseCAST and demonstrate the critical role of the TnsB C-terminal tail in the recruitment of the TnsAB transposase and for the delivery of the transposon DNA to the target site before integration.

According to recent reports, to determine the structure of the PseCAST transpososome holocomplex comprising Cascade, TniQ, TnsC and TnsAB, we used a modified ‘one pot’ affinity co-precipitation strategy to trap the transpososome in a post-integration strand-transfer complex (STC) state (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 7), which has been used previously to visualize transpososome structures because of its stability6,34,36,41,46,47. The assembly used a minimal symmetrized RE donor sequence, which supports transposition in related systems48,49 and is sufficient for the formation of a paired-end PseTnsAB complex45. Cryo-EM analysis of the resulting sample, supported by three-dimensional variability analysis combined with heterogeneous and locally focused refinement, yielded a reconstruction with a global resolution of 3.1 Å (Fig. 3b, Extended Data Table 3 and Extended Data Fig. 8a–d). The reconstruction revealed that the transposase adopts an intertwined, pseudo-twofold arrangement with a TnsA2–TnsB4 stoichiometry to assemble on the structured DNA in an STC configuration (Fig. 3c,d). All seven TnsC subunits are bound to the C-terminal hook motifs of TnsAB (Fig. 3b,c); it is not possible to ascertain which of these are connected to the bound TnsAB or contributed by unbound TnsAB molecules in trans, as the connecting segments (residues 824–843) of TnsAB are unstructured. The target DNA exits from the central channel of the TnsC heptamer and extends towards the TnsAB tetramer assembled on the pseudo-palindromic target site duplication (TSD) region and the adjacent transposon end sequences (Fig. 3a). As in the structure of the TnsAB PEC45, each transposon end is occupied by two TnsB protomers: a proximal catalytic subunit (TnsB.1 or TnsB.2)—the catalytic domain of which engages the other transposon end in trans—and a distal structural subunit (TnsB.3 or TnsB.4) (Fig. 3c). Only two TnsA subunits (TnsA.1 and TnsA.2), bound to the catalytic TnsB protomers, are resolved in the structure. The corresponding interaction interfaces in the structural TnsB subunits are occupied by the bound RE DNA duplexes, precluding TnsA interactions.

Sources indicate that the structure of the PseCAST holocomplex reveals the molecular interactions responsible for the TnsC-dependent recruitment of TnsAB to the target DNA to effect site-specific donor integration. The TnsB.1 subunit is tethered to the C-terminal face of the TnsC heptamer by its β-barrel domain (residues 434–500), positioned at the interface of the TnsC.1 and TnsC.7 subunits (Fig. 3e). TnsC.1 inserts its C-terminal loop—spanning residues 314–322 and including Leu318—into a hydrophobic pocket formed by Val472, Gln467 and Leu441 in the TnsB.1 β-barrel domain (Fig. 3e). In turn, Asn316 of TnsC, situated in the same loop in TnsC.7, interacts through hydrogen bonds with Arg443 and Asn444 in TnsB.1 (Fig. 3e). Aspartate substitutions of Leu318 in TnsC (L318D) or Val472 in TnsB (V472D) resulted in a pronounced reduction in transposition activity in vivo (Fig. 3f). The single TnsC mutation N316A or replacement of TnsC loop residues 316–321 with a (Gly–Ser)3 linker resulted in modestly impaired activity. By contrast, the single TnsB mutations R443E or N444D strongly reduced transposition activity (Fig. 3f), confirming that the formation of this interface is essential for PseCAST-mediated DNA transposition.

It has been revealed that in addition to interactions with TnsC, the β-barrel domain of the catalytic TnsB.1 subunit also interacts with the backbone of the target DNA segment downstream of the TnsC heptamer, forming a network of hydrogen bonds and electrostatic contacts using Arg439, Thr440, Lys447 and Gln449 of TnsB (Fig. 3g). Furthermore, Lys520 and Arg524 in the C-terminal helical domain of TnsB also contact the target DNA backbone. Notably, this domain adopts a helical bundle fold that bridges the catalytic and β-barrel domains in the catalytic TnsB.1 and TnsB.2 subunits. By contrast, the helical domain of the structural TnsB.3 and TnsB.4 subunits forms two stretched helices that are sandwiched between the catalytic domain and DNA-binding domain 2 of TnsAB.1 and TnsAB.2, contributing to intra-subunit contacts.

Together, these insights highlight the functional role of the TnsB β-barrel domain in transpososome assembly. The shape complementarity of the TnsC and TnsB β-barrel interaction surfaces, together with cooperative interactions with the target DNA, provide the structural basis for the molecular ruler mechanism that defines the integration site, enabling the transposon to be inserted at a fixed distance of 49 nucleotides from the crRNA-specified target site. Moreover, the synergistic contacts with two TnsC subunits and the target DNA underlie a checkpoint mechanism that senses target DNA-dependent TnsC oligomerization, thereby explaining the strictly sequential assembly of the transpososome observed in type I-F systems40.

It has been revealed that the structure of the PseCAST transpososome holocomplex captures the TnsAB STC tetramer in a post-integration state (Fig. 4a,b). As in the PEC structure45, the active sites of the TnsA.1 and TnsA.2 subunits interact with the 5′ termini of the transposon ends, adopting a catalytically competent, post-cleavage geometry in which the catalytic triad residues Glu34, Asp71 and Lys87 of TnsA coordinate the 5′-terminal phosphate group and a single Mg2+ ion (Fig. 4c). In contrast to the PEC structure, the catalytic sites of the TnsB.1 and TnsB.2 subunits also assume an activated conformation in which a Mg2+ ion—coordinated by the catalytic triad residues Asp220, Asp304 and Glu340 of TnsB—interacts with the 3′-hydroxyl group of the terminal nucleotide (dG76 in the NTGS) of the target DNA and the phosphodiester group that links the TSD segment to the 3′-terminal nucleotide of the transposon end (Fig. 4d). Furthermore, the catalytic domain establishes contacts with RE and TSD nucleotides that are crucial for STC formation (Fig. 4d). Specifically, Asp225 of TnsB positions an additional Mg2+ ion such that it simultaneously coordinates the phosphate groups of dA(−82) and dG(−80), stabilizing a kink in the DNA backbone at the TSD–RE junction that enables STC formation. The backbone is additionally contacted by Thr222, Arg239 and Ser360 of TnsB (Fig. 4d). Consistent with these observations, alanine substitution of Asp225 (D225A) or a charge-reversal mutation of Arg239 of TnsB (R239E) resulted in a complete loss of PseCAST transposition activity in E. coli, whereas TnsB mutations T222A or S360A only reduced PseCAST activity (Fig. 4e).
