In a recent development, finally, the PseCAST transpososome holocomplex structure highlights a potential allosteric relay mechanism that underlies the target-DNA-dependent catalytic activation of TnsB. In the PEC structure, the β-barrel and C-terminal helical domains of the catalytic TnsB subunits are disordered45. By contrast, both domains are structured in the STC state and interface with the catalytic domain (Fig. 4b) through a network of hydrogen bonds and ionic interactions (Fig. 4f). This is coupled with local structural remodelling of the catalytic domain, resulting in the ordering of an adjacent loop (residues Glu348–Lys369 of TnsB) (Fig. 4g) and an approximately 11-Å concomitant shift of the helix bearing the catalytic Glu340 residue of TnsB (Fig. 4g). The conformational rearrangement marks the transition of the catalytic site from an inactive, post-excision state to an active, strand-transfer configuration that supports Mg2+ coordination and catalytic activity. Consistent with these observations, combined alanine substitutions of Lys567, Gln571 and Asn577 in the C-terminal helical domain of TnsB strongly reduced the transposition activity of PseCAST in E. coli (Fig. 4i). Additional ordering was observed for the N-terminal segment (residues Met1–Pro11) of the TnsA helical domain, which positions the Arg4 residue of TnsA such that it contacts the 5′-terminal phosphate of the cleaved transposon end (Fig. 4c,h), implicating TnsA in TnsB activation. Accordingly, truncation of the TnsA N-terminal segment (ΔMet1–Asn12) resulted in a complete loss of transposition activity (Fig. 4i). Together, the structural observations and their functional validation indicate that the molecular interfaces formed between the C-terminal, β-barrel and catalytic domains of TnsB after binding to the target DNA and TnsC are required to support the integration activity of PseCAST. Both target DNA and TnsC synergistically couple transposase recruitment with domain ordering and catalytic-site remodelling, resulting in the allosteric activation of TnsB for site-specific DNA integration.

Our structural and functional analyses of the PseCAST system comprehensively revealed the molecular mechanism that underlies RNA-guided transposon integration by type I-F CASTs, in which an orchestrated series of interactions and conformational rearrangements couples target recognition with site-specific DNA insertion. Together, these insights support a mechanistic model in which DNA transposition is controlled by a succession of molecular checkpoints (Fig. 5). The formation of the QCascade–TnsC targeting complex requires R-loop completion, enabled by a conformational rearrangement of the Cas8 subunit, including the approximately 90° rotation of the helical bundle domain into a locked conformation. In contrast to the open conformations reported previously for type I-F CAST QCascade complexes9,19,21,37, this locked state positions the PAM-distal target-DNA duplex for binding to TniQ, which facilitates ATP-dependent TnsC assembly on the target DNA by interacting with Cas8 and TniQ. As the locked Cas8 conformation is achieved only with fully matched targets, it acts as a fidelity checkpoint that discriminates against mismatched sites, underpinning the high target specificity of PseCAST. Instead of forming extended filaments as in type V CASTs32,33, PseTnsC assembles into a symmetric heptamer to fully encircle the DNA duplex exiting QCascade. The transposon insertion site is thus defined by the physical footprint and register of the TnsC ring, rather than by TnsB-dependent TnsC depolymerization6,32,33. The initial recruitment of the TnsAB transposase PEC is mediated by the TnsB C-terminal tail hook motifs. As these interactions are dependent on TnsC heptamerization, this step provides another fidelity checkpoint that makes transposition dependent on the correct recognition of the DNA target. Finally, productive target engagement by TnsAB requires conformational ordering of the TnsB β-barrel domain and C-terminal helices, driven by interactions of the TnsB β-barrel domain with the target DNA and the TnsC heptamer. This is coupled with structural remodelling of the TnsB active site into a catalytically competent configuration. Therefore, the TnsC- and target-DNA-dependent catalytic activation of TnsB acts as a final fidelity checkpoint, ensuring that transposon DNA insertion proceeds only once the transposase is correctly anchored to the target DNA. Together, our findings reveal the structural coupling of target DNA engagement and transposase activation, but the precise role of allosteric interactions in the observed conformational rearrangements requires further investigation. We speculate that similar structural coupling is involved in activating TnsAB for transposon excision after interacting with the flanking segments of the donor DNA.

Recent findings suggest that the Cascade–TniQ complex is guided to the target DNA by base-pairing with its crRNA, leading to the initial formation of a partial R-loop. Coordination of the displaced NTGS by the Cas8 helical bundle is coupled with the transition of the bundle from open to closed, full R-loop formation and the stabilization of the double-stranded PAM-distal target-DNA duplex by the TniQ dimer. TnsC is recruited to the target site, where it assembles into a closed heptameric ring by binding to the PAM-distal target-DNA duplex in the presence of ATP, TniQ and Cas8. At the donor site, excision of the transposon DNA by TnsAB involves the formation of a PEC. The PEC is initially recruited by the TnsC heptamer by interacting with the C-terminal TnsB hooks. Interactions with the target DNA and TnsC result in structural remodelling of the β-barrel and C-terminal helical domains of the interfacing TnsB copies, which is allosterically coupled with a conformational rearrangement of the catalytic domains into an active conformation (the asterisks indicate active TnsB sites). The transposon DNA is integrated by two transesterification reactions catalysed by the active sites of the interfacing TnsBs, covalently linking both transposon 3′ ends to the target DNA with 5-base-pair spacing that results in a target-site duplication (TSD).

Directed evolution and structure-guided engineering are powerful complementary strategies for improving CAST activity8,9, recalling previous studies in which structural insights have enabled the rational design of hyperactive variants of the Sleeping Beauty transposase50,51. To provide a structural context for current engineering efforts, we mapped the activity-enhancing substitutions of evoCAST onto the PseCAST holocomplex structure (Extended Data Fig. 9). Two of these, F43S in TnsB and P88T in TnsA, have already been interpreted structurally in the PseTnsAB PEC as potentially facilitating transposon end recognition and stabilizing the cleaved NTGS overhang, respectively. Several of the remaining substitutions in TnsB, which were mostly unresolved in the PEC, can now be interpreted. Y349N, P352T and D396N are found close to the target-DNA substrate, potentially enhancing its binding. Q410K, V526E and Q549R are predominantly surface-facing and thus likely to enhance protein solubility or stability. Q594L, although unresolved in the holocomplex structure, may provide additional hydrophobic interactions to the interface formed between the C-terminal hook and TnsC, which is essential for transposase recruitment. Finally, H464R may promote the interaction between the TnsB β-barrel domain and TnsC through enhanced electrostatic contacts. The substitutions R197I and N314K in TnsC map to the TnsC oligomerization interface and the TnsC–TnsB interface, respectively. Lastly, in addition to the PAM-enhancing mutations N125D and A244N in Cas8, the A410R substitution in the helical bundle likely contacts the PAM-distal target-DNA duplex after R-loop completion (Fig. 5), potentially stabilizing the locked QCascade conformation and promoting TnsC assembly. Together, these insights suggest that evoCAST activity results from the synergistic optimization of DNA binding, intersubunit contacts, folding and solubility. Therefore, future engineering efforts should continue to use both structure-guided and directed-evolution approaches.

In conclusion, the structural findings presented here reveal the molecular mechanisms underpinning RNA-guided transposition by type I CASTs, providing a framework for their further rational engineering for technological applications.

Recent findings suggest that the expression plasmids containing His10–TEV-tagged TniQ and Cas8 (pSL4521), Cas7, Cas6 and the CRISPR array (pSL4522), His6–SUMO–TEV-tagged TnsC (pSL5536) and His6–SUMO–TEV-tagged TnsAB fusion protein (pSL3768) were cloned using standard molecular biology methods including Gibson52 and Golden Gate53 assembly. All plasmids were sequence-verified using whole-plasmid Nanopore sequencing (Genewiz). To clone the expression plasmid containing Cas7, the CRISPR array and Twin-Strep-tagged Cas6 (pMS321), a Twin-Strep-tag54 was added to the C-terminus of cas6 by Gibson assembly: pSL4522 was linearized by PCR using oMS603 and oMS604, and the Twin-Strep-tag was amplified by PCR from a common backbone using the primers oMS605 and oMS606, which contain overhangs compatible with the linearized pSL4522 plasmid. Constructs for expression of His6–MBP-tagged versions of the TnsAB fusion protein and TnsB were generated by PCR amplification of the coding sequence using pSL3768 as template and primer pairs oMS631-632 and oMS634-632, respectively. The PCR products were inserted in the 1C backbone (Addgene; 29654) by ligation-independent cloning55. The His6–MBP-tagged TnsB C-terminal tail (residues 575–613) was prepared by Gibson assembly, using the His6–MBP–TnsB plasmid as a template and the primer pairs oGF181-182 and oGF180-184 to generate the PCR fragments. Plasmids were cloned and propagated in Mach I cells (Thermo Fisher Scientific), purified using the GeneJET plasmid miniprep kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and verified by full-plasmid sequencing or Sanger sequencing (Microsynth). All sequences of primers and parental plasmids used for cloning are provided in Supplementary Tables 1 and 2.

According to recent reports, for Cascade–TniQ protein expression, the plasmid pSL4521 encoding His10–TEV–TniQ and Cas8 and the plasmid pMS321 encoding Cas7, Cas6–Twin-Strep and the crRNA were transformed together in 50 μl of E. coli BL21 Rosetta2 (DE3) cells (Novagen), plated on an agar plate and incubated at 37 °C overnight. A single colony was inoculated in 100 ml of Luria broth (LB) to obtain a starter culture. Both the transformation plate and liquid medium were supplemented with 50 µg ml−1 kanamycin, 50 µg ml−1 streptomycin and 33 µg ml−1 chloramphenicol. After overnight growth at 37 °C and 220 rpm, the starter culture was added to eight 750-ml flasks containing antibiotic-supplemented (kanamycin, streptomycin) LB medium to reach a starting optical density at 600 nm (OD600) of 0.05. Cell cultures were grown at 37 °C with shaking at 110 rpm until an OD600 of 0.6 was reached. Protein expression was induced with 0.4 mM isopropyl β-d-1-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG) for 16 h at 18 °C. Cells were collected by centrifugation (4,000g at 4 °C for 30 min) and resuspended in 100 ml of lysis buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 500 mM NaCl, 5 mM imidazole) supplemented with 1 μg ml−1 pepstatin and 200 μg ml−1 4-(2-aminoethyl)benzenesulfonyl fluoride (AEBSF). The suspension was lysed using a Maximator cell homogenizer at 1,500 bar and 4 °C. The lysate was cleared by centrifugation (40,000g at 4 °C for 40 min) and applied to three 5-ml HisTrap HP columns (Cytiva) connected in tandem and equilibrated in lysis buffer. The columns were washed with 200 ml of HisTrap wash buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 500 mM NaCl, 5 mM imidazole) and eluted with 50 ml of HisTrap elution buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 500 mM NaCl, 250 mM imidazole). Dithiothreitol (DTT) and ATP were added to the eluted sample to a final concentration of 1 mM each. The sample was added to 7 ml of 50% Strep-Tactin affinity resin suspension (IBA Lifesciences) in HisTrap elution buffer. The mixture was incubated at 4 °C on a rotating wheel for 30 min. The protein-bound resin was washed with 70 ml of size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 500 mM KCl, 1 mM DTT) and the sample was eluted with 20 ml of SEC buffer supplemented with 5 mM d-desthiobiotin. Eluted fractions were further purified by SEC using a Superose 6 Increase 10/300 GL (Cytiva) column in SEC buffer. Purified proteins were concentrated to approximately 10 mg ml−1 using a 30-kDa molecular-mass cut-off centrifugal filter (Merck Millipore), flash frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C until further use.

Industry observers note that for TnsC expression, the vector pSL5536 encoding His6–SUMO–TEV–TnsC was transformed in 50 μl of E. coli BL21 Star (DE3) cells (Thermo Fisher Scientific), plated on an agar plate supplemented with 50 µg ml−1 kanamycin and incubated at 37 °C overnight. A single colony was inoculated in 100 ml of kanamycin-supplemented LB to obtain a starter culture. After overnight growth at 37 °C and 220 rpm, the starter culture was added to eight 750-ml flasks containing kanamycin-supplemented LB medium to reach a starting OD600 of 0.05. Cell cultures were grown at 37 °C with shaking at 110 rpm until an OD600 of 0.6 was reached. Protein expression was induced with 0.3 mM IPTG for 16 h at 18 °C. Cells were collected by centrifugation (4,000g at 4 °C for 30 min). Proteins were purified as described previously for the TnsC of Vibrio cholerae40. A cell pellet (corresponding to four 750-ml liquid cultures) was resuspended in 40 ml of lysis buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 1 M NaCl, 5 mM magnesium acetate, 0.2 mM EDTA, 0.1% (v/v) Triton X-100, 5% (v/v) glycerol, 1 mM DTT) supplemented with 1 μg ml−1 pepstatin, 200 μg ml−1 AEBSF and 1 μg ml−1 DNase. The suspension was lysed by ultrasonication (Bandelin Sonopuls HD 3200 equipped with a VS 70 T probe, 1 s on–2 s off cycle, at 20% amplitude for 15 min at 4 °C). The lysate was cleared by centrifugation (40,000 g at 4 °C for 45 min) and applied to two 5-ml HisTrap HP columns (Cytiva) connected in tandem and equilibrated in equilibration buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 1 M NaCl, 0.2 mM EDTA, 5% (v/v) glycerol, 10 mM imidazole, 1 mM DTT). The columns were washed with 90 ml of equilibration buffer and 50 ml of wash buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 1 M NaCl, 0.2 mM EDTA, 5% (v/v) glycerol, 30 mM imidazole, 1 mM DTT), and the proteins were eluted with 10 ml of elution buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 1 M NaCl, 0.2 mM EDTA, 5% (v/v) glycerol, 300 mM imidazole, 1 mM DTT). Elution fractions were pooled and dialysed overnight against 2 l of dialysis buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 1 M NaCl, 0.2 mM EDTA, 1% (v/v) glycerol, 1 mM DTT, 10 mM imidazole) in the presence of 2% (w/w) His6-tagged TEV protease. Any precipitated protein was removed by centrifugation (20,000g at 4 °C for 20 min). The dialysed proteins were applied to two 5-ml HisTrap HP columns (Cytiva) connected in tandem and equilibrated in equilibration buffer. The columns were washed with 60 ml of equilibration buffer, 90 ml of wash buffer and 50 ml of elution buffer. Flowthrough and initial wash fractions were applied to a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL column (Cytiva) equilibrated in SEC buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 1 M NaCl, 0.2 mM EDTA, 1% (v/v) glycerol, 1 mM DTT). Purified proteins were concentrated to approximately 12 mg ml−1 using a 10-kDa molecular-mass cut-off centrifugal filter (Merck Millipore), flash frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C until further use.

It has been revealed that for the expression of His6–SUMO–TEV–TnsAB (pSL3768), His6–MBP–TEV–TnsAB (pMS329), His6–MBP–TEV–TnsB (pMS331) and His6–MBP–TEV–TnsB(575–613) (pGF189), the procedure described for His6–SUMO–TEV–TnsC was followed, except that 0.4 mM IPTG was used to induce protein expression instead of 0.3 mM. For the purification of untagged TnsAB, TnsB or TnsB(575–613), a cell pellet (corresponding to four 750 ml liquid cultures) was resuspended in 40 ml of lysis buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 500 mM NaCl, 5 mM imidazole, 5% glycerol) supplemented with 1 μg ml−1 pepstatin, 200 μg ml−1 AEBSF and 1 μg ml−1 DNase. The suspension was lysed by ultrasonication (Bandelin Sonopuls HD 3200 equipped with a VS 70 T probe, 1 s on–2 s off cycle, at 30% amplitude for 15 min at 4 °C). The lysate was cleared by centrifugation (40,000g at 4 °C for 1 h) and applied to two 5-ml HisTrap HP columns (Cytiva) connected in tandem and equilibrated in lysis buffer. The columns were washed with 50 ml of lysis buffer, and the proteins were eluted in a stepwise gradient (5%, 20% and 100%) of elution buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 500 mM NaCl, 500 mM imidazole, 5% glycerol). Fractions corresponding to the 20% and 100% of elution-buffer concentrations were pooled and dialysed overnight in 2 l of dialysis buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 500 mM NaCl, 5% glycerol, 1 mM DTT) in the presence of 2% (w/w) His6-tagged TEV protease. Dialysed proteins were applied to two 5-ml HiTrap Heparin HP columns (Cytiva) connected in tandem and equilibrated in dialysis buffer, washed with 30 ml of dialysis buffer and eluted in a linear gradient of heparin buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 1 M NaCl, 5% glycerol, 1 mM DTT) over 150 ml (target concentration of heparin buffer: 100%). Peak fractions were pooled and further purified by SEC using a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL column (Cytiva) equilibrated in SEC buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 500 mM NaCl, 1 mM DTT). Purified proteins were concentrated to approximately 15 mg ml−1 using a 50-kDa molecular-mass cut-off centrifugal filter (Merck Millipore), flash frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C until further use. For the expression and purification of His6–MBP-tagged TnsAB, TnsB and TnsB(575–613), the procedures described for untagged TnsAB, TnsB and TnsB(575–613), respectively, were followed, except that the TEV-cleavage and heparin steps were omitted.

Industry observers note that A double-stranded target DNA (dsTarget) was prepared by annealing the synthetic oligonucleotides oMS628 and oMS629 (Supplementary Table 3) in a 1:1 ratio at a final concentration of 100 μM in annealing buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 100 mM KCl). The annealing program consisted of incubation at 95 °C for 5 min, followed by a 1 °C min−1 rampdown until 12 °C was reached. The pull-down procedure involved mixing the assembly buffer (40 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 20 mM MgCl2, 50 mM KCl, 2 mM DTT), 300 pmol of DNA substrate, water and 300 pmol of Cascade–TniQ and incubating this mixture at room temperature for 10 min. Subsequently, ATP or ATPγS (at 1 mM final concentration) was added to the sample, followed by 2,400 pmol of TnsC. The mixture was further incubated at room temperature for 30 min, after which 300 pmol of His6–MBP–TnsB(575–613) or full-length His6–MBP–TnsB was added to the sample to a final volume of 53 μl. After 30 min at room temperature, 147 μl of binding buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 10 mM MgCl2, 300 mM KCl, 1 mM DTT, 0.025% Tween-20, 1 mM ATP or ATPγS) was added to the sample. Then, 10 μl were withdrawn and mixed with 10 μl of water and 5 μl of SDS dye (225 mM Tris-HCl pH 6.8, 50% (v/v) glycerol, 5% (w/v) SDS, 0.05% (w/v) bromophenol blue, 250 mM DTT) to obtain a 5% input control sample for SDS–PAGE analysis. The sample was mixed with 50 μl of 50% amylose resin pre-equilibrated in binding buffer and incubated at 4 °C on a rotating wheel for 1 h. After a short centrifugation (500g at 4 °C for 2 min), the supernatant was discarded and the protein-bound resin was washed three times with 500 μl of binding buffer. Subsequently, 25 μl of binding buffer supplemented with 10 mM maltose was added to the sample. After centrifugation (14,000g at 4 °C for 2 min), 20 μl of supernatant was mixed with 5 μl of SDS dye to obtain an elution sample for SDS-PAGE analysis. Next, 10 μl of 5% input control and 10 μl of elution sample were loaded on a 10% SDS-PAGE gel (Bio-Rad) for each tested condition. For the control samples Cascade–TniQ–TnsC-minus or MBP–TnsB/AB-minus, the respective SEC buffers were used instead of a protein solution. SDS-PAGE gels were imaged using a ChemiDoc Imaging system (Image Lab Touch software v.4.1, Bio-Rad) and analysed using Image Lab (v.6.1.0, Bio-Rad).

A PseCAST pDonor plasmid was first transformed in E. coli BL21 (DE3) cells (NEB). Single colonies were inoculated in a liquid culture and the resulting strains were made chemically competent using standard methods. PseCAST pEffector plasmids encoding a crRNA targeting the lacZ locus (crRNA-4) and all CAST subunits were transformed in the resulting strain and plated on double-antibiotic LB agar plates containing 100 µg ml−1 carbenicillin and 100 µg ml−1 spectinomycin. After approximately 20 h of growth, surviving colonies were scraped from the plates, resuspended in fresh LB medium and re-plated on double-antibiotic LB agar plates supplemented with 0.1 mM IPTG to induce PseCAST protein expression. Cells were incubated for an additional 18–20 h, scraped and resuspended in LB medium. Cells were then lysed and integration efficiencies were measured using qPCR as described previously1. Data were plotted and statistical analyses performed in GraphPad Prism (v.11.0.0, GraphPad). Wild-type plasmid sequences, crRNA-4 and oligonucleotides used for qPCR are listed in Supplementary Tables 1 and 2.

The cryo-EM reconstruction of the QCascade–TnsC targeting complex resulted from an initial attempt to reconstitute the QCascade–TnsC–TnsAB holocomplex. Target- and donor-DNA constructs were prepared by annealing the synthetic oligonucleotides oMS572, oMS573 and oMS576 (target; Supplementary Table 3) and oMS569, oMS570 and oMS571 (donor; Supplementary Table 3) at a 1:1:1 molar ratio to a final concentration of 100 μM in annealing buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 100 mM KCl). The annealing program involved incubation at 95 °C for 5 min, followed by a 1 °C min−1 rampdown until 12 °C was reached. For the target pot assembly, 10× buffer (200 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 1,500 mM KCl, 100 mM MgCl2, 10 mM DTT), water and TniQ–Cascade were gently mixed on ice. The target DNA was added and the sample was incubated at room temperature for 10 min. TnsC and ATP were added to the sample, which was then incubated at room temperature for 15 min. The final target pot volume was 25 μl, containing 4.5 μM of Cascade–TniQ, 4.5 μM of target DNA, 40.5 μM of TnsC, 1 mM ATP, 20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 150 mM KCl, 10 mM MgCl2 and 1 mM DTT. The donor pot was prepared by mixing 10× buffer, water, ATP, TnsAB and donor DNA to a final volume of 25 μl (containing 18 μM TnsAB, 4.5 μM of donor DNA, 20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 150 mM KCl, 10 mM MgCl2, 1 mM ATP and 1 mM DTT) and then incubating the mixture at room temperature for 10 min. However, a white insoluble precipitation was observed in the donor pot at this stage and again after mixing with the target pot and incubating at room temperature for 20 min. This was likely due to TnsAB instability under the conditions used. In fact, the donor pot components were not detected in the subsequent cryo-EM analysis. After mixing the target and donor pots, the sample was centrifuged (14,000g at 4 °C for 10 min) and the pellet discarded. Next, 2.5 μl of supernatant was applied to a freshly glow-discharged (30 s) Quantifoil R 1.2/1.3 Au 300 mesh grid, blotted for 2 s (100% humidity, 4 °C) and plunge-frozen in liquid ethane using a Vitrobot Mark IV plunger (FEI), followed by storage in liquid nitrogen. Cryo-EM data were collected on an FEI Titan Krios G3i system (University of Zurich, Switzerland) operating at 300 kV and equipped with a Gatan K3 direct electron detector in super-resolution counting mode. In total, 9,403 movies were acquired at 130,000× magnification, yielding a super-resolution pixel size of 0.325 Å. Each movie consisted of 47 subframes with a cumulative exposure of 59.672 e− Å−2. EPU automated data-acquisition software for single-particle analysis (v.3.9, Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used for data acquisition, with three shots per hole and a defocus range of −1.0 to −2.4 μm in 0.2-μm increments.

It has been revealed that in total, 9,403 exposures were imported into cryoSPARC56 live (v.4.3) for real-time processing. After patch-motion and patch-CTF (contrast transfer function) correction, 745,080 particles were identified using blob picker (200–300 Å diameter), extracted (extraction box size: 600 pixels; Fourier-cropped to box size: 200 pixels) and classified into 50 two-dimensional (2D) classes. Next, 416,193 particles were selected and three volumes were generated using ab initio reconstruction. One class yielded a recognizable Cascade–TniQ–TnsC volume (108,814 particles) and was used for three-dimensional variability analysis (3DVA; filter resolution: 5 Å; mode: simple); the other two volumes did not contain density for TnsC. Two distinct volumes, resulting from one 3DVA mode, were used as input for heterogeneous refinement to separate the particles of Cascade–TniQ–TnsC from those of Cascade–TniQ only. The two volumes, after a round of non-uniform refinement, were used as inputs for a second heterogeneous refinement, together with one of the volumes from the ab initio multi-class round. This refinement resulted in a volume of Cascade (195,798 particles), Cascade–TniQ (143,494 particles) and Cascade–TniQ–TnsC (76,901 particles). The Cascade–TniQ–TnsC volume was used for non-uniform refinement after particle re-extraction (76,400 particles), yielding a reconstruction at a resolution of 3.07 Å, as calculated by gold-standard Fourier shell correlation (GSFSC). After particle subtraction, a local refinement of the TnsC heptamer generated a 3.44-Å (GSFSC resolution) map. A composite map was obtained by combining the consensus Cascade–TniQ–TnsC and TnsC-focused volumes using the combine_focused_maps function in Phenix57 (v.2.0-5936). Particles corresponding to Cascade only were used as an input for a 3DVA and heterogeneous refinement as described above. One of the resulting volumes, corresponding to 132,574 particles, yielded a 2.86-Å (GSFSC resolution) Cascade reconstruction after particle re-extraction and non-uniform refinement. The Cascade–TniQ volume was fed twice into a heterogeneous refinement. One of the volumes, corresponding to 50,074 particles, yielded a 3.19 Å (GSFSC resolution) reconstruction after particle re-extraction and non-uniform refinement. All maps and models have been deposited in the Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) and Protein Data Bank (PDB) (see Data availability and Extended Data Table 1). A detailed processing workflow is shown in Extended Data Fig. 1. Monomeric initial models of Cas6, Cas7, Cas8, TniQ and TnsC were generated using AlphaFold3 (ref. 58). The AlphaFold3 models were docked manually as rigid bodies in the cryo-EM density map using UCSF ChimeraX59 (v.1.9). The model was real-space refined in Phenix (v.2.0-5936) against the cryo-EM map and then manually in Coot60 (v.0.9.4) using secondary structure, side chain rotamer, Ramachandran and LibG61 nucleic-acid restraints. The nucleic acid model, comprising the crRNA (positions −7 to 52), TGS (positions −60 to 4) and NTGS (positions −4 to 4, 21 to 23 and 34 to 60), was built manually in Coot (v.0.9.4) using PDB accession 7U5D (ref. 21) as a starting point. The cryo-EM density was clear enough to distinguish the DNA register. Refinement statistics are included in Extended Data Table 1. Structure and map figures were prepared using UCSF ChimeraX (v.1.9) and Adobe Illustrator (v.25.4.1, Adobe). The local model-to-map fit for all residues shown for the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC complex in Figs. 1–5 is presented in Supplementary Fig. 1a–f.

In a recent development, the cryo-EM sample of the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC–TnsB hook recruitment complex was obtained using a pull-down approach. The dsTarget and a double-stranded right-end donor DNA (dsRE) were prepared by annealing synthetic oligonucleotides oMS628-629 and oMS576-630 (Supplementary Table 3), respectively, in a 1:1 ratio to a final concentration of 100 μM in annealing buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 100 mM KCl). The annealing program consisted of incubation at 95 °C for 5 min, followed by a 1 °C min−1 rampdown until 12 °C was reached. The target pot was prepared by adding 1,200 pmol of dsTarget to 100 μl of assembly buffer (40 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 20 mM MgCl2, 2 mM DTT), after which KCl solution was added to a final KCl concentration of 230 mM and 1,200 pmol of Cascade–TniQ. The mixture was incubated at room temperature for 10 min, after which ATP and 8,400 pmol of TnsC were added. The sample was then incubated at room temperature for 30 min. The final target pot volume was 200 μl and its buffer composition was 1 mM ATP, 20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 10 mM MgCl2, 1 mM DTT and 230 mM KCl. A donor pot was prepared by mixing 1,200 pmol of His6–MBP–TnsAB and 1,200 pmol of dsRE substrate. The donor pot was brought to a 20 μl final volume using TnsAB SEC buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 500 mM KCl, 1 mM DTT), mixed with the target pot and incubated at room temperature for 30 min. After adding 30 μl of binding buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 10 mM MgCl2, 300 mM KCl, 1 mM DTT, 0.025% Tween-20, 1 mM ATP), the sample was mixed with 40 μl of 50% amylose resin pre-equilibrated in binding buffer and incubated at 4 °C on a rotating wheel for 1 h. After centrifugation (500 g at 4 °C for 2 min), the supernatant was discarded and the protein-bound resin was washed three times with 500 μl of binding buffer. Next, 15 μl of binding buffer supplemented with 10 mM maltose was added and the sample was centrifuged (14,000 g at 4 °C for 5 min). The supernatant was isolated by careful pipetting and centrifuged two additional times. A second elution was performed using 20 μl of maltose-supplemented binding buffer, followed by three centrifugation steps as described above. The two eluates were combined into one sample and used to freeze cryo-EM grids. Two and a half microlitres of sample was applied to a freshly glow-discharged (60 s) Quantifoil R 1.2/1.3 Au 300 mesh grid, blotted for 2.5 s at 100% humidity and 4 °C, plunge-frozen in a cryogenic mixture of liquid ethane and propane using a Vitrobot Mark IV plunger (FEI) and stored in liquid nitrogen. Cryo-EM data were collected on a FEI Titan Krios G3i system operating at 300 kV and equipped with a Gatan K3 direct electron detector in super-resolution counting mode. In total, 11,374 movies were acquired at 130,000× magnification, yielding a super-resolution pixel size of 0.325 Å. Each movie consisted of 37 subframes with a cumulative exposure of 60.947 e− Å−2. EPU automated data-acquisition software for single-particle analysis (v.3.9, Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used for data acquisition, with three shots per hole and a defocus range of −1.0 to −2.4 μm in 0.2-μm increments.

Sources indicate that in total, 11,374 exposures were imported into cryoSPARC live (v.4.7) for real-time processing. After patch-motion and patch-CTF correction, 329,059 particles were identified using blob picker (200–300-Å diameter), extracted (extraction box size: 600 pixels; Fourier-cropped to box size: 200 pixels) and classified into 50 2D classes. The selected 114,608 particles were used as a training set for Topaz picking (350-Å expected particle diameter, 50 particles per micrograph), yielding 463,242 particles, which were extracted (extraction box size: 500 pixels; Fourier-cropped to box size: 250 pixels) and classified in 150 2D classes. Classes corresponding to 189,451 particles were selected and fed into a two-class ab initio reconstruction, resulting in a junk class and a recognizable Cascade–TniQ–TnsC volume (142,343 particles), which was used as input for non-uniform refinement after particle re-extraction. A 2.84-Å (GSFSC resolution) reconstruction was obtained from a final number of 138,834 particles, which was further used for a TnsC-focused local refinement, yielding a 2.96-Å (GSFSC resolution) volume of the heptamer decorated with additional density for each of its seven subunits. A composite map was obtained combining the consensus Cascade–TniQ–TnsC and TnsC-focused volumes using the combine_focused_maps function in Phenix (v.2.0-5936). All maps and models have been deposited in the EMDB and PDB (see Data availability and Extended Data Table 2). A detailed processing workflow is shown in Extended Data Fig. 5. The Cascade–TniQ–TnsC model was rigid-body fitted into the cryo-EM density map using UCSF ChimeraX (v.1.9) and adjusted manually in Coot (v.0.9.4) using the above-mentioned restraints. The DNA duplex was extended by three nucleotides at the 5′ end of the TGS and by two nucleotides at its 3′ end, with the NTGS extended correspondingly. An initial model of the TnsC heptamer bound to seven TnsB(575–613) copies was generated using AlphaFold3 and docked manually. The model placed the last nine TnsB C-terminal residues at the additional densities of each TnsC subunit. The recognizable density of the bulky TnsB residues Trp605 and Phe612 aided in fitting the TnsB hook in the density. Refinement statistics are included in Extended Data Table 2. Structure and map figures were prepared using UCSF ChimeraX (v.1.9) and Adobe Illustrator (v.25.4.1). The local model-to-map fit for all residues shown for the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC–TnsB hook complex in Figs. 1–5 is presented in Supplementary Fig. 1g–m.

The cryo-EM sample of the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC–TnsAB holocomplex was prepared using a pull-down approach. The strand-transfer substrate was prepared by annealing oligos oMS733, oMS734 and oSO146 (Supplementary Table 3) in a 1:1:1 ratio to a final concentration of 100 μM each. The annealing program consisted of incubation at 95 °C for 5 min, followed by a 1 °C min−1 rampdown until 12 °C was reached. Next, 1,000 pmol of substrate, 22.5 μl of assembly buffer A (40 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 20 mM MgCl2, 200 mM KCl, 2 mM DTT) and water were mixed with 2,000 pmol of His6–MBP–TnsAB to a final volume of 45 μl, and the sample was kept on ice for 10 min. In the meantime, 35.8 μl (1,000 pmol) of Cascade–TniQ was mixed with 55 μl of assembly buffer B (40 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 20 mM MgCl2, 100 mM KCl, 2 mM DTT) and 1.6 μl of water to reduce its KCl concentration to 260 mM. This mixture was added to the initial pot and incubated at room temperature for 10 min. ATP (1 mM final concentration) was added, followed by 7,000 pmol of TnsC, reaching a final volume of 155 μl. The mixture was then incubated at room temperature for 30 min. After the addition of 45 μl of binding buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 10 mM MgCl2, 300 mM KCl, 1 mM DTT, 0.025% Tween-20, 1 mM ATP), the sample was mixed with 50 μl of 50% amylose resin pre-equilibrated in binding buffer. The mixture was incubated at 4 °C on a rotating wheel for 1.5 h, and after centrifugation (500 g at 4 °C for 2 min), the supernatant was discarded and the protein-bound resin was washed three times with 500 μl of binding buffer. After adding 25 μl of binding buffer supplemented with 10 mM maltose, the sample was centrifuged (14,000 g at 4 °C for 10 min). The supernatant was isolated by careful pipetting and centrifuged two additional times. Next, 2.5 μl of sample was applied to a freshly glow-discharged (60 s) Quantifoil R 1.2/1.3 Au 300 mesh grid, blotted for 3 s (grid 1) or 2.5 s (grid 2) at 100% humidity and 4 °C, plunge-frozen in a cryogenic mixture of liquid ethane and propane using a Vitrobot Mark IV plunger (FEI) and stored in liquid nitrogen. Cryo-EM data were collected on an FEI Titan Krios G3i system operating at 300 kV and equipped with a Gatan K3 direct electron detector in super-resolution counting mode. In total, 43,220 movies were acquired as two separate datasets (dataset 1, 11,964 movies of grid 1; dataset 2, 31,256 movies of grid 2) at 130,000× magnification, yielding a super-resolution pixel size of 0.325 Å. Each movie consisted of 37 subframes with a cumulative exposure of 60.059 e− Å−2 (dataset 1) or 65.580 e− Å−2 (dataset 2). EPU automated data-acquisition software for single-particle analysis (v.3.9, Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used for data acquisition, with three shots per hole and a defocus range of −1.0 to −2.4 μm in 0.2-μm increments.

For both datasets, the exposures were imported to cryoSPARC live (v.4.7) for real-time processing. Datasets 1 and 2 were pre-processed separately. After patch-motion and patch-CTF correction, particles were identified using blob picker (270–290-Å diameter, elliptical blob), extracted (extraction box size: 600 pixels; Fourier-cropped to box size: 200 pixels) and classified into 100 2D classes. Next, 93,462 particles of dataset 1 and 203,735 of dataset 2 were selected for a two-class ab initio reconstruction, which resulted in a Cascade–TniQ–TnsC volume and a TnsAB tetramer volume. The Cascade–TniQ–TnsC particles were re-extracted with a bigger box size (extraction box size 1,024 pixels, Fourier-cropped to box size 256 pixels) and used for non-uniform refinement. Using a bigger box revealed additional density at the edge of the particles, corresponding to a flexible TnsAB tetramer next to the TnsC density. This volume was low-pass filtered and used to create masks for particle subtraction. After reducing the box size (extraction box size 700 pixels, Fourier-cropped to box size 350 pixels), the signal for Cascade–TniQ was subtracted from the selected set of particles and the TnsABC moiety was locally refined after aligning the volume to the centre of mass of the TnsABC mask. A 3DVA (filter resolution: 5 Å; mode: simple) yielded one reconstruction with clear density for both TnsC and TnsAB and another with a well-resolved TnsC density but only a weak TnsAB density. The volumes were used as input for two rounds of heterogeneous refinement with the initial set of particles. Next, 49,752 were assigned to the TnsAB-bound TnsC volume, re-extracted (576 pixels) and locally refined, focusing on TnsAB. To adjust the box size for the creation of a composite map, the particles were re-extracted with a larger box-size (700 pixels) and re-aligned to the centre of mass of the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC mask, yielding a 49,606-particle set. An ab initio reconstruction, followed by non-uniform refinement, resulted in a Cascade–TniQ–TnsC–TnsAB consensus volume at 3.10 Å GSFSC resolution. Using the consensus map, new masks were generated for the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC, TnsC and TnsAB moieties as described above. The masks were used for particle subtraction of the TnsAB signal and local refinement of the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC complex. To improve the signal of the TnsB hooks bound to TnsC, a final particle subtraction of the Cascade–TniQ signal was followed by local refinement of TnsC. The TnsAB local refinement was repeated using the final set of 49,606 particles to match the rest of the volumes. This procedure yielded focused cryo-EM maps for the TnsAB tetramer, the hook-bound TnsC heptamer and the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC-hook complex at GSFSC resolutions of 3.36 Å, 3.30 Å and 3.09 Å, respectively. After re-alignment of the TnsAB volume, the global consensus map and the locally refined maps were combined into a composite map using the volume maximum function of ChimeraX (v.1.9). All maps and models have been deposited in the EMDB and PDB (see Data availability and Extended Data Table 3). A detailed processing workflow is shown in Extended Data Fig. 8. The QCascade–TnsC–TnsB hook model was rigid-body fitted in the cryo-EM density map using UCSF ChimeraX (v.1.9) and adjusted manually in Coot (v.0.9.4) using the above-mentioned restraints. The density corresponding to the tetrameric TnsAB was rigid-body fitted using our previously determined TnsAB PEC structure (PDB 9T7L)45. Missing regions in the protein and nucleic acid chains were built manually in Coot (v.0.9.4) with the aid of an AlphaFold3 model of TnsAB. It was not possible to determine whether the hooks bound to TnsC could be assigned to any of the TnsB copies observed in the structure, as the region between the hook and the last modelled TnsB residue (TnsB(586-604)) is disordered. It should also be noted that the 7:7 TnsC:hook observed stoichiometry probably reflects the excess of bait (His6–MBP–TnsAB) used in pull-down preparations, rather than the physiological interaction ratio, which was observed to be 7:4 in other transpososome structures6,36,41. Refinement statistics are included in Extended Data Table 3. Structure and map figures were prepared using UCSF ChimeraX (v.1.9) and Adobe Illustrator (v.25.4.1). The local model-to-map fit for all residues shown for the holocomplex in Figs. 1–5 is presented in Supplementary Fig. 1n–r.

Liverpool are finally starting to find their feet under Andoni Iraola.

The Reds record-breaking additions Alexander Isak and Florian Wirtz have found form under the Spaniard, and Rio Ngumoha has continued his astronomical trajectory.

As is usually the case, Liverpool's upturn in form has led to interest in many of their stars from across Europe.

For several stars it feels like their time in Merseyside is coming to a natural end, but for others a move away would come as a surprise to the Anfield faithful.

Julian ward won't be looking to let any of Liverpool's best players go mid-season, but that hasn't stopped one European giant from trying to pry a duo away.

Bayern Munich have some of the best attacking talent in the world.

Hary Kane has just won the Ballon d'Or, Michael Olise is one of the most sought-after players in the world and Luis Diaz has continued his brilliance since moving on from Merseyside.

The German giants have concerns over the long-term futures of Olise and Jamal Musiala however, and as a result are targeting a double swoop for Florian Wirtz and Rio Ngumoha.

That's according to an article from TEAMtalk, which states the German side are eying the Liverpool pair as well as Manchester City's Jeremy Doku as contingency planning begins for Olise and Musiala's potential exits.

The club's interest in both of the Liverpool pair extends back some way, with Bayern being heavily linked with both players in the past, but news of a potential move for both is upcoming.

Any offer would have to be astronomical for Liverpool to consider the sale of either star, so the notion that they may sell both players to the same club is almost unthinkable.

There may have been a willingness to listen to offers for Wirtz in the past, but the German has turned a corner in the last six weeks and has a clear place in Iraola's prepares.

Bayern may well try and sign the Liverpool duo, but it will likely be a firm no from Ward and the Anfield hierarchy.

  • Former Manchester United forward Rasmus Hojlund aimed a dig at Manchester City after scoring against them for Napoli in the Champions League.
  • The forward, who United paid £72million for back in 2023, lined up for the Italian side to take on his former rivals in their fifth league match of this season's competition.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By LEWIS BROWNING, SPORTS REPORTER.

Published: 17:58 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 19:15 EST, 24 November 2026.

Former Manchester United forward Rasmus Hojlund aimed a dig at Manchester City after scoring against them for Napoli in the Champions League.

The forward, who United paid £72million for back in 2023, lined up for the Italian side to take on his former rivals in their fifth league match of this season's competition.

He was yet to score in Europe this campaign for a Napoli side who had been struggling to even reach the play-off qualification spots, but that all changed on Tuesday night.

Hojlund opened the scoring after half-time of the 2-2 draw when he fired low past Gianluigi Donnarumma to condemn City to a 10th game in a row conceding a goal.

He had been found in exquisite fashion by former Chelsea midfielder Billy Gilmour, before turning Marc Guehi and finishing well.

And his celebration caught the eye, as he held up one finger and appeared to shout 'one team in Manchester' in the direction of the home fans.

Former Manchester United forward Rasmus Hojlund taunted Manchester City fans after scoring against them on Tuesday.

Hojlund did well to take on a pass from Billy Gilmour before firing low into the goal.

After the game, he confirmed he did indeed jibe at Enzo Maresca's side but insisted it was all in good faith.

'Yeah, it's good banter,' he said on TNT Sports. 'There's a rivalry between Manchester City and United and I have a past with United.

'That's my club. Nothing against Manchester City. It was good to score here.'.

The strike was Hojlund's third goal of the season in 11 games as he continues to try and find his feet again after a disastrous spell in England.

Having arrived from Atalanta as a 20-year-old three years ago, there were hopes he would be the man to lead the Red Devils' forward line for years to come.

In his first season, he scored 17 goals in all competitions, including 10 in the Premier League, but things went downhill rapidly.

Recent findings suggest that he would only score another nine goals for the club before being shipped out on loan to Napoli halfway through last season. In total, he netted 26 times for United in 95 games.

In the summer, he joined Napoli permanently, with the Italians coughing up £38m - a £34m loss for United, who are 19th in the Premier League.

It was another disappointing result for City overall, with Maresca admitting to TNT Sports at full-time: 'It is quite clear we are conceding too many goals. It is something we need to adjust, and we are able to adjust that.'.

By Matthew Cooper | 26 Nov 2026 12:22.

Peterborough United will be looking to pick up an important victory when they welcome rivals Cambridge United to the Weston Homes Stadium on Saturday.

The hosts currently sit 22nd in the League One table, while the visitors are 11th.

Peterborough head into this local derby after ending a four-match winless run last weekend when they beat promotion chasers Plymouth Argyle 2-0.

Harry Ashfield opened the scoring in the first half, before Harry Leonard converted a penalty in stoppage-time to secure all three points.

The win was a welcome boost for Robbie Savage's side, who are fighting for survival and remain in the relegation zone with 13 points from 14 games.

However, they will be looking to carry the momentum of last weekend's win into Saturday's clash, with the Posh targeting back-to-back league victories for the first time since February.

It is also worth noting that Peterborough have a strong recent record against their rivals, having won their last five meetings across all competitions.

Cambridge, meanwhile, are without a win in their last five league games and suffered a disappointing 3-0 home defeat to league leaders Stockport County last Saturday.

Ollie Norwood broke the deadlock early in the second half with a stunning free kick, before Ethan Ennis doubled their lead and Gassan Ahadme scored an unfortunate own goal.

The defeat leaves the U's 11th with 21 points from 15 matches, having suffered just one defeat in their first 10 games before going five without a win.

Head coach Neil Harris has admitted his side have not been "tough to play against" in recent weeks and is keen for them to "get back to being that team".

Peterborough could welcome back Ben Woods and Luca Mendonca on Saturday, but they are both unlikely to start even if they are fit.

Savage is expected to keep faith with the team that beat Plymouth last weekend, with Leonard set to lead the line with support out wide from Bolu Shofowoke and Owura Edwards.

Cambridge may be forced to make at least one change, with the availability of Kelland Watts in doubt after he was forced off against Stockport.

Patrick Bauer could replace Watts in defence, while Louis Appere is set to start up front with support from Zak Bradshaw and Ben Knight.

Bass; Johnston, Feeney, Hughes, Mills; Jones, Ashfield; Shofowoke, Williams, Edwards; Leonard.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There will be some games where Mikel Arteta has no choice but to tweak the XI, rest some tired legs and give his second-choice attackers the chance – although given the option he may wish to pick the same team every week.

Recent findings suggest that the three massive guns of his attack were primed and ready to come on in the next break in play when Arsenal at last broke through in this, their second Champions League league phase game of the season against some stubborn opposition from Ligue 1. Lille had sat deep against an Arsenal attack without Bukayo Saka, Martin Odegaard and Kai Havertz, and the French club were past the hour when it all finally broke.

Industry observers note that that was a superb finish from Jurrien Timber who, with two touches, demonstrated that in the modern era even defenders are capable of the kind of moments of skill and composure that we once assumed were only within the capacity of the best attackers. He gave Arsenal the lead just as Mikel Arteta had decided he had seen enough from some of his second-choice attackers – Viktor Gyokeres, Noni Madueke and Mikel Merino. They had created some chances and at times looked promising, but as soon as the substantial three were on the difference was obvious.

According to recent reports, this touch and finish from Jurriën Timber 😮‍💨 Arsenal lead against Lille! 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/WPrcA5ZrQ1 https://t.co/L2B6YsNDXo.

According to recent reports, “We had moments in the game in the first half … [when] we arrived in very dangerous positions,” Arteta mentioned. “With a lot of advantage, our technical quality wasn’t good enough to deliver moments of real threat and especially to be able to sustain the attack, so we allowed certain transitions.” He said that he made some changes at half-time, as managers are wont to do, and that things improved but the real change was clear when he made the substitutions.

“It was a joy to watch,” Arteta mentioned. “The three goals were unbelievable, the connections, the timings, the quality they delivered to score. Three different players and a lot of players participating in those goals, so overall very, very happy.” He had played Myles Lewis-Skelly at left-back again to give Riccardo Calafiori a rest. Saka had been ill during the week and not in a position to start.

Industry observers note that in the opposing technical area was Davide Ancelotti, the 37-year-old son of Carlo, with his father’s trademark slow amble to the edge of the technical area. Young Ancelotti had drilled his team well, but once they were exposed to the high-pace recovery and sharp passing geometry of the Arsenal substitutes there was to be no coming back. Saka made the second for Eberechi Eze who had started the game on the left and the Arsenal No 7 scored the third himself. The home fans sang again about being champions of England and they certainly looked the part.

It didn't take Arsenal long to double their lead ⚡️ Eberechi Eze scores to make it 2-0 🎯 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/WPrcA5ZrQ1 https://t.co/BVMieESgbi.

It took a while. Arteta got ever more sour in his dealings with Richard Hempel, the giant German fourth official. Bruno Guimarães hustled as best he could in midfield and might have won a penalty. But essentially Arsenal lacked the subtle attacking edge that distinguishes the best from the rest in this competition. You could see it immediately in the way that Odegaard hunted for the ball for the second goal and then turned urgently to attack Lille. The third goal was a passing sequence from Saka to Odegaard to Havertz and back to Saka for the finish.

Arsenal are on fire now 🔥 Bukayo Saka extends their lead to 3-0 💥 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/WPrcA5ZrQ1 https://t.co/ZbCmhueaXo.

According to recent reports, the Arsenal players wore black armbands to mark the passing, aged 94, of Ken Friar, the club’s life vice-president. He had served the club from 1945 to 2014 and was variously club secretary, managing director and a driving force in building the stadium in which they now play. Even Arteta, no sentimentalist, insisted on beginning his press conference with a tribute.

For Arteta’s players, there will be a much bigger test than this one in Munich next week against Bayern. Arsenal have already won in Naples but a victory at Bayern would be significant beyond that. Arsenal have won all but one of their 10 games this season – that major defeat at the Amex Stadium, almost one month ago. They clearly have another gear to go to when required although ideally, Arteta would not always have to ask it of the same players. Olivier Giroud back at the Emirates ❤️ https://t.co/TPBgcNDsVW.

Arsenal pay tribute to one of the club’s greatest custodians this evening following the news of Ken Friar’s death aged 92. Friar worked in various roles at the club across more than 70 years, and a bridge from Drayton Park to Emirates Stadium is named in his honour.

A statue at the end of the bridge is a nod to the chance meeting the 11-year-old Friar had with Arsenal manager George Allison in 1945, while playing football outside Highbury with his friends.

As Sam Dean wrote earlier today, finishing the story: “Allison was so impressed by Friar’s enthusiasm that he told him to report to his office at 9am the next day. Friar did as he was instructed and his reward was a job offer: he became a messenger at the stadium on match days. He was paid 12 and a half pence per week.”.

Friar was a long-serving member of the Arsenal board, before stepping back in 2020 and becoming life president.

Arsenal’s players will wear black armbands.

A post shared by Sam Dean (@samjdean_tel).

After signing his new Arsenal contract last week, Mikel Arteta described May’s Champions League final defeat as “poison in his veins,” and last season’s campaign demonstrated the benefits of finishing top of the league phase.

Arsenal enjoyed home second legs all the way through to the final after winning eight from eight, and in a 50:50 draw they fell into a considerably kinder bracket.

Sometimes it can be hard to gauge the importance of these league-phase matches, but Arteta will strive for another perfect record to give Arsenal the best possible chance of going deep in the competition again.

Fixtures against Bayern Munich and Real Madrid are likely to determine whether Arsenal finish in the top two, but there is still a job to be done against Lille this evening.

Arsenal have played against 10 different French opponents in European competition but have never faced Lille, who are managed by Davide Ancelotti, son of five-time Champions League winner Carlo.

In a recent development, lille sell their best players every summer. After finishing third in Ligue 1 last season they lost Ayyoub Bouaddi and Matias Fernandez-Pardo to Manchester City and Newcastle United for a combined £130m. They have claimed 10 points from their first five league games of the season and led Paris St-Germain 2-0 before being pegged back in stoppage time.

Leading the line for Lille is 40-year-old Olivier Giroud, who scored 105 Arsenal goals in 235 appearances between 2012 and 2018. After leaving the Emirates, Giroud went on to score against Arsenal for Chelsea in the 2019 Europa League final, but he can still expect a warm reception.

Arsenal’s home record in the Champions League has been formidable since they returned to the competition under Arteta in 2023. They have won all 11 home group-stage or league-phase matches, conceding just three goals (two of those were shipped against Kairat Almaty in a dead rubber).

Arteta’s scope for rotation has been reduced by injuries to Piero Hincapie and Martin Zubimendi, but tonight’s game should offer Eberechi Eze and Viktor Gyokeres a chance to impress, while Jurrien Timber needs minutes to build his fitness.

Juventus sell out Venezia game as Omonia sales pass 35,000

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (442 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Juvefc

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Juventus have sold out Sunday's Serie A home game against Venezia despite a long injury list.
  • Juventus go into Sunday’s home game against Venezia still short of players.
  • Industry observers note that general sale for the fixture opened at 3pm on Tuesday 6 October.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Juventus have sold out Sunday's Serie A home game against Venezia despite a long injury list. Strong early sales for the Europa League visit of Omonia Nicosia keep the club in line for another strong European crowd.

Juventus go into Sunday’s home game against Venezia still short of players. Several remain unavailable for Sunday’s 12:30 kick-off. Edon Zhegrova has trained with the group and is considered available. Celik, Cambiaso, Nico Gonzalez and Kalulu remain out, Sport Mediaset reported. For Spalletti, a full home crowd arrives in the middle of a busy run of games.

Industry observers note that general sale for the fixture opened at 3pm on Tuesday 6 October. Supporters living in the province of Venezia could buy only if they held an active Juventus Card. The fixture belongs to the 2026-27 Serie A Enilive season.

This season every Juventus match ticket is digital. Each one is managed through the Allianz Stadium App.

Sources indicate that season-ticket holders who cannot attend can list their seat on resale.juventus.com. The club, not the seller, sets the resale price. A few of those listings are now all that remains for supporters who missed the general sale, ANSA reported.

The season-ticket terms also reward turning up. To keep first refusal on a 2027-28 season ticket, a holder must use the seat for at least 70 per cent of matches. That means at least 13 of the 19 league games.

The Europa League has drawn big numbers to Turin this season. Against NEC, 39,308 match tickets were sold, with away fans counted separately. No away figure was released for the Rennes visit, but that section was full.

In a recent development, the Rennes game finished 2-2 on 22 October. Juventus needed a second-half Woltemade penalty to draw after trailing 2-1.

Omonia Nicosia are next. Bookings for the Cypriot club’s visit still trail the two earlier European crowds.

In a recent development, juventus have set strict conditions for the fixture. Supporters of Cypriot nationality may buy tickets only for the away section. The club has warned that breaking UEFA rules can lead to cancelled tickets and refused entry.

According to recent reports, taken together, the figures are consistent with a home support that keeps buying despite the injury list. The weekend league fixture will be followed by a European night that is already well on its way to another large crowd.

Juventus host Omonia Nicosia in the Europa League on 26 November.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Obviously, this is still miles away from where they need to be but, the fact that only seven points separate them and first-placed Arsenal is excellent news.
  • Right now, it's unclear where Liverpool are going to finish in England's top flight but, if they keep performing to the standard they showed on Sunday against Manchester United, they'll be storming their way up the table.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Andoni Iraola has now managed to get Liverpool to fourth in the Premier League table.

Obviously, this is still miles away from where they need to be but, the fact that only seven points separate them and first-placed Arsenal is excellent news.

Right now, it's unclear where Liverpool are going to finish in England's top flight but, if they keep performing to the standard they showed on Sunday against Manchester United, they'll be storming their way up the table.

But, for them to do this, improvements need to be made to their squad as, all of their other title rivals will be adding extra firepower to their ranks.

So, the fact that the January transfer window is now just over a month away is rather exciting.

Especially with all the players that they've just been linked with.

Liverpool see Gustavo Varela as a 'long-term target'.

Liverpool have several problem areas among their ranks that need addressing.

Obviously, since they're one of the biggest clubs in the world, they won't have any problem finding players who want to join.

However, the prices that Premier League clubs have to pay instantly have extra money added on top of them.

That's why only a certain number of deals can be struck by Liverpool in each window.

Moves for the future are also laid out with a latest enhancement from Football Insider sharing that the Reds' recent links with Monza striker Gustavo Varela are for the 'long-term' rather than the short-term.

"Liverpool will not prioritise a move to sign Monza striker Gustavo Varela in January, sources have told Football Insider," they wrote.

"The 21-year-old has emerged as a target for the Reds, having struck 11 goals from his opening 11 games in Serie A so far this term.

"The Reds are "keeping tabs" on the Portuguese youngster, with several top Italian clubs also having their "eyes fixed on him" at the moment.

"However, sources say that Varela is viewed as more of a long-term option at Anfield, and the club are not likely to make a move for him this winter.

"Monza are relaxed over their frontman's future for now, but they know that further interest from top clubs is inevitable if he continues to perform.".

Liverpool's interest in Gustavo Varela could mean that they're changing to a two striker formation.

Liverpool only have two fit strikers among their ranks at the moment.

Alexander Isak is one of them and, since he was the Reds' record signing, he's obviously going to be Iraola's striker.

Lewis Koumas is the other and, even though his manager likes him, the fact that Hugo Ekitike is edging closer to a return will certainly worry him.

Before he got injured last term, Ekitike was easily Liverpool's best player and, they probably wouldn't have qualified for the Champions League if it wasn't for him.

So, the fact that Varela is now emerging as a potential option for the Reds on their shortlist certainly raises a few questions.

The easiest explanation for this move would be that, eventually, Iraola wants to move to a two striker formation while having Varela and Koumas as his back-up options.

Obviously, there are now guarantees that this will play out like that but, if that is the case, a major tactical change could be on its way to Anfield in the next couple of years.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Both aiming to halt their respective rotten runs of second-tier form, Millwall and Burnley lock horns at The Den in search of much-needed Championship points on Saturday afternoon.
  • The Lions were sentenced to another loss by promotion-chasing Stoke City earlier in the week, whilst the Clarets claimed an unwanted record in their 2-0 home defeat by Birmingham City.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Carter White | 26 Nov 2026 12:22.

Both aiming to halt their respective rotten runs of second-tier form, Millwall and Burnley lock horns at The Den in search of much-needed Championship points on Saturday afternoon.

The Lions were sentenced to another loss by promotion-chasing Stoke City earlier in the week, whilst the Clarets claimed an unwanted record in their 2-0 home defeat by Birmingham City.

After suffering just four Championship away defeats last season on their way to a third-placed finish, Millwall picked up their sixth loss on the road in 2026-27 at Stoke on Wednesday night.

The Lions extended their losing run to four consecutive matches following a lacklustre first-half display at the bet365 Stadium, where in-form striker George Hirst bagged a game-clinching brace for the hosts.

Winning just one of their past eight second-tier matches (D1 L6), Alex Neil's side have plummeted down to 18th spot in the Championship standings, a mammoth nine points behind the current top-eight pace.

Following four straight losses on the road, Millwall are in desperate need of some home comforts this weekend, however, the Lions have enjoyed victory in just one of their past six (D2 L3) competitive contests at The Den.

One of a multitude of problems facing head coach Neil ahead of a hectic festive period, the South Londoners are struggling in attack since the summer departure of Femi Azeez, scoring only once across their past four matches.

Whilst Millwall are experiencing a saddening fall from grace relative to last season, Saturday's visitors Burnley are in the midst of a full-blown crisis, with the recently-relegated side right now sleepwalking towards League One.

A 2-0 defeat by Birmingham at Turf Moor on Wednesday night made it 24 consecutive home league fixtures without a win for the Clarets - the longest such streak in the history of English football.

Despite this, head coach Fabio Celestini opted for the glass-half-full approach during his post-match media duties, insisting that Burnley bested Blues outside of the two boxes during the Lancashire loss.

The optimistic Swiss boss needs to increase his side's effectiveness in the decisive moments to avoid the same fate as Nicky Hayen, though, as the Clarets are winless in their opening five matches (D3 L2) with the 51-year-old at the helm.

Joining Premier League strugglers Manchester United on just the single league victory so far this season, Burnley are currently occupying 23rd position in the Championship rankings, four points from safety.

After accusing a number of his players of "not taking part in the game" at Stoke on Wednesday, it is safe to say that Millwall boss Neil is planning changes to his XI this weekend.

That indirect jab was likely commenting on the displays of Milhailo Ivanovic, Tairyk Arconte and Jenson Metcalfe, with the trio replaced at half time.

Derek Mazou-Sacko will start in the middle of the park, and influential Belgian Casper de Norre is set to return to the matchday squad.

Zak Sturge's absence reduces the hosts' options at left-back, with the 22-year-old picking up a straight red card during the defeat by Queens Park Rangers last Saturday.

Burnley also have a suspended player for this weekend's clash, with Wales international Connor Roberts out of action following his dismissal at Cardiff City on November 7.

The Clarets could make attacking alterations after firing a blank against Birmingham, with Marcus Edwards and Jamie Vardy pushing for starts.

Millwall possible starting lineup:.

Jensen; Osei-Tutu, Taylor, Cooper, Doughty; Kelly, Mazou-Sacko; Sykes, Neghli, Lisbie; Dykes.

Burnley possible starting lineup:.

Weiss; Walker, Alleyne, Julio, Pires; Cullen, Raghouber; Ramazani, Ramsey, Amdouni; Vardy.

After a soft display at Turf Moor earlier in the week, it is hard to imagine Burnley coping with the physical challenge posed by a trip to The Den.

Millwall were much-improved in the second half at Stoke and should be relatively confident of putting their relegation-threatened visitors to the sword.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Manchester United have been handed a potential boost in their pursuit of Sporting CP left-back Maxi Araujo, who is reportedly keen on a move to Old Trafford.
  • The Uruguay international caught the attention of United officials during Wednesday's 2-2 draw in Lisbon, having been monitored by the club for several months.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Lewis Blain | 26 Nov 2026 12:28.

Manchester United have been handed a potential boost in their pursuit of Sporting CP left-back Maxi Araujo, who is reportedly keen on a move to Old Trafford.

The Uruguay international caught the attention of United officials during Wednesday's 2-2 draw in Lisbon, having been monitored by the club for several months.

However, a potential January deal could prove difficult given the asking price and Mauricio Pochettino's limited transfer budget.

According to Sport Witness, a source close to the situation has indicated that Araujo 'wants to join' United, with mutual appreciation between the player and the Premier League outfit.

Recent findings suggest that united first showed interest in the 26-year-old earlier this year but failed to strengthen at left-back during the summer. Araujo subsequently extended his Sporting contract until 2030, which includes an €80m (£67m) release clause.

However, it's believed a fee closer to £50m could actually be enough to secure his services in the January transfer window, despite his upcoming contract and substantial salary in Portugal.

United officials reportedly watched him closely during Wednesday's Champions League meeting, with Araujo playing the full 90 minutes.

The left-back has made 15 appearances this season and is viewed as a potential solution to United's problems in the position.

Luke Shaw has missed the last eight matches with a muscle injury, while youngster Harry Amass is also among the club's recognised options. Both players have contracts expiring in 2027, adding further uncertainty to the position.

Araujo's performance against United offered Pochettino an opportunity to assess a potential transfer target at close quarters.

Operating in an advanced left wing-back role, the Uruguayan registered two shots, created one chance, won three fouls and completed six progressive passes. He also made six defensive contributions, including three interceptions, per Sofascore.

It was not necessarily a spectacular individual display, but his all-round contribution attracted praise from the Portuguese press and demonstrated the qualities United could benefit from on the left flank.

Araujo could provide the attacking thrust and defensive work rate required to solve a problem position, although the financial implications are significant.

A reported £50m asking price would represent a sizeable investment, particularly with United believed to have less than that available for multiple positions in January.

Pochettino may be impressed by what he saw in Lisbon, but convincing the hierarchy to spend such a large proportion of their budget on one full-back could be difficult when central defence and striker reinforcements are also needed.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Michael Carrick had urged his Manchester United players to come out and fight. But nobody could have imagined quite how Lisandro Martínez would interpret that message.

By the end of an extraordinary evening in Madrid, where United went 1-0 down inside a minute and never recovered against Atlético Madrid, Martínez had blown the lid off any pretence of all being well at the club as he rolled out a lacerating assault on the club’s executives.

United had come into this getting battered from all sides and when Pablo Barrios put Atlético ahead, Jamie Carragher’s pre-match assessment about how things could get “very messy, very quickly” for all involved at Old Trafford must have been ringing in the ears of the travelling supporters.

According to recent reports, ATLETICO ARE AHEAD IN JUST 53 SECONDS! ⚡️ A nightmare start for United at the Metropolitano Stadium 😬 https://t.co/TdOwoXxopn.

Sources indicate that they certainly know how to make life difficult for themselves. Leny Yoro’s 74th-minute red card pretty much ended hopes of them taking something from the game.

Recent findings suggest that ademola Lookman scored Atlético’s second soon after and Carrick was staring at another defeat. And so they now move on to a substantial game at Leeds on Sunday. This was not the result Carrick would have wanted – and that is before what happened off the pitch.

Ademola Lookman PUNISHES a 10-man Man United 💥 https://t.co/GHKYIHGhNC.

Another defeat intensified the pressure on Carrick but Martínez left nobody under any illusions that he felt the finger should be pointed not simply at another manager or the players, but the hierarchy above him.

It was extraordinary to see a player speaking out so publicly in this fashion against his own bosses.

But Martínez pulled no punches, even going as far as singling out Jason Wilcox, the director of football, as he criticised the club’s summer transfer business and effectively accused the club of failing Carrick and the players in the window.

To what extent Martínez’s comments mirror the views of the wider dressing room is unclear, but you have to wonder where Carrick and United go from here.

It has been revealed that on the one hand, Martínez was providing a show of support for his manager by attacking the people above him. At the same time, he has presented Carrick with a disciplinary problem to address.

Lisandro Martínez did NOT hold back after United's loss to Atletico 😬👀 https://t.co/OGo25Pzd30.

And United have enough troubles as it is without a senior member of Carrick’s dressing room turning so squarely against the club’s power brokers.

Martínez was probably only giving voice to what many fans have been saying since an underwhelming transfer window closed with more questions than answers. But for a player to talk in such blunt, excoriating terms resonated more loudly than anything a supporter or United’s most caustic critic could say.

The message was simple: you can sack all the managers you want but until you pull together a squad worthy of United’s name and give the man at the helm the tools to compete, the club will struggle to escape this cycle of mediocrity.

No one can reasonably argue United’s window was a success. They went into it with the hopes of landing Elliot Anderson and other premium midfielders but ended up going for numbers over proven quality or pedigree. Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba were not a trio of signings anyone expected at the start of summer, not even the club itself.

There were glaring issues to address in defence, not least at left-back, and at centre-forward but a quality alternative to Luke Shaw never materialised and no back-up was signed for Benjamin Sesko, who was missing for four months with a shin injury that has since resurfaced and which could keep him out for a while yet.

According to recent reports, having done so well to lead United to third and take them back into the Champions League, Carrick would have expected further backing than he got in the summer. Ever the company man, he has been too polite to criticise that lack of investment. But the cat is out of the bag now Martínez has had his say.

It now places the spotlight on Wilcox. United head to Elland Road on Sunday and that was the scene of Rúben Amorim’s final meltdown as manager. Two days after he blew up in a meeting with Wilcox at United’s Carrington training base, Amorim took aim at the director of football and others at the club, demanding they “do their job” and repeatedly declaring that he had come to Old Trafford to “be the manager, not to be the coach”.

It is remarkable to think that, 10 months on, United head back to Leeds with just as many questions as there were back then.

United’s worst start to a league season for 40 years has ensured Carrick is already under pressure, but Martínez is very much of the view that it is no longer enough for the manager and the players to keep carrying the can and that the credibility and suitability of those who recruit the players and make the decisions must now be called into question.

Recent findings suggest that that Martínez picked this game to speak out was interesting. United, lost, yes, and the manner of Atlético’s opening goal from Barrios after 53 seconds was shocking. But United at least went down fighting on this occasion and had fashioned enough good chances to at least draw level before Yoro’s harsh 74th-minute red card swung a delicately poised match decisively in Atlético’s favour.

Lookman made it 2-0 soon after, but Atlético, having looked like they would run all over United in those opening 10 minutes, were made to work hard for their victory.

It has been revealed that united cannot keep shooting themselves in the foot like they did in the first minute. Carrick had gone with a three-man midfield to shore things up and made his team more comfortable and yet they were opened up in double quick time by two passes through the middle.

Still, you only needed to look across at United’s opponents to appreciate how chaotic it had become at Old Trafford.

Diego Simeone’s reign at Atlético covers a period stretching two years longer than the post-Ferguson era and in many ways his teams have represented everything United have not been in that time: well constructed and thought through, unified, stable, organised, hungry, aggressive, uncompromising and with a flash of devilment.

If United were not in crisis before this, they are now.

The two sides had contrasting fortunes in their opening fixtures in this competition, Man Utd beating Azerbaijan’s Sabah 4-0 at Old Trafford a month ago while Atléti were defeated by Liverpool who came back from 1-0 down to win 2-1.

But domestically it is the other way round – Michael Carrick’s side have made the club’s worst start in the league for 40 years with one win, three draws and two defeats and have been knocked out of the League Cup. Those of us who watch them regularly – purely because of occupational obligations in this instance – have been surprised by how poor they have been. The results have been bad but the performances even worse.

They seem to lack players who can play on the front foot, who have the athletic dynamism required in this league and too many self-indulgent forward players who either can’t be bothered to help out their team-mates or cannot concentrate long enough to do so. Spooked by their lack of pace in defence and midfield, they are hidebound by caution, dropping ever deeper, ever more reliant on counter-attacking despite the blatant disconnect between the front four and back six. If they drift through this match and Sunday’s trip to Elland Road, Carrick may join the long list of Ineos-driven managerial mis-steps.

Back in the days of Diego Godín, Gabi, Juanfran et all, six wins a draw and a defeat would have had goals for of about 10 and goals against of maybe three.

Simeone is a martinet about attitude not systems or styles and his team have evolved, with the World Cup-winner Alex Baena, who has scored four goals so far, driving them on. He has reintegrated Julián Alvarez, too, after his brazen attempt to force a move to Barcelona so incensed Atléti fans that it seemed they would drive him out of the club. Simeone refused to let Alvarez get his own way and he is now buckling down. Ten years ago Simeone would have bitten his head off.

In a recent development, the one surviving veteran in the squad from that first of El Cholo’s Liga winning sides and the two Champions League finals, victory in which would represent Simeone’s crowning achievement, is the midfielder Koke.
