Each black dot represents one biological replicate (WT: n = 6; Setdb1 cKO: n = 3). Data were combined across three independent experiments for WT and two independent experiments for Setdb1 cKO. Bars indicate means. Significance was assessed using Welch’s unpaired t-test, P = 0.007. d, Separation scores for the HC and EC regions of the locus. In the schematic, red regions represent heterochromatin and grey regions represent euchromatin. e, HC domain size as a fraction of total locus volume in terms of Rg. For d and e, distributions are shown as violin plots. Horizontal lines and numbers indicate medians. Significance was assessed using a two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test with Benjamini–Hochberg correction. Adjusted P values for Rad21 cKO versus WT, WT versus Setdb1 cKO and Rad21 cKO versus Setdb1 cKO, respectively: P = 1.5 × 10−103, P = 3.6 × 10−101 and P < 1 × 10−230 in d and P = 1.1 × 10−23, P = 2.3 × 10−71 and P = 2.6 × 10−229 in e. **P < 0.01, ****P < 0.0001. f, ORCA traces from each condition with the heterochromatin domain and Pcdh enhancers labelled. g, Percentage of mOSNs expressing each Pcdh gene across genotypes. Pcdhb1 is excluded.h, Change in percentage of mOSNs expressing Pcdha genes as a function of each gene’s distance to the HS5-1 enhancer in Rad21 cKO relative to WT. i, Change in percentage of mOSNs expressing Pcdha genes as a function of each gene’s distance to the heterochromatin domain boundary determined by nChIP–seq at the Pcdha cluster in Setdb1 cKO relative to WT.

Industry observers note that individual traces reflected these structural changes. Single molecules showed distancing of Pcdh enhancers from the heterochromatin domain in Rad21 cKO OSNs relative to WT (Fig. 5f), which was further supported by changes in the distance of each locus position relative to the heterochromatin domain centre (Extended Data Fig. 10d). Meanwhile, the heterochromatin domain seemed less compact and more intermixed with euchromatin in Setdb1 cKO OSNs relative to WT (Fig. 5f), which was further supported by an increase in the entropy of each locus position in Setdb1 cKO (Extended Data Fig. 10e). These data suggest that Pcdh enhancers require cohesin to approach the heterochromatin domain and contact target promoters, whereas heterochromatin keeps the promoters in a compact and ordered environment.

It has been revealed that to evaluate how these changes in Pcdh locus architecture affect stochastic Pcdh gene expression, we performed single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq). Ablation of Rad21 resulted in widespread downregulation of Pcdh expression in favour of Pcdhac2, the Pcdha gene most proximal to the HS5-1 enhancer, which also resides in euchromatin (Fig. 5g,h and Extended Data Fig. 10f,g). This gain in expression of enhancer-proximal Pcdh genes was not observed at the Pcdhg cluster, suggesting distinct enhancer–promoter specificities at the two clusters (Fig. 5g and Extended Data Fig. 10f,g). By contrast, ablation of Setdb1 resulted in upregulation of Pcdha10–12 and Pcdhgb6–b7, the genes closest to the heterochromatin–euchromatin boundaries at the locus (Fig. 5g,i and Extended Data Fig. 10f,h). Enhancer–promoter contact frequencies reflected these expression changes in both genotypes (Extended Data Fig. 10i,j).

These results indicate that DNA loop extrusion and heterochromatin compaction cooperate to establish Pcdh locus architecture and promote an unbiased enhancer–promoter search space at the locus. While cohesin is required for Pcdh enhancers to gain access to the heterochromatin domain housing Pcdh promoters, the compaction of the domain expands the ability of the enhancers to find target promoters. Thus, although generally viewed as antagonistic processes35, both cohesin and heterochromatin-driven chromatin compartmentalization are indispensable for proper Pcdh expression.

Sources indicate that here we show that heterochromatin spatially partitions the Pcdh locus into a compacted domain housing Pcdh promoters and multiple open regions housing Pcdh enhancers. Transcription from chosen promoters occurs within the heterochromatin domain, and enhancers must access the domain to engage target promoters (Extended Data Fig. 10k). Counterintuitively, Pcdh transcription can read through hundreds of kilobases without dissolving the compacted state of the locus (Extended Data Fig. 10k). We further demonstrate that Pcdh locus architecture and proper Pcdh expression are achieved through cooperation between heterochromatin-mediated compaction and cohesin-mediated DNA loop extrusion.

Sources indicate that our findings challenge the prevailing view that heterochromatin is a physically inaccessible chromatin structure. Heterochromatin compaction was initially proposed to sterically hinder the transcriptional machinery and thereby repress gene expression36,37. However, rather than acting as an impenetrable barrier, our data indicate that heterochromatin can support active transcription while retaining a compact 3D organization. These findings add to a growing body of evidence suggesting that heterochromatin is not intrinsically inaccessible and can support transcription. For example, 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI)-dense centromeric and pericentromeric heterochromatin are actively transcribed and accumulate abundant RNA despite their highly condensed appearance38. Furthermore, transcription can stabilize H3K9me3-modifying enzymes39,40,41, and dense heterochromatin nonetheless allows passage of transcription factors42 and large macromolecules43, including RNA polymerase II (ref. 44).

Sources indicate that these observations have motivated an alternative model of heterochromatin organization, wherein domain-scale compaction emerges from frequent intra-domain interactions that serve to reinforce the epigenetic state of the domain rather than directly silence the underlying DNA through steric exclusion. By this model, distal genomic loci are brought into proximity by the activity of heterochromatin reader and writer proteins, as readers bound to heterochromatin marks on one chromatin fibre might promote deposition of the same modification by writers on another fibre. This 3D reader–writer activity establishes a positive feedback loop that reinforces the heterochromatic state of the domain. Heterochromatin compaction thus functions to concentrate this feedback, ensuring it acts primarily back on the existing heterochromatin to stabilize its epigenetic state, rather than spreading or diluting to neighbouring euchromatin45,46.

Although heterochromatin has been proposed to be crucial for epigenetic memory at the Pcdh locus11,12, we found that chosen Pcdh promoters do not segregate from flanking promoters retaining the silent state, contrasting with the behaviour of chosen promoters in H3K27me3 heterochromatin29,47. This unexpected organization argues against domain-scale spatial segregation as a primary mechanism for heterochromatin-mediated memory of Pcdh gene choice. Instead, these data suggest that a more local compartmentalization of active and inactive genes might develop, with biophysically distinct microcompartments, or ‘pockets’, of active chromatin containing expressed genes forming within the heterochromatin domain. This model is consistent with the presence of both highly dynamic and more stable HP1 populations within the same heterochromatin environment48 and structural heterogeneity of heterochromatin compartments, as revealed by recent single-molecule footprinting49 and chromatin tracing46 studies.

Lastly, beyond classical examples of heterochromatic genes, such as the lt and rl genes in Drosophila3,4,5, the intermixed spatial organization of active and inactive genes within H3K9me3-enriched chromatin domains discussed here may reflect a more general property of gene regulation within heterochromatic territories—with particular relevance to genes arranged in clusters, such as OR6 and KZFP genes7. We propose that domain-scale spatial segregation of active and inactive genes might not be required at these clusters to accommodate and maintain expression of subsets of genes within a more broadly repressive chromatin domain. Furthermore, as we have shown here for Pcdh genes, these loci might also require the coordinated integration of genome folding mechanisms across scales—from higher-order heterochromatin compartmentalization to enhancer–promoter interactions mediated by various looping factors50—to achieve genomic architectures required for precise and selective gene activation.

In summary, our findings illustrate how seemingly silent chromatin domains can coordinate gene expression and invite a reconceptualization of heterochromatin from a singularly repressive chromatin environment to one that can, when properly configured, permit active transcription.

In a recent development, mice were treated in compliance with the rules and regulations of the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) at the University of California, San Francisco under the IACUC protocol AN-170364-03F. For ORCA experiments involving RNA imaging, postnatal day 11 mice were used. For ORCA experiments involving conditional knockouts, mice older than postnatal day 35 were used to allow time for the knockout to take effect. Rad21 cKO mice were generated by crossing Rad21 conditional allele mice51 to Omp-ires-cre mice (Omptm1(cre)Jae) harbouring a Cre-inducible tdTomato allele (ROSA26-tdtomato, Gt(ROSA)26Sortm14(CAG-tdTomato)Hze/J). Setdb1 cKO mice were generated using the same strategy. Setdb1 conditional allele mice were purchased from Shanghai Model Organisms (C57BL/6Smoc-Setdb1tm1(flox)Smoc, NM-CKO-190052). For the nChIP–seq experiments, cells were sorted from Krt5–GFP (labelling HBCs), Ngn1–GFP (labelling INPs) and Omp-ires–GFP (labelling mOSNs) mice. Primers used for genotyping mice are listed in Supplementary Table 1.

Industry observers note that mice were perfused with 30 ml of ice-cold PBS followed by 30 ml of freshly prepared, ice-cold 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA). Tissue from the mouse OE was dissected and incubated in 4% PFA with gentle rocking at 4 °C for 6 h. Tissue was then transferred to 30% sucrose in 1 × PBS, incubated with gentle rocking at 4 °C until sunk, then embedded in OCT. For ORCA experiments, OE tissue was sectioned coronally at 6 μm onto glass coverslips (Biooptechs, 40-1313-03191) coated with chromium potassium gelatin. Slides were coated as described previously52. For immunohistochemistry experiments, OE tissue was sectioned coronally at 20 μm onto Superfrost Plus slides (Fisherbrand, 1255015). ORCA coverslips were stored at −80 °C until use; immunohistochemistry slides were stored at −20 °C until use.

Industry observers note that for a breakdown of all ORCA-related experiments in the present study, see Supplementary Table 4. The genomic coordinates of the ORCA barcodes tiling the Pcdh locus are listed in Supplementary Table 5.

Industry observers note that RNA and DNA probes were designed and hybridized as previously described52, with minor modifications as follows. Briefly, for combined RNA/DNA imaging experiments, RNA probes were hybridized and imaged first. Tissue sections mounted on coverslips were fixed in freshly prepared 4% PFA at room temperature for 10 min, followed by three washes in 1 × PBS. Sections were then permeabilized for 10 min at room temperature in 1% Triton X in 1 × PBS, followed by two washes with 1 × PBS. Next, sections were incubated for 5 min at room temperature in a protease solution consisting of 0.1 mg ml−1 pepsin (Sigma Aldrich, 501784863) in 10 mM HCl and washed twice in 0.1 M glycine in 1 × PBS to improve RNA hybridization efficiency. Sections were then cleared in 8% sodium dodecyl sulfate at room temperature for 10 min and washed three times in 2 × SSC, reducing background fluorescence. Following clearing, sections were incubated in Hybridization Buffer (2 × SSC, 50% formamide, 0.1% Tween) for 35 min at room temperature. Then, 2,500 ng of primary RNA probes diluted in Hybridization Solution (2 × SSC, 50% formamide, 10% dextran sulfate, 0.1% Tween) were added to the sections, covered with coverglass and incubated overnight (12–20 h) at 42 °C. The following morning, samples were washed twice for 10 min in 2 × SSC at 42 °C, washed once in 2 × SSC at room temperature, then imaged. After RNA imaging, samples were re-fixed in 4% PFA for 5 min at room temperature, washed three times in 2 × SSC, re-permeabilized for 10 min in 1% Triton X-100 at room temperature and washed three times in 2 × SSC. Sections were subsequently incubated for 5 min in 0.1 M HCl and washed three times in 2 × SSC. Pre-hybridization was performed for 35 min as for RNA, then 5,000 ng of DNA probes diluted in Hybridization Solution were added to sections and covered with coverglass. Sections were then incubated on a 90 °C hotplate for exactly 7 min and transferred to 42 °C overnight. The following morning, samples were washed twice in 2 × SSC for 10 min at 42 °C, once in 2 × SSC at room temperature, then incubated in a post-fix solution (2% glutaraldehyde, 8% PFA in 1 × PBS) for 30 min. Samples were then washed three times in 2 × SSC and imaged.

It has been revealed that for ORCA experiments not involving RNA imaging, samples were fixed, permeabilized, cleared, treated with HCl, pre-hybridized and hybridized as described above, but omitting the protease step. Inclusion of the protease step was found to substantially improve RNA staining and was therefore used only for experiments that included RNA imaging. For ORCA experiments involving fluorescent protein labelling (for example, tdTomato signal in Rad21 cKO and Setdb1 cKO), samples were first fixed and washed, imaged for the fluorescent protein and then processed for DNA ORCA as described above. Throughout all procedures, care was taken to prevent sections from drying at any point in the protocol to minimize tissue shrinkage between RNA or protein imaging rounds and subsequent DNA imaging rounds.

In a recent development, samples hybridized with primary probes were imaged on a previously described custom microscopy and microfluidics setup29,52. RNA and DNA readout barcodes were labelled sequentially with a 750 dye complementary to the readout barcodes on primary probes. All RNA and DNA probes share a common sequence that was labelled with a Cy3 dye complementary to this sequence, referred to as the fiducial. Fiducial probes were added before the first imaging round and imaged alongside each barcode. Fiducial signal was subsequently used for drift correction and alignment across imaging rounds. For RNA imaging, the fiducial signal captures all stained RNAs, whereas for DNA imaging it appears as discrete puncta, with each punctum representing one Pcdh locus.

In a recent development, OE tissue was first stained for H3K9me3 as follows. Tissue on glass coverslips was fixed for 10 min in 4% PFA, washed twice in 1 × PBS, quenched for 5 min in PBS containing 0.1 M glycine and washed again in PBS. Tissue was permeabilized with three 5-min washes in PBS containing 0.1% Triton X-100, then blocked in PBS containing 1% BSA and 200 U ml−1 RNase inhibitor (Latest England Biolabs, M0314L). Primary antibody incubation was performed overnight at 4 °C using rabbit anti-H3K9me3 antibody diluted 1:1,000 in blocking buffer (Abcam, ab8898). The following morning, tissue was washed three times for 5 min each in PBS containing 0.1% Triton X-100, then incubated with donkey anti-rabbit Alexa Fluor 647 secondary antibody diluted 1:1,000 in blocking buffer (Invitrogen, A31573). Tissue was then washed three times for 5 min each in PBS containing 0.1% Triton X-100. Samples were stored at 4 °C in PBS protected from light until imaging. To image OE tissue with STORM, an imaging buffer was prepared immediately before use as follows. A dilution buffer was first prepared containing 50 mM NaCl and 200 mM Tris pH 8.0. A glucose oxidase/catalase oxygen-scavenging solution was prepared by combining 700 μl of dilution buffer, 49 mg of glucose oxidase and 175 μl of catalase, centrifuging at maximum speed for 1 min and collecting 800 μl of supernatant. STORM imaging buffer was prepared by adding 800 μl of glucose oxidase/catalase oxygen-scavenging solution, 8 ml of 50% glucose and 400 μl of β-mercaptoethanol to 32 ml of dilution buffer.

For each field of view, fresh STORM imaging buffer was flowed onto the sample immediately before imaging. H3K9me3 STORM videos were acquired at five axial positions using the 635-nm laser at maximum power and an exposure time of 0.5 s per frame. The first and fourth videos contained 3,000 frames, whereas the remaining videos contained 2,500 frames. Fresh STORM imaging buffer was flowed onto the sample after the third video to maintain fluorophore blinking during prolonged imaging. Further frames were acquired after addition of fresh buffer because extra illumination time was required for photobleaching before robust fluorophore blinking could be observed.

STORM videos were acquired across multiple axial planes rather than using astigmatism-based 3D STORM with a cylindrical lens53, because high tissue background made accurate fitting of astigmatic spot widths unreliable. The five axial planes were separated by 750 nm and sampled a 3.0-μm axial range centred on the plane with strongest H3K9me3 signal. Subsequent ORCA imaging of the same samples was acquired using Z-stacks containing matched axial planes to those imaged by STORM.

Fluorescently tagged WGA, which labels cell membranes, was used to align fields of view across imaging sessions (for example, to align H3K9me3 STORM, RNA and Pcdh DNA images). First, 3 μl of 1 ng μl−1 WGA was diluted in 600 μl of 2 × SSC, added to samples for 15 min, then washed off with 2 × SSC immediately before imaging. For RNA and Pcdh DNA imaging, the fiducial channel was imaged alongside the WGA signal at the end of each imaging session. For H3K9me3 STORM, WGA images for each field of view were taken immediately following completion of STORM acquisition. For imaging of fluorescent proteins tagging mOSNs, WGA was imaged simultaneously in a different channel alongside the fluorescent protein. When aligning images across RNA and DNA imaging rounds, images from each field of view were first aligned to the fiducial signal acquired with WGA, and fields of view were subsequently registered across imaging modalities using the WGA signal. The WGA signal additionally enabled 3D cell segmentation (described below).

All imaging was performed on a custom microscopy and microfluidics setup as previously described29,52. The details of the microscopy setup are also listed on the 4DN data portal and Mirco-Meta App54 under Stanford-Boettiger_lab_ORCA_Nikon_Eclipse_Ti2-U_Scope3.

Recent findings suggest that three-dimensional cell segmentations were generated from the WGA signal acquired during RNA imaging. We trained a Cellpose55 algorithm to identify cell outlines in individual sections of WGA images. This algorithm was then run on every section of WGA Z-stack images for each field of view. To connect the resulting two-dimensional (2D) cell segmentations into 3D cell segmentations, we applied ultrack56, an algorithm initially designed to track cells over time in time-series data, to the 2D segmentations for each stack, effectively treating the Z dimension as time. Ultrack produced 3D cell segmentations that matched WGA staining (Extended Data Fig. 3a). We used ultrack, as we found Cellpose’s performance with 2D images to be superior to its performance with 3D images for OE sections stained with WGA.

Industry observers note that segmented cells were classified into distinct cell types on the basis of RNA transcripts within each segmentation as follows. RNA puncta were first identified from 3D stacks using storm-analysis (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7679267), which identifies their X, Y position in each frame and is robust to overlapping spots. The Z position of each punctum was computed by fitting the axial fluorescence intensity profile to puncta with a common X, Y position (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7698979). RNA puncta were then mapped to cell segmentations and segmentations were classified by cell type as follows: for each cell, counts of Icam1, Ascl1, Tex15, Gap43 and Omp transcripts were log-transformed, Z-scored and combined into marker-specific scores corresponding to HBCs (Icam1), GBCs (Ascl1), INPs (Tex15), iOSNs (Gap43) and mOSNs (Omp high, Gap43 low). Cells were assigned to the cell type with the highest score, subject to further marker-based rules (Tex15+ cells were forced to INP and not allowed to be mOSN; HBC labels were forbidden in Gap43+ or Omp+ cells). A confidence score was defined as the difference between the top two scores, and cells with low confidence or ambiguous profiles were labelled ‘undetermined’. To map DNA loci to each segmentation, the X, Y, Z coordinates of DNA loci were transformed by the image alignments computed between WGA images. Each locus was then mapped to a classified cell from its respective field of view and assigned that cell’s label.

Sources indicate that for ORCA experiments involving protein rather than RNA staining, DNA loci were classified as belonging to a particular cell type (namely, mOSNs) on the basis of the fluorescent signal of tdTomato. Apart from Fig. 1 and Extended Data Fig. 2d,e, data in all figures come from cells classified as mOSNs.

Industry observers note that after aligning images from RNA and DNA imaging rounds, the X, Y, Z positions of RNA puncta and DNA loci were registered into a common coordinate system. For each DNA locus, we computed the 3D Euclidean distance to every RNA punctum in the same field of view in voxel units, where X–Y coordinates are in pixels and Z is in imaging planes. A locus was classified as ‘transcribing’ for a given gene if at least one RNA punctum for that gene lay within a 3D distance of 8 voxel units, and as ‘non-transcribing’ otherwise. This threshold corresponds to 1.23–1.60 μm in physical space, depending on how the separation between DNA and RNA puncta is distributed across the X–Y and Z axes. The threshold of 8 voxel units was chosen on the basis of the distribution of nearest RNA distances across all DNA loci for each Pcdh RNA, which was consistently bimodal, with one population less than 8 voxel units and another greater than or equal to 8 voxel units.

In a recent development, STORM videos were processed frame by frame using the 2dfixed multi-emitter-fitting algorithm from storm-analysis (https://github.com/ZhuangLab/storm-analysis). Initial frames dominated by saturated fluorescence before photobleaching were excluded. Single-molecule localizations in each frame were identified using a 10-sigma detection threshold and fit with a fixed-width 2D Gaussian model using an initial Gaussian sigma of 1.3 pixels. Drift correction was not applied during fitting. Localizations were fit independently for each axial imaging plane, and each localization was assigned the Z position of its corresponding imaging plane for downstream analysis.

H3K9me3 STORM signal around Pcdh loci in mOSNs was quantified as the number of STORM localizations within a 324-nm radius, corresponding to 3 pixels, of the X–Y position of the fiducial signal of each locus. Similar results were obtained using different radius sizes. For each locus, localizations were counted from the STORM imaging plane or planes nearest to the locus in Z. If the locus was located in the same Z plane as a STORM video, only localizations from that plane were used. If the locus was located between two STORM imaging planes, localizations from both planes were included and linearly weighted according to their proximity to the locus Z position. For example, for a locus located at Z plane 26 between STORM videos acquired at planes 25 and 28, localizations from plane 25 were weighted by 2/3 and localizations from plane 28 were weighted by 1/3. For the analyses in Fig. 2f, the same quantification was performed using the X, Y and Z position of the ORCA barcode containing the Pcdh gene being analysed, rather than the fiducial position of the locus.

For the simulations in Fig. 2c, randomized positions were used to compare H3K9me3 STORM signal at observed Pcdh loci with signal expected at other positions within the same nuclei. For each of 1,000 simulations, one random position was selected for each observed Pcdh locus from the same cell and Z plane, thereby controlling for non-uniform axial distribution of H3K9me3 STORM signal within individual cells. H3K9me3 STORM signal was quantified at each randomized position using the same 324-nm radius and Z-plane weighting scheme described above. The median STORM signal from each simulation was used to generate a null distribution, which was compared with the observed median STORM signal around Pcdh loci to calculate an empirical P value. The same randomization and quantification procedure was performed for putative Tex15 transcription sites in INPs for Extended Data Fig. 7d. Putative Tex15 transcription sites were identified from Tex15 RNA FISH z-stacks by detecting bright 3D regional maxima. For each field of view, the Tex15 stack was smoothed with a 3D Gaussian filter and thresholded to identify local maxima corresponding to candidate nascent RNA puncta. The intensity threshold was empirically chosen by visual inspection across fields of view to retain bright Tex15 transcription sites while excluding dimmer spots probably corresponding to mature transcripts.

For visualization of H3K9me3 STORM localizations together with ORCA traces in three dimensions (Extended Data Fig. 7a), STORM localizations from each axial imaging plane were shown with a randomized Z position drawn from a truncated Gaussian distribution centred on the corresponding STORM imaging plane. The Gaussian had a standard deviation of 1.2 imaging-plane units and was truncated to ±3.5 imaging-plane units around the plane centre. This jittering was used only to create smooth 3D renderings of STORM signal across the sparsely sampled axial planes and was not used for quantitative analyses.

Image processing (drift correction and localization of spots) was performed as described previously29,52 using ORCA analysis tools (https://github.com/BoettigerLab/ORCA-public).

In a recent development, before downstream analyses, ORCA traces were quality filtered on the basis of barcode detection. For each experiment, we computed the number of detected barcodes per trace. Median barcode detection per trace was calculated to be around 40–60 barcodes, and we restricted our analysis to traces with ≥25 detected barcodes. We further filtered out traces with unnaturally high barcode detection, keeping only traces with ≤86 barcodes detected. For each retained trace, the 3D positions of detected barcodes were ordered by genomic position. Next, barcodes with consistently poor detection or abnormal labelling (for example, failed strand displacement) were assigned estimated positions by linear interpolation in traces for which the immediately flanking barcodes were detected. This selective interpolation was applied to 2–5 barcodes per experiment. For contact frequency map analyses, such as those presented in Figs. 1e and 3e–g, we further interpolated missing barcodes using a maximum gap length of three consecutive missing barcodes. This interpolation preserved the major features of contact frequency maps while improving their smoothness. Different maximum gap lengths were tested. Gap lengths greater than three did not produce measurable further smoothing, whereas allowing larger interpolations produced abnormally short adjacent-barcode distances. For all other analyses, raw detected barcode positions were used, with only the selective interpolation of poorly labelled barcodes described above.

For contact frequency analyses, we chose contact thresholds near the average distance between adjacent barcodes in a spatially contiguous region of the locus. These thresholds ranged from 170 to 220 nm across experiments. We also conducted a threshold parameter sweep to verify that observed contact patterns were robust to a range of thresholds around the selected value, and varying the contact threshold within a reasonable range did not qualitatively alter any within-experiment effects. Thresholds were used to call contacts between all barcode pairs in an experiment. The thresholds used for each experiment are listed in Supplementary Table 4.

According to recent reports, enhancer–promoter barcode pairs were assigned on the basis of previously reported regulatory relationships between Pcdh cluster enhancers and their target promoters13,15,25,57, together with the ORCA locus positions containing the corresponding genes and enhancers. All Pcdha genes were assigned the HS5-1 enhancer (barcode 27), whereas Pcdhb genes were assigned the HS18-22 enhancer (barcode 78) and Pcdhg genes were assigned the HS16-17 enhancer (barcode 76). Enhancer–promoter contact frequencies were extracted from contact frequency matrices generated from max-gap-3 interpolated polymer coordinates, as described above. For ORCA barcodes containing multiple Pcdh promoters, combined gene labels were used.

We defined the geometric centre of an ORCA trace as the median X, Y, Z position of all detected barcodes in that trace. For the distance-to-centre profiles in Fig. 1i, we computed the Euclidean distance between each barcode and this centre on a per-trace basis, then plotted, for each position, the median distance across all traces. When distances to the centre of the heterochromatin domain were measured in Fig. 4c and Extended Data Figs. 9a–d and 10d, the heterochromatin centre was defined as the median X, Y, Z position of barcodes assigned to the heterochromatin domain (barcodes 2–14 and 29–67), and the distances of relevant locus positions to this centre were measured. When distances to the centre of a euchromatin region were measured in Extended Data Fig. 9a–d, the centre was defined as the median X, Y, Z position of barcodes assigned either to the euchromatin stretch between the Pcdha and Pcdhb clusters (barcodes 15–28) or to the euchromatin stretch downstream of the Pcdhg cluster (barcodes 68–90), depending on the specific locus position being analysed.

Radius of gyration (\({R}_{{\rm{g}}}\)) was used as a single-number measure of the spatial spread of a set of barcodes around its geometric centre47. For a set of \(N\) barcodes with 3D coordinates {\({r}_{i}\)}, we first calculated the centre \(c\) as the coordinate-wise median position, then defined \({R}_{{\rm{g}}}\) as \({R}_{{\rm{g}}}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{N}{\sum }_{i=1}^{N}{||}{r}_{i}-c{{||}}^{2}}\). The \({R}_{{\rm{g}}}\) of the heterochromatin domain was primarily evaluated. In Fig. 5e, the heterochromatin domain \({R}_{{\rm{g}}}\) was calculated as a fraction of the trace-wide \({R}_{{\rm{g}}}\).

For each isoform measured in Fig. 4a, the promoter barcode was assigned on the basis of the ORCA locus position containing the respective Pcdh gene. The heterochromatin compartment was defined as barcodes 2–14 and 29–67. The euchromatin compartment was defined on the basis of the cluster of the promoter being analysed: barcodes 15–28 for Pcdha promoters, and barcodes 68–90 for Pcdhb and Pcdhg promoters. The promoter barcode itself was excluded from the compartment to which it belonged. For each trace, a promoter-to-heterochromatin centre distance was calculated as the median Euclidean distance between the promoter barcode and all heterochromatin compartment barcodes. Promoter-to-euchromatin centre distances were calculated analogously as the median Euclidean distance between the promoter barcode and all barcodes in the corresponding euchromatin compartment.

In Extended Data Fig. 10e, entropy was calculated for the distance distributions between pairs of locus positions as described previously58. For each barcode pair, we pooled 3D distances across all traces within each genotype separately, then normalized each genotype’s distances by that genotype’s own median distance for the pair to account for length-scale differences between experiments. We then pooled the normalized distances from both genotypes together and set common histogram bin edges (50 bins) using the 1st and 99th percentiles of this pooled, normalized distribution, so that entropy values were computed on the same scale for both genotypes. Using these shared bin edges, we separately estimated each genotype’s distribution, normalized bin counts to probabilities pk and computed Shannon entropy as \(S=-{\sum }_{k}{p}_{k}{\log }_{2}({p}_{k})\), such that higher S reflects broader, more variable distances and lower S indicates more narrowly peaked, reproducible distances. For each locus position, we calculated its entropy with respect to all other positions, averaged these pairwise entropies per position and compared the resulting mean entropies between Setdb1 cKO and WT.

According to recent reports, to quantify spatial segregation between heterochromatic and euchromatic regions of the Pcdh locus, we calculated a separation score as follows. For each polymer, we designated heterochromatin locus positions (barcodes 2–14 and 29–67) as region A and euchromatic locus positions (barcodes 15–28 and 68–90) as region B, computed all pairwise 3D distances and took the median distance between A and B (heterochromatin–euchromatin) and the median distance within A (heterochromatin–heterochromatin). The separation score was defined as the ratio of these two medians (medianA–B/medianA–A), such that higher values indicate that the heterochromatin domain is more spatially separated from neighbouring euchromatin. This score was computed per trace for WT, Rad21 cKO and Setdb1 cKO and compared across genotypes.

Sources indicate that to validate the specificity of RNA probes targeting Pcdha and Pcdhg isoforms, plasmids encoding Pcdha and Pcdhg variable exons fused to mCherry under control of a CMV promoter were generated through FastCloning59. Plasmid sequences were validated using Plasmidsaurus. Plasmids were transfected into Cath.a-differentiated cells grown in eight-well Ibidi glass-bottom plates (Ibidi, 80827). Cells were seeded at a density of 40,000 cells per well in 220 μl of media and transfected after 24 h of growth using lipofectamine (Invitrogen, L3000001). Each well was then stained with primary RNA probes according to the procedure described above. For 12 plasmids across each of the Pcdha and Pcdhg clusters, three wells were transfected, with each well stained by a different ORCA readout barcode. Only wells that were labelled with a readout barcode mapping to the Pcdh isoform they were transfected with produced signal.

Recent findings suggest that FACS isolation of mouse OSNs was performed as previously described15. In brief, mice were euthanized with CO2 followed by cervical dislocation and OE tissue was immediately dissected. Cells were then dissociated into a single-cell suspension by incubating freshly dissected tissue with papain for 30–40 min at 37 °C according to the Worthington Papain Dissociation System. After dissociation and filtering through a 35-μm cell strainer, cells were resuspended in 1 × PBS with 2% fetal bovine serum (FBS), DNase (0.0025% final concentration) and DAPI. Fluorescent cells were sorted on a FACS Aria Fusion cell sorter (BD Biosciences) with BD FACSDiva 9.0.1 software. Cells were sorted into 1 × PBS + 2% FBS. FACS gating strategies used to isolate GFP+ and tdTomato+ mOSNs are shown in Supplementary Fig. 1.

Sources indicate that scRNA-seq experiments were performed as previously described15. In brief, cells were dissociated from OE tissue from 4- to 5-week-old mice as described above. About 70,000 mOSNs were FACS-isolated. Complementary DNA and library preparation were performed using the 10x Genomics Single Cell 5′ Gene Expression workflow, and libraries were sequenced using a NovaSeq SP100 PE50 and a NextSeq 2000 P2 200 through the UCSF Gladstone Genomic Core and the UCSF Center for Advanced Technology. Sequencing data were processed using 10x Genomics Cell Ranger 6.0.1. Data analysis was performed using Seurat60,61 and custom scripts. Cells were filtered to retain cells with 1,000–10,000 detected genes and less than 5% mitochondrial reads. Counts were then normalized using Seurat’s NormalizeData with log normalization and a scale factor of 10,000. See Supplementary Tables 2 and 3 for further details on scRNA-seq analysis and statistics.

For analyses in Fig. 5 and Extended Data Fig. 10, Pcdh isoform choice was analysed in mOSNs defined by detected Omp expression and no detected Gap43 expression using raw unique molecular identifier counts. A Pcdh isoform was considered detected in a given mOSN if one or more unique molecular identifier-corrected reads were assigned to that gene. For each condition, the percentage of mOSNs expressing each Pcdh isoform was calculated as the fraction of mOSNs with detected expression of that isoform. Changes in Pcdh choice across genotypes were calculated as percentage-point differences relative to WT. Data for single-cell experiments represent one biological replicate per condition.

nChIP–seq was performed as previously described62. Briefly, live cells were sorted from papain-dissociated mouse OE; in experiments for which spike-ins were included to enable quantification of ChIP signal across conditions, HEK293T cells at around 70% confluency were trypsinized, washed with PBS and added at a ratio of 0.75% to the sorted mouse cells. (HEK293T cells were grown in RPMI or DMEM media supplemented with 10% FBS and 1 × penicillin-streptomycin, incubated at 37 °C and 5% CO2, and tested for mycoplasma (ATCC Universal Mycoplasma Detection Kit) before use in experiments.) Live sorted cells were pelleted in a swinging bucket centrifuge (800g, 15 min, 4 °C) and then resuspended in Buffer 1 (0.3 M sucrose, 60 mM KCl, 15 mM NaCl, 5 mM MgCl2, 0.1 mM EGTA, 15 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 0.1 mM PMSF, 0.5 mM DTT, 1 × Roche cOmplete EDTA-free protease inhibitors). Cells were lysed on ice for 10 min by adding an equal volume of Buffer 2 (0.4% Igepal CA-630, 0.3 M sucrose, 60 mM KCl, 15 mM NaCl, 5 mM MgCl2, 0.1 mM EGTA, 15 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 0.1 mM PMSF, 0.5 mM DTT, 1 × Roche cOmplete EDTA-free protease inhibitors). Nuclei were pelleted (1,000g, 10 min, 4 °C) and resuspended in MNase buffer (0.32 M sucrose, 4 mM MgCl2, 1 mM CaCl2, 50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 0.1 mM PMSF, 1 × Roche cOmplete EDTA-free protease inhibitors). Resuspended nuclei were treated with MNase (Sigma) at 37 °C, and the reaction was quenched with the addition of EDTA to a final concentration of 20 mM. Two fractions of solubilized chromatin were collected; nuclei were pelleted (10,000g, 10 min, 4 °C) and fraction S1 was collected and stored at 4 °C overnight. Nuclei were resuspended in Dialysis Buffer (1 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 0.2 mM EDTA, 0.1 mM PMSF, 1 × Roche cOmplete EDTA-free protease inhibitors) and rotated overnight at 4 °C. Insoluble material was pelleted (10,000g, 10 min, 4 °C) and fraction S2 was retained. MNase treatment was optimized to yield predominantly mono-nucleosomes in the S1 fraction and predominantly di-nucleosomes, tri-nucleosomes and some larger chromatin fragments in the S2 fraction. S1 and S2 DNA concentrations were measured by HS DNA Qubit after RNase A treatment. Equal volumes of S1 and S2 fractions were pooled, and total yields were estimated. In spike-in experiments, chromatin input was not always equalized across immunoprecipitations, as spike-in normalization accounts for differences in input.

Recent findings suggest that MNase-digested chromatin was diluted in Wash Buffer 1 (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 10 mM EDTA, 125 mM NaCl, 0.1% Tween-20, 1 × Roche cOmplete EDTA-free protease inhibitors), and 5% inputs were reserved. Histone H3 lysine 9 tri-methyl antibody (H3K9me3, Abcam ab8898) was added, and the binding reaction was rotated overnight at 4 °C. For each immunoprecipitation, 20 μl of Dynabeads Protein G (Invitrogen) were blocked overnight with 2 mg ml−1 yeast transfer RNA and 2 mg ml−1 BSA in Wash Buffer 1. The next day, blocked beads were added to antibody-bound chromatin and rotated for 1–3 h at 4 °C. Chromatin-bound beads were washed at 4 °C a total of four times with Wash Buffer I, three times with Wash Buffer II (5 mM Tris pH 7.5, 17.5 mM NaCl, 0.01% NP-40, 1 mM EDTA, 1 × Roche cOmplete EDTA-free protease inhibitors), and one time with Tris-EDTA buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 1 mM EDTA). Two 15-min elutions were conducted at 37 °C in Elution Buffer (1% SDS, 250 mM NaCl, 2 mM DTT). ChIP DNA and input DNA were column purified using Zymo ChIP DNA columns (Zymo Research, D5205 or D5201).

Industry observers note that libraries were prepared using the Ovation Ultralow V2 DNA-Seq Library Preparation Kit (Tecan Life Sciences). The quality of the libraries was assessed by Bioanalyzer and quantified using a combination of Bioanalyzer and Qubit. Libraries were pooled and sequenced on a NextSeq 2000 (Gladstone Institutes), NextSeq 500/550 (UCSF Center for Advanced Technology) or NovaSeq X (Chan Zuckerberg Initiative Biohub San Francisco).

Industry observers note that data processing and analysis was conducted in accordance with previous literature63,64. For spike-in experiments, adapters were trimmed with cutadapt with --minimum-length 18 and checked for sequencing quality control with FastQC. Reads were aligned with Bowtie2 to a concatenated mouse and human genome (mm10 + hg38) in which the spike-in chromosomes were pre-labelled with a ‘_hg38’ suffix. Alignments were split by chromosome using bamUtil’s splitChromosome function, and samtools’ merge command was used to collect mouse and human alignments separately. Then, duplicates were marked and removed using Picard MarkDuplicates, and the spike-in chromosome suffix was stripped. Alignments with mapping quality < 30 were removed using samtools, and read counts aligning to the mouse and human genomes were used to calculate spike-in scaling factors.

According to recent reports, as in the original ChIP-Rx method describing quantitative spike-in normalized ChIP followed by sequencing, our spike-in corrections normalized for the number of spike-in reads in the immunoprecipitation63. We sequenced every input as well, allowing us to adjust for the variability in spike-in read fraction in each input64,65. The spike-in adjusted coverage signal, \({z}_{i}\), was calculated from counts per million (CPM)-normalized coverage values, \({x}_{i}\), with the equation \({z}_{i}={x}_{i}\cdot \frac{{S}_{\mathrm{in}}}{{T}_{\mathrm{in}}}\frac{{T}_{\mathrm{ip}}}{{S}_{\mathrm{ip}}}\), where \({S}_{\mathrm{in}}\) and \({T}_{\mathrm{in}}\) are the number of spike-in (human) and target (mouse) reads in the inputs, respectively, and \({S}_{\mathrm{ip}}\) and \({T}_{\mathrm{ip}}\) are the number of spike-in (human) and target (mouse) reads in the immunoprecipitations, respectively. Bigwig files were generated from Deeptools bamCoverage using --scaleFactor of \(\frac{{S}_{\mathrm{in}}}{{T}_{\mathrm{in}}}\cdot \frac{{T}_{\mathrm{ip}}}{{S}_{\mathrm{ip}}}\), --binSize 10, --minMappingQuality 30 and --normalizeUsing CPM. In Fig. 5c, to compare spike-in-normalized nChIP–seq values from different experiments, we batch-corrected using the average of the scale factors from the WT samples within each experimental batch. Significance was assessed and confirmed using both a Welch’s unpaired t-test and a two-way ANOVA (main effects only).

Recent findings suggest that for experiments without spike-ins, adapters were trimmed and the first 4 nucleotides of each read removed with cutadapt (v1.9.1; -u 4, --minimum-length 18). Reads were aligned to mm10 with Bowtie2. BigWig files were generated with deepTools bamCoverage in 10-base-pair bins from unextended reads, normalized to 1 × genome coverage (reads per genomic content; effective genome size 2,407,883,318; chr. X, chr. Y and chr. M excluded from normalization).

Immunohistochemistry for RAD21 was performed as described previously15. A similar staining protocol was performed for SETDB1, with minor modifications to the blocking buffer composition to improve signal. Sections were removed from −20 °C, washed in 1 × PBS for 5 min at room temperature, then washed three times in 0.1% PBS-Triton X for 5 min. Sections were incubated in blocking solution (3% BSA, 0.2% Tween in 4 × SSC) for 1 h at room temperature. Primary antibody incubation proceeded overnight (12–16 h) at 4 °C in a humidified chamber. The following morning, sections were washed three times in 0.1% PBS-Triton X for 5 min at room temperature, then incubated in secondary antibody at room temperature for 1 h. Samples were then washed three times in 0.1% PBS-Triton X for 5 min at room temperature and mounted under coverslips with antifade mounting medium with DAPI (Vector Laboratories, H-2000-2). For RAD21 staining, primary antibody was added at 1:100 in blocking buffer (Invitrogen, PA5-28344). For SETDB1 staining, primary antibody was added at 1:250 in blocking buffer (Thermofisher, MA5-47120). For both RAD21 and SETDB1, secondary antibody was added at 1:1,000 in blocking buffer (Invitrogen donkey anti-rabbit 647, A31573).

The Hi-C data in Extended Data Fig. 2b and bulk RNA-seq data in Fig. 3b were previously published and re-analysed as described15.

(k) Model of Pcdh transcription from a megabase-scale heterochromatin domain. Pcdh enhancers lie outside the heterochromatin domain containing Pcdh promoters. Cohesin-mediated loop extrusion brings enhancers into the domain to engage promoters, with transcription initiating from within the domain. After promoter activation, transcription can proceed in the absence of enhancer—promoter engagement. Transcription reads through downstream Pcdha and Pcdhg genes residing within the heterochromatin domain, and domain-scale compaction is maintained.

Derby County vs Watford - prediction, team news, lineups

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (531 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Darren Plant | 26 Nov 2026 12:49.
  • Derby County and Watford square off at Pride Park on Saturday afternoon as two of the worst performing teams in the division.
  • While the Rams sit at the bottom of the Championship table, Watford are only five points ahead of them and with a head coach taking charge of his first Hornets match.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Darren Plant | 26 Nov 2026 12:49.

Derby County and Watford square off at Pride Park on Saturday afternoon as two of the worst performing teams in the division.

While the Rams sit at the bottom of the Championship table, Watford are only five points ahead of them and with a head coach taking charge of his first Hornets match.

When Derby travelled to Molineux to face Wolverhampton Wanderers on Tuesday night, they would not have necessarily expected to earn anything from one of the form teams in the division.

However, despite having troubled Wolves during the opening half hour, the Rams succumbed to a 3-0 defeat and allowed their opponents to have the most shots (39) by any team in the Championship in 11 years.

John Eustace has now overseen 11 defeats in 17 league matches, and it is realistic to assume that he may be sacked if Derby lose this game.

In four of their last eight outings, Derby have conceded at least three goals, while they have only netted more than once in a fixture in 13 outings.

On a positive note, the East Midlands outfit did win their last contest at Pride Park, overcoming Bolton Wanderers by a 3-1 scoreline on November 6.

Meanwhile, Watford head into this encounter with former Romania and Legia Warsaw boss Edward Iordanescu in the dugout for his first game in English football.

The Hornets have accumulated seven points from seven matches, hardly a disaster at this stage of the season.

Nevertheless, back-to-back defeats have been posted at Sheffield United and against Blackburn Rovers without scoring a goal.

Despite holding leaders Middlesbrough to a goalless draw before the November international break, Watford have now failed to score in three successive matches.

Furthermore, they have collected just one point from eight away matches this season, that 1-1 draw at Wrexham in August being followed by seven consecutive defeats on their travels.

Derby County Championship form:.

Oscar Fraulo and Bobby Clark are both pushing for a return to the Derby midfield.

Jack Robinson may return to the defence, whether that be as a central defender in a back three or left-back in a back four.

Eustace must decide whether to use Rhian Brewster in an unfamiliar wing-back role for the second game in a row, but Sammie Szmodics remains in a packed treatment room.

Iordanescu will be forced into at least two Watford changes through Mattie Pollock and Jordan Zemura serving suspensions.

Branimir Mlacic and Marc Bola appear likely to deputise, while Edo Kayembe, Rocco Vata and Othmane Maamma will also be considered for opportunities further up the pitch.

Derby County possible starting lineup:.

Widell-Zetterstrom; Clarke, Sanderson, Robinson; Nyambe, Ozoh, Mowatt, Clark, Brewster; Fuseini, Morris.

Watford possible starting lineup:.

Ravaglia; Traore, Mlacic, Coulibaly, Bola; Kayembe, Kyprianou, Bravo; Vata, Doumbia, Maamma.

With Watford transitioning to a new head coach, it is difficult to predict how they may perform. Nevertheless, this is a must-win match for Derby and Eustace, and we are backing the Rams to net a late goal to edge this contest.

Breaking: Kean’s new tibia injury rules former Juventus striker out of Como v Juventus

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (519 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Juvefc

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that moise Kean has broken down again in Como training, three weeks after treatment that was meant to fix his shin.
  • Moise Kean has suffered a fresh tibia injury in training with Como.
  • Como’s statement of 17 November gave no recovery date.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that moise Kean has broken down again in Como training, three weeks after treatment that was meant to fix his shin. The former Juventus striker is set to miss about two more months, so he will not face his old club on 29 November.

Moise Kean has suffered a fresh tibia injury in training with Como. The former Juventus striker is now undergoing further medical tests. Sky Sport Italia reported that he will be out for about two more months. That timeline rules him out of Como’s home game against Juventus.

Como’s statement of 17 November gave no recovery date. The club promised an update once more information was available.

In a recent development, the upcoming problem follows a treatment that was meant to end his shin trouble. On 30 October, Como’s update described his treatment at the Cugat Institute in Barcelona as successful. The club put his recovery at about five weeks. His progress was to be reviewed every day.

It has been revealed that that initiative has now collapsed. Kean had been out since early October. The original injury came while he was playing for Italy against France on 2 October. That match was the first leg of a Nations League tie.

The setback is a heavy blow for Como. In Serie A, his outings for the club added up to 160 minutes. He has yet to score, including in his single Champions League game. He joined from Fiorentina on an initial loan, with an obligation to make the move permanent. At Fiorentina he scored 27 league goals in two seasons, 19 of them in 2024/25. Before that, he came through the Juventus academy.

Industry observers note that without him, Como will have to rely on Douvikas up front. The club may also look for a striker in January.

For Juventus, the news removes one threat from a crucial stretch. Como are their next opponents after Venezia. The game is the Sunday evening fixture a week later, in round 13 of Serie A. Kick-off is at 20:45.

Como 1907 is pleased to announce the signing of Italian international forward Moise Kean from @acffiorentina on an initial loan, with an obligation to make the move permanent.

Official statement ➡️ https://t.co/PJKnFXS9Xp pic.twitter.com/4F30ROYFUT.

— Como1907 (@Como_1907) September 1, 2026.

Luciano Spalletti’s side need results. Juventus sit six points behind fourth place and have averaged just over 1.6 points per game, according to Corriere dello Sport. The paper sees the run of fixtures as decisive for the push for a Champions League place. It warns that dropping points against Venezia would force Juventus to win every remaining game of 2026 to stay in touch with the top four.

According to recent reports, the schedule offers little respite after the trip to Como. Juventus host Udinese on 6 December and Monza on 14 December. They then travel to Roma on 19 December.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Liverpool are at the moment fourth in the Premier League table.

If they finish in this position by the end of the term, they'll qualify for the Champions League again.

But, in reality, they should be aiming for a much higher finish.

They have spent over £600 million on new players across these last couple of years and, with that amount of spending, you'd expect them to be one of the best teams in the world.

That clearly isn't the case as, around a month ago now, they were beaten 3-2 by Fenerbahce which is probably their low point of the season.

However, this latest news to emerge from Anfield could change everything.

Liverpool and Rio Ngumoha are getting closer to agreeing a newly introduced deal.

One of the biggest stories to emerge from the 2026-27 season so far is about what's going to happen to Rio Ngumoha.

The Englishman was promoted to Liverpool's first-team squad by Arne Slot last term and, since then, he's never really looked back.

Talk of him extending his contract, which expires in 2028, has been rife since the 2026-27 season got fully underway with some rumours about him potentially switching Liverpool for Munich at some point.

Fortunately, this deal never came to fruition and now, the Reds are in the driving seat to lock him down.

And, thanks to a fresh revision from TEAMtalk, that looks like exactly what's about to happen.

"Ngumoha is primed to put pen to paper on a newly introduced and much improved contract at Anfield," they wrote.

"Bayern Munich are once again sniffing around the player amid a raft of injuries and problems with their forward line.

"However, sources tell us Liverpool are close to finalising a new deal that will ensure Ngumoha continues to terrorise Premier League defences for years to come.".

Rio Ngumoha is the future of Liverpool's attack.

This season, Ngumoha has featured 15 times for Liverpool and has contributed to four goals.

Three of them have come as assists for his teammates and, whether he's been used on the left or right-wing, he's always put in plenty of effort.

As mentioned, Ngumoha's effort hasn't gone unnoticed with clubs such as Bayern Munich trying their hardest to strike a deal with him.

Obviously, Liverpool would never let that happen but it does prove how high the Englishman's ceiling actually is.

Right now, Ngumoha might not be a guaranteed starter but, in the future when certain players exit or Liverpool's tactics change, he's likely to be one of the first names on Liverpool's team sheet.

The former Chelsea man may only be 18 years old but, as long as Liverpool keep him around, their attack will be sorted for at least one attacker so, here's hoping these rumours of a deal being close to completion are true and that the Reds can lock their 'game-changer' down soon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Manchester City play like this what a loss their football will be to the Premier League – and the Champions League – if they are heavily sanctioned later this season.

Industry observers note that in what turned out to be a match for the ages, a night of brilliant, unbridled attack, we were treated to the ultimate game of two halves as the back-to-back European champions Paris St-Germain took City apart for 45 minutes. And then were left holding on.

City will hope this is a sign of what is to come in their Premier League fight. But with a different result. After suffering a resounding defeat at the hands of the Premier League’s independent commission, with 114 of the 115 charges against them proven, they maintain their innocence and are mounting an appeal.

Could they make a comeback? It would be incredible and highly improbable if they did so but, out on the pitch, and 3-0 down after a first half in which they were in danger of being humiliated by PSG, they created enough opportunities to save themselves.

Sources indicate that the data backed that. City’s expected goals (xG) was 2.57 while PSG’s was 1.83. City had 27 shots to 15 and had more possession and more passes. Enzo Maresca made a triple substitution to devastating effect, especially with the introduction of new signings Ayyoub Bouaddi and Iliman Ndiaye.

In a recent development, in the end they clawed back two goals, both scored by Erling Haaland, who now has 61 in 60 games in this competition – seventh outright in the all-time list, before Ruud van Nistelrooy. And 37 of those for City, overtaking Sergio Agüero’s club record.

Erling Haaland gets his second of the night, and the game could be back on 🔥 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/sFZ0eT2Egz.

Sources indicate that it could have been a hat-trick. It could even have been four as Haaland, taking the captain’s armband as Rúben Dias was withdrawn during the interval, clipped the top of the crossbar with a header and then was denied by goalkeeper Matvei Safonov as the striker slid in.

Industry observers note that “Even with 3-0 in the first half, with the amount of chances we created in the second half, we deserved more. Luis [Enrique, PSG’s coach] remarked at the end of the game that they were quite lucky,” Maresca claimed before being asked whether he would relish facing PSG again, later in this competition. “My feeling is we are there. We are close,” he added.

Did City deserve a draw? No one was predicting that at half-time as they were suffering as comprehensive a defeat as was inflicted by the commission. Accused of “sham” contracts to inflate income, this was a sham of a performance, made all the more emphatic because of how brilliant PSG, and their exceptional 21-year-old winger Désiré Doué, were.

There is a certain irony that it was PSG who inflicted this defeat, ending City’s run of eight wins from eight in all competitions under Maresca.

It was a meeting of two clubs empowered more than any other by the riches of Gulf states: Abu Dhabi versus Qatar. Both have also had their run-ins over money. Both were sanctioned, but escaped full bans by Uefa for breaching financial fair play rules.

The question, also, was: would the eighth meeting of these clubs in the Champions League in the last 11 seasons be the last for some time?

So we should savour it and we did. That included Pep Guardiola on his first return to the Etihad – in a sign of solidarity – after quitting at the end of last season. Will Australia push for fossil fuel exit at UN talks?

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (979 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In its role as president of negotiations at the UN climate talks in Turkey, Australia is being pressured to guide nations toward unified action on slashing the greenhouse gas emissions that are generated in large part by burning fossil fuels.
  • The nation has pledged to lead by example at the summit through a strong commitment to renewable energy, electrification and reduced reliance on planet-heating coal, oil and gas.
  • "Renewable energy, grids, storage and electrification are creating opportunities to strengthen resilience, improve energy security, and reduce emissions at the same time," said Chris Bowen, Australia's climate change and energy minister, in October during a meeting in Fiji ahead of the COP climate conference.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In its role as president of negotiations at the UN climate talks in Turkey, Australia is being pressured to guide nations toward unified action on slashing the greenhouse gas emissions that are generated in large part by burning fossil fuels.

The nation has pledged to lead by example at the summit through a strong commitment to renewable energy, electrification and reduced reliance on planet-heating coal, oil and gas.

"Renewable energy, grids, storage and electrification are creating opportunities to strengthen resilience, improve energy security, and reduce emissions at the same time," said Chris Bowen, Australia's climate change and energy minister, in October during a meeting in Fiji ahead of the COP climate conference.

"These are proven, commercial and scalable today. Now is the moment for faster implementation.".

Sources indicate that yet Australia is also the world's third-largest exporter of fossil fuels. And unlike France and Germany, or island nations from Fiji to the Bahamas that are highly vulnerable to a changing climate, the COP31 co-president has not yet committed to phasing them out.

As calls grow for the country to set a clear route to a clean energy future, critics say its vague promise to transition away from polluting sources of power does not go far enough.

Australia is home to 56% of the world's coal mine projects right now in the pipeline, notes environmental nonprofit, 350.org.

Andreas Sieber, head of political strategy at the organization, is calling on the country, the world's second-largest coal exporter, to reverse course and announce an "overdue coal phaseout date" during the COP31 conference.

"Australia needs to walk the walk and follow Germany's example and commit to a phaseout," mentioned Melanie Pill, founder of The Climate Project, an Australia-based climate policy advisory.

The argument to end fossil fuel production is not only about cutting emissions but reducing dependence on energy systems that rely on volatile oil and gas markets, she explained.

"A fossil phaseout in the face of the enduring and escalating conflict in the Middle East is in the interest of everyone," Pill told DW.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

This is especially true for Australia's diesel-reliant Pacific neighbors, who spend up to 25% of GDP on fossil fuel imports — as opposed 6% on health — according to a report by the Institute for Climate Risk and Response at the University of Newly introduced South Wales.

As lead negotiator at the UN climate talks, Australia can "flip the narrative" on a fossil fuel phaseout, using the challenge of energy security as a justification, mentioned Pill.

This opportunity could be lost, however, if Australia fails to address fossil fuel exports that accounted for 80% of its total carbon footprint in 2022 — and near 5% of global emissions.

While the nation is a world leader in rooftop solar, and generates around half of its electricity from renewables, this progress is "being undone by its continued approval of more fossil fuels for export," stated Simon Bradshaw, COP31 lead and climate expert at Greenpeace Australia Pacific.

He noted that the Labor government of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has approved the construction, expansion or extension of 38 coal, oil and gas projects since coming to power four years ago on a pro-climate platform.

"You cannot aspire to lead on climate abroad if you're not getting your own house in order," mentioned Thomas Houlie, climate and energy policy analyst at Climate Analytics, a global climate policy institute.

In 2025, when Australia approved the extension of a major gas export project in the country's west until 2070, Albanese justified the move in the name of a balance between "security of energy supply" and "support [for] the transition which reduces our emissions.".

The country has publicly backed a global transition away from the fossil fuels driving the global temperature rise linked to extreme heat and drought. Both through the Global Stocktake agreed at the 2023 UN climate summit, and via the inaugural "transitioning away" summit in Colombia this April, at which Australia and 56 countries pledged to develop a fossil fuel exit road map.

But these commitments are not reflected in Australian resources policy, or its domestic rollout of clean power infrastructure.

"While the government has set a renewables target for electricity, it leaves plenty of blind spots in other sectors," said Houlie, adding that emission reductions in industry and transport have been limited and that the push to achieve an 82% renewables target for the electricity grid by 2030 is behind schedule.

In its role as lead negotiator at COP31, Australia has promised to ensure that any final conference text serves to "elevate the views and the experiences" of small Pacific nations in its region, from Vanuatu to Tuvalu.

These island countries that generate low emissions yet suffer extreme climate impacts from worsening cyclones or rising seas are "sick of Australia's double talk on climate," mentioned Shiva Gounden, head of Pacific at Greenpeace Australia Pacific.

In a recent development, australia must commit to "substantial upcoming funding contributions" to help Pacific neighbors adapt to the climate emergency and achieve energy independence, said his colleague Bradshaw. He reiterated the need to concurrently create a "national road map" away from coal and gas production and export.

A Climate Analytics report co-authored by Houlie outlines a fossil fuel phaseout pathway for Australia that can begin immediately. This includes an end to coal power generation by 2034 and a rapid reduction in oil and gas consumption, with renewables generating almost all the country's electricity by 2040. Fossil fuel export projects would be eliminated, and existing ones shuttered before becoming obsolete.

"This co-presidency is a golden opportunity for Australia to step up and commit to a phaseout," said Houlie.

Breaking: Le Havre vs. Strasbourg - prediction, team news, lineups

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Seye Omidiora | 26 Nov 2026 13:09.
  • Two of Ligue 1's struggling sides meet in Saturday's gameweek 12 encounter, as winless Le Havre host third-bottom Strasbourg at Stade Oceane.
  • The bottom club remain the only side without a victory in the French top flight after 11 matches, leaving their survival prospects looking increasingly bleak even at this stage of the campaign.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Seye Omidiora | 26 Nov 2026 13:09.

Two of Ligue 1's struggling sides meet in Saturday's gameweek 12 encounter, as winless Le Havre host third-bottom Strasbourg at Stade Oceane.

The bottom club remain the only side without a victory in the French top flight after 11 matches, leaving their survival prospects looking increasingly bleak even at this stage of the campaign.

Le Havre's 14th-placed finish last season, just three points above Nice in the relegation playoff spot, offered little encouragement ahead of the 2026-27 campaign, and those concerns have proved justified.

Le Club Doyen have not won a top-flight fixture since beating Lorient 2-0 on the final day of last season, with their miserable start prompting Didier Digard's dismissal at the end of October.

Valerien Ismael's first match in charge of the basement club began brightly when Josh Maja scored after three minutes against Troyes; however, they held that advantage for just 15 minutes before eventually losing 3-1.

Conceding three more goals left Les Ciel et Marine with the competition's joint-worst defensive record, having shipped 25, while their tally of 10 scored surpasses only Angers' nine.

Even victory would do little to transform the Dean Club's position, as they enter this weekend eight points behind the relegation playoff spot and nine adrift of safety.

Nonetheless, the hosts must avoid defeat to Vitor Matos's Strasbourg, who occupy that playoff position.

Le Racing's disappointing start has already cost Hugo Oliveira his job, with Matos replacing his Portuguese compatriot during the international break.

The newly introduced manager's debut did not go to plan, with Le RCS losing 1-0 to Brest despite an encouraging performance in which they attempted 15 shots to their opponents' 16; Le Racing also created two chances deemed clear-cut to Brest's one.

Looking to build on that display, Le RCS target their fourth victory of the campaign this weekend, although it would be only their second since early October.

Maximum points could lift Matos's men out of the playoff spot and as high as 13th, although escaping the bottom three also requires Auxerre, Troyes or Le Mans to slip up.

The hosts have several absentees, with Felix Mambimbi (Achilles), Timothee Pembele (muscle), Rassoul Ndiaye (muscle), Daren Mosengo (ankle), Stephan Zagadou (ACL), Sota Nakamura (leg) and Lionel Mpasi (Achilles) all sidelined.

Enzo Koffi begins a two-match suspension following his late dismissal against Troyes last weekend, ruling him out of Saturday's encounter and December's trip to Lens.

Only six players have surpassed Maja's five league goals this season, but the Nigerian's efforts have brought little reward for a Dean Club side repeatedly undermined by defensive frailties.

Strasbourg have several potential game-changers, with Gessime Yassine registering four goals and three assists, Giovanni Reyna scoring three, Conrad Harder and Dario Essugo contributing two goals and an assist and Sebastian Nanasi setting up three.

However, Reyna is unavailable due to a muscle problem, while Fabio Balde (leg), Oso (knock) and Joaquin Panichelli (ACL) are also sidelined.

Le Havre possible starting lineup:.

Bodart; Sasso, Seko, Touba; Ouziad, Mwanga, Ebonog, Richardson, Jelert; Maja, Fofana.

Strasbourg possible starting lineup:.

Jorgensen; Antwi, Doukoure, Coulibaly, Hogsberg; Essugo, El Mourabet; Yassine, Nanasi, Godo; Harder.

Maja's scoring form offers Le Havre some encouragement, but conceding 25 goals in 11 matches suggests that their defensive problems remain too pronounced for an immediate recovery.

Strasbourg created enough chances to trouble Brest in Matos's first match and should find greater reward against the division's joint-leakiest defence.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pierre Sage felt Crystal Palace were “really far off” his expectations after suffering a 3-2 away Europa League defeat by his former side Lyon.
  • Corentin Tolisso opened the scoring for the hosts and Ernest Nuamah doubled Lyon’s advantage late in a first half devoid of any shots on target for the visitors.
  • Yéremy Pino halved the deficit five minutes after the break, before Pavel Sulc restored the two-goal lead, and substitute Daichi Kamada’s late goal proved a mere consolation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pierre Sage felt Crystal Palace were “really far off” his expectations after suffering a 3-2 away Europa League defeat by his former side Lyon.

Corentin Tolisso opened the scoring for the hosts and Ernest Nuamah doubled Lyon’s advantage late in a first half devoid of any shots on target for the visitors.

Yéremy Pino halved the deficit five minutes after the break, before Pavel Sulc restored the two-goal lead, and substitute Daichi Kamada’s late goal proved a mere consolation.

“At the end, we were frustrated by the result, but in the first half we have to be frustrated in the way we play,” remarked Sage, speaking to PalaceTV.

“I think we didn’t play this first half. We are really far off our standards in the mental side of the play, in the tactical side of the play, because the players are too high between our lines and we really struggled a lot with that.

“When you give back the ball to your opponent, you suffer a lot and we were better in the second half. You cannot win this kind of game by playing only one half.”.

Sage’s side got the better of his predecessor, Oliver Glasner, after they bounced back to beat Nottingham Forest 3-1 at Selhurst Park on Sunday.

After that victory, the Frenchman called for more consistency from his team, but on Thursday night was left ruing missed opportunities and goals conceded too easily by last season’s Conference League winners.

Sources indicate that sage was sacked by Lyon in January 2025 after a 14-month spell with the Ligue 1 outfit. Like Glasner’s, his own reunion ended in disappointment.

According to recent reports, he told Uefa: “It’s a very disappointing return because we lost. I can’t take satisfaction from coming back home or seeing familiar faces when the result isn’t there.

“The scoreline may have been close, but there was a substantial difference in the way the two teams played.

“We improved considerably after the break and gave ourselves a chance, but conceding that third goal made things difficult.

“I think our second-half efforts deserved an equaliser, although winning would have been a generous reward given that we only really played [to our level] for one half.”.

Sources indicate that the veteran captain said: “It has been a long time coming. The fans were up for it, the players were up for it so we’re very happy with the performance.”.

When asked about Evanilson’s header, which Smith supplied the assist for, he replied: “It wasn’t my best cross but I put it in an area, what a finish from him and I think we deserved that little bit of luck.

“From there on we went on to win the game but in the second half we got a little bit tired but the quality that came off the bench is great and we look forward to Sunday now.

“It’s a great header, he deserved it because he has worked very hard this season and many more to come from him.”.

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of Thursday night’s European football with Crystal Palace, Sunderland and Bournemouth in Europa League action, and Brighton hosting Kauno Zalgiris in the Uefa Conference League.

In a recent development, palace manager Pierre Sage managed Lyon between November 2023 and January 2025, and another sub-plot is American businessman John Textor’s involvement with the French club. The former Palace shareholder was the reason the club missed out on Europa League participation last season because Lyon were in the same competition and thus Palace were considered in breach of multi-club ownership rules. Textor sold his stake in Palace, but despite the club’s best efforts they had to settle for the Conference League, a competition they subsequently won.

Palace could have been three or four down against Nottingham Forest at the weekend but fought back for a much-needed Premier League victory. They made a winning start in Europe, beating Lech Poznan 4-0 at Selhurst Park in their opening Europa League game.

In a recent development, bournemouth and Sunderland also made winning starts, despite both teams’ poor form domestically. Sunderland travel to Portuguese side Torreense, while Sturm Graz are the opposition for Bournemouth’s first ever European game at the Vitality Stadium (or Dean Court if you prefer). Bournemouth continue to be without Justin Kluivert, Eli Junior Kroupi and Alex Scott because of injury.

Brighton are favourites to win the Conference League and play their first game in the competition against Lithuanian club Kauno Zalgiris. Lifting the trophy in Istanbul at the end of the season would assure Brighton of a place in next season’s Europa League, though given their Premier League form and Manchester City’s predicament, Champions League qualification could be a realistic aspiration. Brighton won with 10 men at Sunderland on Saturday, and were successful in their appeal against Pascal Struijk’s red card.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Lewis Blain | 26 Nov 2026 13:11.

Arsenal could face an unexpected transfer decision in January, with Kepa Arrizabalaga's future at the Emirates Stadium uncertain.

The Spanish goalkeeper is understood to be unhappy with his current situation and is not ruling out a mid-season departure.

A potential exit would leave Gunners boss Mikel Arteta needing to consider an additional goalkeeper, despite other areas of his squad appearing to require greater attention.

Kepa joined Arsenal from Chelsea in July 2025 and spent the past 18 months as David Raya's deputy, making 12 appearances in all competitions, including just one in the Premier League.

He has started only twice this season, with his latest appearance coming in Tuesday's 1-1 draw against Borussia Dortmund in the Champions League, when Raya was unavailable through injury.

Reports in Spain (via Sport Witness) have linked the 32-year-old with Valencia, with sporting director Braulio Vazquez reportedly exploring the possibility of bringing him back to LaLiga.

It is understood that there is nothing concrete at this stage, with Kepa yet to receive a formal approach or offer from the Spanish club.

The shot-stopper has also not held talks with Arsenal over his future, although the possibility of him initiating discussions with the club's hierarchy has not been ruled out.

Kepa's contract at the Emirates runs until 2028, but his future remains uncertain, with Valencia potentially revisiting their interest in the January window.

Arsenal have obvious priorities elsewhere, particularly in attack, where additional options on the wing and at centre-forward could strengthen Arteta's squad as they look to defend their Premier League crown.

However, allowing Kepa to leave in January, even on loan, would create an unexpected problem between the posts.

With Raya, Kepa and Illan Meslier currently providing the goalkeeping options, losing the Spaniard would leave the Gunners needing to consider another addition to maintain sufficient cover.

The club would surely prefer to avoid that situation until the summer, and that makes sense given the other areas that could demand investment.

Unless Kepa pushes for an exit or Valencia make an offer that Arsenal are willing to consider, keeping him until the end of the season would appear the simplest solution.
