Industry observers note that we confirmed these findings using the complementary tEC-iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R clonal tracing model (Extended Data Fig. 11a–i). Whereas Cherry+ and Cherry+ Nr2f2ΔEC/ΔEC endothelial cells contributed similarly to arteries, eGFP-PIK3CAH1047RNr2f2ΔEC/ΔEC cells were detected in 35% of arteries, compared with 10% for eGFP-PIK3CAH1047R cells (Extended Data Fig. 11c,e). Moreover, most eGFP-PIK3CAH1047RNr2f2ΔEC/ΔEC cells that reached arteries did not form lesions, whereas eGFP-PIK3CAH1047R cells consistently generated small arterial lesions (Extended Data Fig. 11c,f). Nevertheless, eGFP-PIK3CAH1047RNr2f2ΔEC/ΔEC cells continued to overexpand within the capillary plexus (Extended Data Fig. 11g–i). Together, these findings demonstrate that NR2F2 mediates the PIK3CA-driven block in arterial differentiation but is dispensable for mutant cell hyperproliferation in non-arterial vessels.

To investigate how PIK3CAH1047R activation induces NR2F2 expression, we analysed endothelial cells in culture. Nr2f2 transcript levels increased within 24 h after 4-OHT-induced recombination and remained elevated thereafter (Extended Data Fig. 12a). NR2F2 protein levels increased by 72 h (Extended Data Fig. 12b–d). To test whether Nr2f2 induction depends on PI3K signalling, endothelial cells were treated with the PI3Kα-selective inhibitor alpelisib (BYL719). PI3Kα inhibition reduced Nr2f2 mRNA and protein levels in a dose-dependent manner, accompanied by reduced p-AKT levels (Extended Data Fig. 12e–h). Similarly, alpelisib reduced NR2F2 transcript and protein levels in patient-derived endothelial cells with activating PIK3CA mutations (Extended Data Fig. 12i,j).

To investigate the transcriptional mechanisms underlying NR2F2 induction, we focused on FOXO transcription factors, major downstream effectors of PI3K signalling7,32, with FOXO1 the predominant family member in endothelial cells33. PI3K–AKT signalling inhibits FOXO1 through phosphorylation-dependent nuclear exclusion7,32 and, consistent with this, FOXO1 was excluded from the nucleus in vascular lesions of Pik3caH1047R mutant mice (Extended Data Fig. 12k,l). We next examined whether FOXO1 directly regulates NR2F2. Analysis of published RNA-seq, assay for transposase-accessible chromatin with sequencing (ATAC–seq), FOXO1 chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP–seq) and H3K27ac ChIP–seq datasets from human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) expressing constitutively nuclear, PI3K-resistant FOXO1(A3)34,35 revealed sustained repression of NR2F2 transcripts and protein, reduced chromatin accessibility at the NR2F2 locus and FOXO1 binding to a vein-specific NR2F2 enhancer (Fig. 5g and Extended Data Fig. 12m–v). FOXO1(A3) increased occupancy at this enhancer while reducing H3K27 acetylation and chromatin accessibility, consistent with direct transcriptional repression (Extended Data Fig. 12p).

Industry observers note that conversely, endothelial deletion of Foxo1 markedly increased Nr2f2 transcript and protein levels (Fig. 5h,i). Finally, induction of PIK3CAH1047R in HUVECs increased NR2F2 expression, whereas the PI3K-resistant FOXO1(A3) suppressed this response (Fig. 5j). Together, these findings establish FOXO1 as a transcriptional repressor of NR2F2 and define a PI3K–FOXO1–NR2F2 axis through which oncogenic PIK3CA disrupts arterial differentiation.

According to recent reports, using the vasculature as a model, we show that the consequences of PIK3CAH1047R are dictated by endothelial cell context. Depending on the differentiation state of the affected endothelial cell, the mutation promotes pathological proliferation, remains phenotypically silent or disrupts differentiation (Extended Data Fig. 13). This context-dependent model provides a mechanistic explanation for the marked predominance of capillary and venous lesions, and the rarity of arterial lesions, in PIK3CA-driven vascular disease. More broadly, it may also help to explain why PIK3CA-associated overgrowth preferentially affects mesoderm-derived tissues and suggests that similar principles probably apply to other pathogenic PIK3CA variants, which exhibit comparable lesion distributions in patients3.

Genetic lineage tracing revealed that endothelial cells expressing endogenous Pik3caH1047R persist in mature arteries without eliciting a detectable phenotype. Consistently, embryonic expression of Pik3caH1047R in Tie2+ cells does not give rise to arterial lesions32. This finding is unexpected given the broad endothelial expression of Pik3ca and the prominent role of PI3Kα signalling in all endothelial cells33. However, basal PI3K signalling is comparatively low in arteries and is not increased by endogenous Pik3caH1047R expression. By contrast, forced overexpression, enhances PI3K signalling and induces mild overgrowth in arterial endothelial cells that have not yet completed differentiation, suggesting that these cells require higher signalling levels to mount a pathological response than venous or capillary endothelial cells. Nevertheless, increased PI3K signalling does not induce overgrowth or NR2F2 expression in fully differentiated arteries. Likewise, reducing shear stress or Notch signalling, key pathways in the acquisition and maintenance of arterial identity30,34,35, does not restore responsiveness to Pik3caH1047R. These findings suggest that arterial endothelial cells possess multiple layers of protection that may also underlie their broader resistance to other mutations36. Future studies are needed to determine how microenvironmental cues, including extracellular matrix composition and mural cell interactions, contribute to this resistance.

We also find that PIK3CAH1047R disrupts arterial differentiation at early developmental stages. During angiogenesis, a subset of tip cells acquires a pre-arterial identity by expressing canonical arterial markers (such as CXCR4, UNC5B, HEY1 and DLL4)30,37,38 and migrates retrogradely into nascent arteries to support arterial expansion. Pik3caH1047R disrupts this transition by inducing an early hyperproliferation response followed by Nr2f2 upregulation and loss of arterial identity. Supporting a causal role for NR2F2, Nr2f2 deletion restored the ability of Pik3caH1047R tip cells to contribute to arteries, consistent with previous studies demonstrating that NR2F2 antagonizes pre-arterial specification26. More broadly, our findings align with evidence that PI3K signalling promotes venous specification39,40, suppresses arterial differentiation41 and favours a stemness state42. Similar effects have been reported in other tissues, where PIK3CAH1047R biases ageing oesophageal progenitor cells towards self-renewal and induces dedifferentiation during mammary tumorigenesis14,15. In parallel, we show that proliferation blockade in Pik3caH1047R-expressing pre-arterial cells limits lesion formation, but neither reduces NR2F2 expression nor restores arterial contribution of mutant cells. These findings indicate that impaired arterial differentiation cannot be explained solely by proliferative exclusion43,44. Conversely, NR2F2 depletion did not block lesion growth or endothelial proliferation, despite previous reports implicating NR2F2 in cell cycle regulation25,45. Together, these findings indicate that PIK3CAH1047R-driven endothelial proliferation and the NR2F2-mediated arterial differentiation defect are functionally separable downstream outputs.

Our findings identify a transcriptional mechanism linking PI3K activation to NR2F2 induction. Previous studies revealed that TIE2–PI3K signalling stabilizes NR2F2 protein during venous specification39 and that NR2F2 is elevated in PI3K-driven prostate tumours46. We show that PI3K signalling also promotes NR2F2 transcript and protein expression by inhibiting FOXO1. This is consistent with the established role of FOXO factors as nuclear effectors of PI3K signalling, including in PIK3CA-related vascular malformations47, and with the vascular overgrowth caused by endothelial FOXO1 loss48. Notably, FOXO1 has been reported to promote NR2F2 transcript and protein expression in pancreatic β cells49, whereas our data identify FOXO1 as a direct NR2F2 repressor in endothelial cells. Although the molecular basis of this difference remains to be determined, it is consistent with the context-dependent transcriptional activity of FOXO factors and NR2F2 regulation50,51 and may reflect differences in enhancer use and FOXO1 occupancy. Given that additional transcription factors regulate endothelial NR2F2 expression52,53,54, defining how they cooperate with or compete with FOXO1 will help to explain this context-dependent regulation.

In a recent development, together, our findings show that the pathological consequences of oncogenic PIK3CA activation depend not only on signalling strength but also on developmental state and endothelial identity. Differentiated arterial cells resist pathological overgrowth, whereas pre-arterial cells undergo an NR2F2-mediated differentiation defect alongside increased proliferation. These functionally separable responses help to explain the vessel-type specificity of PIK3CA-driven vascular malformations.

Mice were housed in individually ventilated cages under specific-pathogen-free conditions. All mice were crossed onto the C57BL/6J genetic background. Both male and female pups were used for retinal experiments.

Recent findings suggest that the following mouse strains were used in this study. Pdgfb-creERT2-eGFP (pan-endothelial Cre line)55 mice were provided by M. Fruttiger. Cdh5(PAC)-creERT2 (pan-endothelial Cre line)56, Bmx(PAC)-creERT2 (arterial-endothelial Cre line)57 and Esm1(BAC)-creERT2 (tip-endothelial Cre line)58 mice were obtained from R. Adams. The R26-mTmG59 mice express membrane-targeted Tomato in the absence of Cre activity and this switches to membrane-targeted GFP expression after Cre activation, enabling cell lineage visualization and tracking. Pik3catm1.1Waph/+ mice, which harbour a Cre-inducible H1047R point mutation in the endogenous Pik3ca locus, were provided by W. Phillips60. In this allele, loxPsites flank exon 20, which is replaced after Cre recombination by a downstream version containing a CAT-to-AGG substitution at codon 1047. The two loxPsites are only 419 bp apart, making this region highly recombinogenic. Consistent with this, robust phenotypes are observed even at low doses of 4-OHT19. We occasionally observed vascular overgrowth in regions lacking GFP labelling, suggesting the presence of mutant cells in which the reporter allele had not recombined. Rosa26CAG-LSL-H2B-Cherry/H2B-GFP-2A-HAHuPIK3CAH1047R mice (hereafter iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R) overexpress the human PIK3CAH1047R cDNA along with H2B-eGFP-V5 (details are provided in the next section and Extended Data Fig. 5). The Nr2f2flox/flox mouse line61, provided by S. Y. Tsai, was used for conditional deletion of Nr2f2. The Foxo1flox/flox mouse line62 was used for conditional deletion of Foxo1. A list of all mouse lines and genotyping primer sequences is provided in Supplementary Table 1.

According to recent reports, to induce CreERT2 activity in pups, 4-OHT (Sigma-Aldrich, H7905) was dissolved in ethanol to prepare a 10 mg ml−1 solution. The stock solution was aliquoted and stored at −20 °C. Pups received intragastric injections in volumes adjusted to deliver the doses specified in the figures. To achieve the desired recombination pattern (such as sparse mosaic recombination, efficient recombination or recombination of multiple alleles), the 4-OHT dose was titrated for each CreERT2 line and experimental configuration (Supplementary Table 2).

Recent findings suggest that to inhibit proliferation, pups received palbociclib (70 mg kg−1 in distilled H2O; Selleckchem S1116; intraperitoneal (i.p.), P3–P5) or mitomycin C (10 mg kg−1 in PBS, Sigma-Aldrich, M4287, i.p., P4–P5). To modulate blood flow and inhibit the Notch signalling pathway, pups received captopril (4.125 mg kg−1 in PBS; Sigma-Aldrich, C4042; i.p., P4–P5) or DAPT (100 mg kg−1 in DMSO/peanut oil; Calbiochem, 565770; subcutaneous, P4–P5). DAPT stock (10 mg ml−1) was prepared by dissolving 5 mg in 50 µl DMSO at 40 °C for 10 min and diluting in 450 µl peanut oil. To assess endothelial cell proliferation, pups were injected i.p. with 100 μg of EdU and euthanized 2 h later. EdU incorporated into the retina was detected using the Click-iT EdU Alexa Fluor 594 Imaging Kit (Invitrogen, C10339).

It has been revealed that to generate the iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R (Rosa26CAG-LSL-H2B-Cherry/H2B-GFP-2A-HAHuPIK3CAH1047R) mouse line, we introduced the DNA insert containing the H2B-eGFP-V5-2A-HA-humanPIK3CAH1047R gene by CRISPR–Cas9-mediated homologous-dependent repair, in the previously targeted iChr2-Mosaic mouse embryonic stem (ES) cell line31. To generate the donor construct of interest, we first obtained the HA-huPIK3CAH1047R sequence from the plasmid pBabe-puro-HA-huPIK3CAH1047R (Addgene, 12524) and cloned it into plasmid SO107 (Addgene, 99617)31, which contained the LoxP2-H2B-eGFP-V5-2A cassette. We then inserted the H2B-eGFP-V5-2A-HA-huPIK3CAH1047R cassette into the donor vector JP6 (Addgene, 99627), which contains the hygromycin-resistance gene. This resulted in the generation of the donor vector NA453, containing the complete donor construct of interest (Extended Data Fig. 5). ES cells of the G4 genetic background63 were cultured in standard ES cell medium consisting of DMEM supplemented with GlutaMax (31966-047, Gibco), 15% FBS (tested for germline transmission), 1× non-essential amino acids (Hyclone, SH3023801), 0.1% β-mercaptoethanol (Sigma-Aldrich, M7522), 1× penicillin–streptomycin (Lonza, DE17-602E) and leukaemia inhibitory factor. ES cells were maintained on dishes coated with a feeder layer of mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs). For each nucleofection, 2.5 × 106 ES cells were resuspended in 100 µl nucleofection solution containing 1.5 µg of circular px330 plasmid (NA505), encoding the guide RNA sequence (Guide3, GTTGCCTATGAGAGGCTAGAC), and 3.5 µg circular donor plasmid (NA453) containing the H2B-eGFP-V5-2A-HA-huPIK3CAH1047R sequence and the PGK-hygromycin resistance cassette (Extended Data Fig. 5). After nucleofection, 5 µl or 30 µl of the cell suspension was plated into separate wells on a six-well plate containing MEF feeder layers. Then, 7 days after hygromycin selection, 24 isolated ES cell colonies were picked for cryopreservation and subsequent screening. PCR with the flanking primers identified clones with correct homologous recombination and targeted insertion. After identifying correctly targeted ES cell clones, the functionality of the targeted allele was validated by transient transfection of a Cre-expressing plasmid. Positive clones were expanded and microinjected into C57BL/6J host blastocysts. Chimeric mice with a high degree of agouti coat colour were subsequently bred to achieve germline transmission of the targeted allele.

Sources indicate that mice were euthanized by decapitation, and their eyes were isolated and incubated on ice in 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA; Sigma-Aldrich, 158127) in PBS for 1 h. Retinas were dissected and fixed for an additional 1 h in 4% PFA on ice, washed three times in PBS and incubated overnight at 4 °C in blocking buffer (1% BSA, 3% donkey serum and 0.3% Triton X-100 in PBS) with gentle agitation. For NR2F2 staining, retinas were subjected to antigen retrieval by boiling for 20 min in 0.01 M citrate buffer (pH 6, Sigma-Aldrich, W305600) before permeabilization. Retinas were then incubated overnight at 4 °C with specific primary antibodies diluted in blocking buffer. In iFluMosaic-PIK3CA retinas, the antigen-retrieval step required for NR2F2 staining abolished the GFP signal and prevented detection with anti-GFP antibodies; therefore, the retinas were incubated overnight with anti-GFP antibodies before antigen retrieval. After washing three times in PBST (0.1% Tween-20 in PBS), the retinas were incubated for 30 min at room temperature in PBLEC buffer (1% Triton X-100, 1 mM CaCl2, 1 mM MgCl2 and 1 mM MnCl2 in PBS (pH 6.8)). Secondary Alexa-Fluor-conjugated antibodies or isolectin GS-B4 (IB4) were incubated with retinas in PBLEC buffer for 2 h at room temperature or overnight at 4 °C. After three additional washes with PBST, retinas were flat-mounted onto microscope slides with Mowiol (Calbiochem, 475904), supplemented with the anti-fade reagent DABCO (1.4-diazabicyclo-(2.2.2)octane; Sigma-Aldrich, D27802) or Fluoromount-G (SouthernBiotech, 0100-01). For FOXO1/ERG co-immunostaining, an additional blocking step was included because both primary antibodies were raised in the same species, thereby preventing cross-reactivity. After the incubation with the anti-FOXO1 antibody and its corresponding secondary antibody, retinas were incubated with AffiniPure F(ab′)2 fragments donkey anti-rabbit IgG (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 711-006-152, 1:100) in PBS for 1 h at room temperature. The retinas were then washed, briefly fixed with 4% PFA, blocked again and incubated with the primary Alexa-Fluor-647-conjugated anti-ERG antibody. A list of all of the primary and secondary antibodies is provided in Supplementary Table 3.

According to recent reports, mouse endothelial cells were isolated from the lungs of adult mice (both female and male) aged 3 to 6 weeks. Under sterile conditions, lungs were minced and digested in 4 U ml−1 dispase II (Roche, 04942078001) in Hanks’ balanced salt solution (Gibco, 14170-112) for 1 h at 37 °C with constant agitation. Tissue was further dissociated by pipetting to obtain a single-cell suspension, and digestion was stopped with Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (DMEM; Corning, 10-013-CV) supplemented with 10% FBS (Biowest, S1810-500) and 1% penicillin–streptomycin (Gibco, 15140-122). Cells were resuspended in PBS and incubated for 30 min at room temperature with rat anti-CD144 (Cdh5; BD Biosciences, 55289) antibody-coated magnetic Dynabeads (Invitrogen, 11035). CD144+ cells were washed in PBS containing 0.5% BSA and sorted by magnetic separation. CD144+ cells were plated on 0.5% gelatine-coated 12-well plates (Sigma-Aldrich, G1890) and cultured in complete DMEM/F12 (PromoCell, C-30140) supplemented with 20% FBS, 1% penicillin–streptomycin and two vials of endothelial cell growth supplement/heparin (ECGF/H; PromoCell, C-30120). Once confluent, a second selection with CD144-antibody-coated magnetic Dynabeads was performed for 1 h at room temperature. Cells were trypsinized, magnet-sorted, resuspended in F12 complete medium and cultured in a six-well format. Cells were maintained at 37 °C under a 5% CO2 atmosphere and used for experiments up to passage 5. Primary cells were not tested for mycoplasma contamination. Mouse endothelial cells used in Fig. 5i,j were isolated from Cdh5(PAC)-creERT2Foxo1flox/flox lungs as described previously64.

According to recent reports, to induce CreERT2-mediated recombination in vitro, mouse lung endothelial cells isolated from Cdh5(PAC)-creERT2iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R mice were treated with 5 μM 4-OHT for 6 h, with ethanol-treated cells as controls, and cultured for a further 72 h. Then, 1 day before immunofluorescence analysis, cells were replated at low confluency onto gelatine-coated coverslips in 12-well plates. At 4 h before collection, the culture medium was replaced with starvation medium, after which cells were processed for immunofluorescence. For mouse lung endothelial cells isolated from Pdgfb-creERT2-Pik3caH1047R/+ mice, recombination was induced by treatment with 2 μM 4-OHT for 6 h, with ethanol-treated cells as controls, followed by the indicated experimental conditions before collection for immunoblot or qPCR analysis. For mouse lung endothelial cells isolated from Cdh5(PAC)-creERT2Foxo1flox/flox mice, recombination was induced with 250 nM 4-OHT or vehicle control (DMSO), and cells were analysed 72 h after treatment.

Pooled HUVECs were purchased from Lonza (CC-2519) and cultured in EBM endothelial cell growth basal medium (EBM, Lonza, CC-3121) supplemented with EGM endothelial cell growth medium SingleQuots kit (Lonza, CC-4133) and 10% FBS (Life Technologies). Human embryonic kidney (HEK293FT) cells were used to produce lentiviruses and purchased from Life Technologies (R70007). HEK293FT cells were cultured in DMEM (Gibco, 31966-021) supplemented with 10% FBS (Life Technologies) and gentamicin (500 µg ml−1, Lonza, 17-518L). Cells were purchased from commercial suppliers, visually inspected for expected morphology and used for a limited number of passages. No further authentication was performed in-house. All cells were tested negative for mycoplasma and maintained at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere with 5% CO2.

Industry observers note that for doxycycline-inducible lentiviral expression of PIK3CAH1047R, a V5-PIK3CAH1047R-encoding cDNA was cloned into the pLVX-TetOne-Puro vector (Takara, 631847). For CRISPR–Cas9-mediated genome editing, gene-specific gRNA sequences (Supplementary Table 4) were cloned into a plentiCRISPRv2 plasmid co-expressing Flag-tagged Cas9 nuclease and a puromycin-selection marker (Addgene, 52961). Lentivirus production was performed by co-transfection of HEK293FT cells with pMD2.G (Addgene, 12259), psPAX2 (Addgene, 12260) and transfer plasmids. Transfections were performed using the Lipofectamine 2000 transfection reagent (Life Technologies, 11668027) as previously described65. Viruses were collected 48 and 72 h after transfection and filtered through a 0.45-μm filter. HUVECs were transduced with lentiviruses for 16 h in the presence of 8 μg ml−1 polybrene (Santa Cruz, sc-134220) and selected with 1 μg ml−1 puromycin (InvivoGen, ant-pr-1). Lentiviral expression of PIK3CAH1047R was induced by stimulating HUVECs with 600 ng ml−1 doxycycline (Sigma-Aldrich, D9891) for 72 h.

Subconfluent HUVECs were transduced with custom-made adenoviruses (Vector Biolabs) to overexpress constitutively nuclear human FOXO1 (FOXO1A3-Flag) or control (CMV-null) adenoviruses (Vector Biolabs, 1300). For adenoviral transductions, HUVECs were incubated in EBM medium (Lonza, CC-3121) containing 0.1% (v/v) BSA (Sigma-Aldrich, 1595) for 4 h and transduced with the respective viruses for an additional 4 h in the presence of 8 µg ml−1 polybrene (Santa Cruz, sc-134220). HUVECs were then washed five times with Hank’s balanced salt solution (Gibco, 14175095) and cultured for the indicated times in EBM basal medium supplemented with 10% FBS and EGM SingleQuots.

Gene-specific gRNA sequences to target the NR2F2-1345 enhancer were designed using CHOPCHOP66. For each target gene, we used three independent gRNAs and co-transfected them with packaging vectors for lentivirus production. After transduction, puromycin was used to select a pool of CRISPR–Cas9-mediated mutant HUVECs. The knockout efficiency was confirmed by PCR analysis of gDNA isolated from transduced cells. Single guide RNA sequences and genotyping primers are provided in Supplementary Table 4.

Cells were washed with warm 1% PBS containing Mg2+ and Ca2+ (Gibco, 14080-055), fixed for 15 min in 4% PFA and washed again with warm PBS. For staining, cells were permeabilized for 5 min with 0.4% Triton X-100 in PBS, followed by a 1 h incubation in blocking buffer (2% BSA in PBS). After washing with PBS, cells were incubated for 1 h at room temperature with primary antibodies diluted in blocking buffer. Subsequently, secondary AlexaFluor-conjugated antibodies were diluted in blocking buffer and added to the cells for a 1 h incubation at room temperature. After additional washes with PBS, cells were incubated with DAPI (Invitrogen, D1305; 1:500) for 1 min and then mounted on microscope slides with Fluoromount-G (Southern Biotech, 0100-01). A list of all of the antibodies is provided in Supplementary Table 3.

Recent findings suggest that human endothelial cells were isolated from patient biopsies of vascular malformations. These biopsies were obtained during therapeutic surgical resection, with informed consent and approval from the Biomedical Committees at Hospital Sant Joan de Déu, Hospital Santa Creu i Sant Pau, Hospital Universitari de Bellvitge and Hospital Universitario Germans Trias i Pujol (codes PR264/16, PIC-96-16 and PI-21-171). Experiments adhered to the WMA Declaration of Helsinki and the Belmont Report. Data were stored in a secure database maintained by Hospital Sant Joan de Deu. Biopsies were homogenized and digested in dispase II (Roche, 04942078001) and collagenase A (Roche Diagnostics, 10103586001) for up to 1.5 h at 37 °C, with continuous movement. The tissue was dissociated by pipetting into a single-cell solution, then inactivated with DMEM (10% FBS, 1% penicillin–streptomycin). Cells were resuspended in 0.5% BSA in PBS and incubated with CD31-antibody-coated (Agilent Dako, M0823, JC70A) magnetic beads (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 11041) for 1 h at room temperature. The CD31+ fraction was magnetically sorted, resuspended and cultured in 0.5% gelatine-coated wells in EGM2 medium (PromoCell, C-39211) supplemented with 10% FBS, 1% penicillin–streptomycin (EGM2 complete) at 37 °C and 5% CO2 until confluency. Cells were then subjected to a second CD31-based magnetic selection. Mycoplasma testing was not performed on primary cells. To validate the presence of the mutation in isolated endothelial cells, genomic DNA was extracted according to the manufacturer’s protocol (Thermo Fisher Scientific, K182001) and detected by next-generation sequencing. For the vascular malformation (VM) 64, we obtained from 1,572 reads, c.3140A>G (H1047R) with a 45.86% variant allelic frequency and for the VM90 from 461 reads, c.2740A>G (E545G) with 48.37% variant allelic frequency.

Cells were lysed in ice-cold lysis buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.4), 5 mM EDTA, 150 mM NaCl and 1% Triton X-100, supplemented with protease (Roche, 11836153001) and phosphatase (Sigma-Aldrich, 4906837001) inhibitors. The protein concentration was measured using the Pierce BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 23225) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Total cell lysates were resolved on 10% SDS–polyacrylamide gels using a Mini-Protean Tetra Vertical Electrophoresis Cell (Bio-Rad, 1658004) and subsequently transferred onto nitrocellulose membranes using a Mini Trans-Blotcell system (Bio-Rad, 1703930). Membranes were blocked with 5% milk in TBST (TBS containing 0.1% Tween-20) and incubated with appropriate primary antibodies diluted in 2% BSA in TBST. Secondary antibodies were diluted in 5% milk in TBST. Immunoblots were visualized using ECL (0.1 M Tris-HCl, pH 9.35, 2.2 mM luminol, 2.2 mM p-coumaric acid and 0.06% H2O2). Western blots shown in Fig. 5i,j and Extended Data Fig. 12o,s were performed as described previously65. Information on all antibodies is provided in Supplementary Table 3. Uncropped western blot images are provided in Supplementary Fig. 2.

RNA was extracted using the Maxwell RSC SimplyRNA Cells Kit (Promega, AS1390) according to the manufacturer’s instructions and RNA quality was assessed using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer. Reverse transcription was performed using 500 ng of RNA from cell lysate samples with the High-Capacity cDNA Reverse Transcription Kit (Applied Biosystems, 4368814). qPCR was performed using a QuantStudio 7 Flex system with SYBR Green real-time PCR master mix (Applied Biosystems, A46110). RNA isolation, cDNA synthesis and qPCR for Fig. 5h and Extended Data Fig. 12n,r,u were performed as previously described65. Primer sequences and TaqMan assay IDs are provided in Supplementary Table 4.

To inhibit PI3Kα activity, mouse lung endothelial cells isolated from Pdgfb-creERT2Pik3caH1047R/+ mice were treated with ethanol or 4-OHT for 6 h, followed by vehicle or the PI3Kα-selective inhibitor alpelisib (BYL719; at 1 or 5 µM) for an additional 66 h. Patient-derived endothelial cells isolated from venous malformations were treated with vehicle or BYL719 (1 µM or 5 µM) for 72 h before downstream analysis. To inhibit proliferation in vitro, mouse lung endothelial cells isolated from Pdgfb-creERT2Pik3caH1047R/+ mice were cultured for 24 h in DMEM/F12 supplemented with reduced growth factors (10% FBS, 1% penicillin–streptomycin and endothelial cell growth supplement/heparin (ECGF/H)) to limit baseline proliferation and achieve approximately 40% confluency. Cells were then treated with palbociclib (2 μM) or vehicle (PBS), followed 6 h later by the addition of 4-OHT (2 μM) or ethanol while maintaining palbociclib treatment. Cells were collected 24 h after 4-OHT treatment for western blot, qPCR analysis and flow cytometry.

For EdU incorporation assays, EdU (10 μM) was added 2 h before collection. Cells were processed using the Click-iT EdU Alexa Fluor 647 Flow Cytometry Assay Kit (Invitrogen, C10634) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Data were acquired on a BD FACSymphony A1 cell analyser and analysed using FlowJo (v.10.1, BD Biosciences). Cells were gated based on forward and side scatter to exclude debris and doublets before analysis as illustrated in Supplementary Fig. 3.

Recent findings suggest that imaging was performed with Leica Stellaris 8, Leica TCS SP5, Zeiss LSM 980 and Zeiss LSM900 confocal microscopes, operated with LAS X v.4.8.2, LAS AF v.2.7 and Zen v.3.9 software, respectively. Adobe Photoshop (v.25.12.0), Adobe Illustrator (64-bit, v.29.0.1), ImageJ v.1.54b, CellProfiler v.4.2.6 and Imaris v.10.1 were used for image processing and quantification. All images shown in the figures are maximum intensity projections. Images were taken from at least three retinal areas in each retina and are representative of at least four retinas analysed for each genotype unless otherwise stated. The identification of retinal vascular lesions and their locations was performed by observing IB4 in ×10 images. Vascular malformations were defined based on abnormal vessel morphology and GFP+ clonal expansion. In capillary beds, lesions were identified as focal regions displaying abnormal vessel enlargement compared with the surrounding capillary plexus and associated clusters of GFP+ endothelial cells. In veins and arteries, malformations were defined by the presence of GFP+ endothelial cell clusters indicative of clonal expansion, together with abnormal vessel enlargement compared with control vessels. Retinal vascularity was measured using the IB4 channel by adjusting the threshold to select IB4+, followed by quantification of the percentage of IB4+ area relative to the total retinal surface. Vessel width was determined by measuring the average diameter at three different points along each vessel. GFP+ cell expansion was quantified by calculating the percentage of GFP+ area within the IB4+ area. For capillary analysis, images containing only capillary beds were used. To quantify GFP+ cells in veins and arteries, IB4 staining was used to delineate the vascular area, and vessel-specific regions of interest (ROIs) corresponding to arteries or veins were manually selected. For quantification of aEC-GFP+ endothelial cells, the analysed area was defined by a fixed ROI (200 × 550 μm (P6 retinas), 200 × 630 μm (P9 retinas) and 500 × 1,200 μm (P12 retinas)) to maintain consistent arterial length across replicates and to avoid including other vascular types. In P21 retinas, aEC-GFP+ cells were spread across various vessel types, so the ROI for quantification included the entire vascular plexus. To quantify vascular p-S6 intensity, a manual threshold was set to obtain the GFP+ area and define the ROI. The integrated density of p-S6 was then measured within the GFP+ area. In iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R mice, p-S6 integrated density was quantified separately in Cherry+ (WT) or eGFP+ (PIK3CAH1047R) cells after manual delineation of IB4+ areas containing each recombinant cell population. In both cases, the background signal (mean grey values) was measured in adjacent IB4-negative regions. The corrected total fluorescence (CTF) was calculated using the following equation: CTF = integrated density – (vascular area × mean grey background value). αSMA, CX37 and UNC5B expression in endothelial cells was quantified by measuring the mean intensity within GFP+ areas. Endothelial cell proliferation was quantified as the percentage of ERG+ endothelial cell nuclei co-immunostained positive for Ki-67 or EdU relative to the total number of ERG+ nuclei within the GFP+ area. In the iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R model, proliferation was quantified separately for Cherry+ and eGFP+ nuclei as the percentage of Ki-67+ nuclei relative to the total number of Cherry+ or eGFP+ nuclei, respectively. Nuclear FOXO1 positivity was quantified as the percentage of FOXO1+ERG+ nuclei relative to the total number of ERG+ nuclei within the GFP+ area. NR2F2 levels were assessed by manual scoring of nuclear immunofluorescence intensity in ERG+ endothelial cells. Endothelial nuclei with strong and unequivocal nuclear signal were classified as NR2F2high, nuclei with weak but discernible nuclear signal as NR2F2low and nuclei lacking detectable nuclear signal were classified as NR2F2negative, including after a substantial increase in display intensity during image visualization. Scoring was performed using identical acquisition settings across samples. Quantification of Cherry+ and eGFP+ endothelial cells in iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R retinas was performed manually, differentiating their presence in capillaries, veins and arteries. Vascular lesions were classified based on size as small (<10 PIK3CAH1047R cells), medium (between 10 and 35 PIK3CAH1047R cells) or large (>35 PIK3CAH1047R cells) based on manual counting of PIK3CAH1047R mutant cells. The incidence of arteries populated with PIK3CAH1047R cells was determined as a percentage in relation to the total number of arteries containing any recombinant cell. The relative arterial vessel width in iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R retinas was assessed by comparing vessel diameter in a central region containing recombinant cells with adjacent regions of the same vessel lacking recombinant cells.

In a recent development, in cultured endothelial cells, maximum-intensity projections of confocal images were analysed using CellProfiler (v.4.2.6). DAPI, eGFP, Cherry and Ki-67 signals were defined as primary objects. Nuclei were identified based on DAPI staining and used to generate secondary objects for p-S6 quantification. CellProfiler assigned p-S6 intensity to individual nuclei and classified cells as p-S6+ or p-S6−. WT and PIK3CAH1047R endothelial cells were quantified by identifying Cherry+DAPI+ and eGFP+DAPI+ cells, respectively.

Recent findings suggest that FOXO1-bound Nr2f2 enhancer identification was performed according an approach described previously67. In brief, enhancer marks from three published datasets were used to identify putative enhancers: (1) open chromatin as assessed by ATAC–seq in mouse P6 retina endothelial cells (MRECs)68; (2) enriched EP300 binding in Tie2-cre+ cells from embryonic day 11.5 mouse embryos69; and (3) binding of the ETS factor ERG, which marks all known endothelial cell enhancers, in HUVECs70. Putative enhancer regions were then assessed for FOXO1(A3) binding47,65, identifying the FOXO1-bound NR2F2-1345 enhancer. For in vivo validation, the NR2F2-1345 enhancer sequence was cloned into the E1b-GFP-Tol2-Gateway vector71 using the Gene Synthesis service from Genewiz (part of Azenta Life Sciences). F0 mosaic transgenic zebrafish embryos were generated using Tol2-mediated integration72. All animal procedures were approved by a local ethical review committee at Oxford University, licensed by the UK Home Office and conducted in accordance with ARRIVE guidelines. All zebrafish (KLC strain) were maintained in groups. Embryos were maintained in E3 medium (5 mM NaCl, 0.17 mM KCl, 0.33 mM CaCl2, 0.33 mM MgSO4) at 28.5 °C. To image, all embryos were dechorionated and anaesthetized with 0.01% tricaine methanesulfonate in E3 medium. For analysis of transgenic zebrafish, single embryos were transferred into a flat-bottom 96-well plate, mounted in 0.1% TopVision low-melting-point agarose (Thermo Fisher Scientific, R0801) in E3 medium with tricaine methanesulfonate (Merck, A5040). GFP reporter gene expression was screened with a Zeiss LSM 980 (Carl Zeiss) confocal microscope at 32–72 h post-fertilization. Whole zebrafish were imaged using the ‘tile scan’ command, combined with z-stack collection, at 488 nm excitation and 510 nm emission for eGFP.

Sources indicate that to target tip endothelial cells, recombination was induced with 25 mg kg−1 4-OHT at P1 and P2 in Esm1(BAC)-creERT2R26-mTmG (control) and Esm1(BAC)-creERT2R26-mTmG;Pik3caH1047R (mutant) mice. Retinas were collected at P6 and processed fresh for enzymatic dissociation using the Neural Tissue Dissociation Kit (P) (Miltenyi Biotec, 130-092-628). After dissociation, the cell suspension was incubated with CD31 MicroBeads (Miltenyi Biotec, 130-097-418) and subjected to two consecutive rounds of magnetic separation using MS columns (Miltenyi Biotec, 130-042-201) and an OctoMACS Separator (Miltenyi Biotec, 130-042-109). Cells were resuspended in 0.04% BSA in PBS and processed for scRNA-seq using the 10x Genomics platform. Two independent experiments were performed on separate days using independent cohorts of control and mutant mice, with retinas pooled per genotype (Exp1: n = 5 control, n = 3 mutant; Exp2: n = 4 control, n = 4 mutant).

In a recent development, mouse lung endothelial cells isolated from Pdgfb-creERT2Pik3caH1047R/+ mice were treated in vitro overnight with 2 μM 4-OHT to induce recombination and expression of Pik3caH1047R, while ethanol-treated cells were used as a control (WT cells for Pik3ca). The medium was then changed to F12 complete, and cells were collected 48 h post-induction. Cells were detached with trypsin, centrifuged, subjected to debris removal (Miltenyi Biotec, 130-109-398) and finally resuspended in 0.04% BSA in PBS. For the scRNA-seq, three independent biological replicates were pooled for each treatment condition.

Single cells were encapsulated into emulsion droplets using the Chromium Controller (10x Genomics) with the 3′ Next GEM kit (v3 chemistry) or the Chromium GEM-X Single Cell 3′ Kit v4 for in vitro and in vivo samples, respectively. Libraries were prepared according to the manufacturer’s protocol, targeting a recovery of around 10,000 cells per sample. Sequencing was performed on the Illumina NovaSeq X 25B platform using 2 × 150 bp paired-end reads. Raw sequencing data were processed using Cell Ranger (v.7.0.1 or v.8.0.1) and aligned to the mouse reference genome (mm10) using the default parameters. For the in vivo datasets, raw UMI count matrices were corrected for ambient RNA contamination using CellBender (v.0.2.1)73. This approach models background RNA from empty droplets and infers corrected expression counts for cell-containing droplets using a probabilistic framework. Corrected matrices were used for downstream analyses.

According to recent reports, all scRNA-seq datasets (in vivo and in vitro) were processed using a unified analytical pipeline in R (v.4.2.2) with the Seurat package (v.4.9.9)74. CellBender output count matrices were imported using a custom function designed to read H5AD files in R. Each sample was initially processed independently. tEC-GFP and tEC-Pik3caH1047R samples were initially analysed separately to prevent the pronounced transcriptional changes associated with the mutation from dominating the global data structure and obscuring the physiological organization of the tEC-GFP retina. After independent quality control, dimensionality reduction and clustering, endothelial cells were identified within each genotype based on canonical marker expression. The endothelial subsets from tEC-GFP and tEC-Pik3caH1047R samples were subsequently combined and jointly reanalysed to enable direct comparison of endothelial states across genotypes while retaining an accurate representation of the WT retinal vasculature. Within each condition, control filtering was applied to remove low-quality cells and uninformative genes. Cells were excluded if they contained fewer than 250 detected genes, more than 20% mitochondrial transcripts or exhibited a complexity index greater than 0.8. Genes with zero counts across all cells were removed. Potential doublets were estimated using DoubletFinder (v.2.0.3) on a per-sample basis75. Although doublets were not removed from the dataset, they were excluded from downstream differential expression analyses. Data normalization was performed using Seurat’s NormaliseData function with the LogNormalise method and a scale factor of 10,000. Highly variable genes (HVGs) were defined based on the distribution of non-zero gene expression counts, selecting a threshold corresponding to the third quartile plus 100 genes. Data were then scaled using ScaleData, and then a principal component analysis (PCA) was performed using RunPCA. To correct for batch effects across biological replicates, datasets were integrated using the Harmony algorithm (v.1.2.3)76, applied to PCA embeddings. The sample identity (ID) was used as the batch variable, enabling alignment of cells across replicates while preserving biological variability. Harmony-corrected principal components were used for downstream analyses. Graph-based clustering was performed by constructing a shared-nearest-neighbour graph using FindNeighbours, followed by community detection with the Louvain algorithm implemented in FindClusters. To specifically analyse the vascular compartment, endothelial cells were identified based on canonical marker expression (Pecam1 and Cdh5) and computationally subsetted. A secondary, endothelial-focused analysis pipeline was then applied, including re-identification of highly variable features, normalization, scaling, PCA and Harmony integration76. Multiple clustering resolutions (0.1, 0.3 and 0.5) were evaluated, with a resolution of 0.3 selected as it best recapitulated known endothelial cell subpopulations (for example, tip, arterial, venous and proliferative endothelial cells). Cluster annotation was performed using a one-versus-all differential expression approach with Seurat’s FindAllMarkers function, applying the Wilcoxon rank-sum test and Bonferroni correction for multiple testing.

It has been revealed that in the in vivo retinal endothelial cell dataset, GFP expression was used to identify recombined endothelial cells. To enable GFP quantification, the GFP coding sequence was appended to the standard mouse reference genome (mm10), and raw sequencing reads were aligned against this modified reference using 10x Genomics Cell Ranger v.8.0.1. This allowed simultaneous quantification of endogenous transcripts and GFP expression. To identify GFP-expressing cells, GFP transcript levels were examined across the dataset. Density plots of log-normalized GFP expression revealed a bimodal distribution, which enabled the application of a stringer classification threshold (log-normalized expression > 1.5). Cells with log-normalized GFP expression of greater than 1.5 were classified as GFP+, whereas cells with expression at or below this threshold were classified as GFP−.

It has been revealed that differential expression analysis was performed by comparing mutant (GFP+ Pik3caH1047R) and WT (GFP+ WT) cells within defined endothelial cell populations using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test implemented in Seurat (FindMarkers). To enhance robustness and account for sparsity inherent to single-cell data, a complementary pseudobulk approach was applied. Raw counts were aggregated at the sample level (grouped by ID and phenotype) using AggregateExpression, treating each mouse as an independent biological replicate. The resulting count matrix was analysed using DESeq2 (v.1.38.3)77, applying a generalized linear model based on the negative binomial distribution. Concordance between single-cell and pseudobulk approaches was assessed by correlating log2[FC] values across clusters and evaluating overlap of significantly regulated genes (adjusted P < 0.05). A high level of agreement in both magnitude and direction of gene regulation was observed. Based on this consistency, Wilcoxon-derived results were used for downstream visualization and functional analyses due to their higher sensitivity, while pseudobulk results served as an independent validation of biological signal.

Recent findings suggest that average expression profiles were calculated for each endothelial population using Seurat’s AverageExpression function and HVG. The 1,500 most variable genes were scaled by gene and hierarchically clustered using Pearson correlation distance and average linkage. Analyses included either all endothelial cells from tEC-GFP retinas, irrespective of GFP status, or only traced GFP+ endothelial cells from tEC-GFP and tEC-Pik3caH1047R retinas. In the latter, populations were additionally stratified by genotype. Heat maps were generated using ComplexHeatmap (v.2.15.4).

To control for potential biases from unequal cell numbers between conditions (GFP+ Pik3caH1047R versus GFP+ WT), we implemented a bootstrapped downsampling strategy. For each endothelial cell subtype, 1,000 iterations of random subsampling were performed. In each iteration, the condition with more cells was downsampled to match the size of the smaller group, thereby generating balanced datasets. Differential expression was recalculated in each iteration using the Wilcoxon test (FindMarkers, with logfc.threshold = 0 and min.pct = 0). For each gene, the frequency of significance (adjusted P < 0.05) and the consistency of log2[FC] direction were recorded across iterations. This approach confirmed that the identified transcriptional signatures were stable and reproducible, supporting their interpretation as robust biological features of the mutant phenotype rather than artefacts driven by differences in cell numbers.

The expression of Nr2f2 and proliferation scores across GFP+ WT and GFP+ Pik3caH1047R endothelial cells were estimated. Cell cycle and proliferation scores (the sum of S and G2/M phases) were computed using ccAFv278. Biological thresholds were established: the Nr2f2 threshold was set at the 99th percentile of reference WT arterial and artery capillary cells, and proliferation status used a cut-off of 0.1. Cells were categorized into Nr2f2 status, proliferation status and a joint status (double high, Nr2f2 high, proliferation high or low/basal).

It has been revealed that RNA velocity was inferred with scVelo in GFP+ endothelial cells and further analysed using CellRank v.2. GFP+ WT and GFP+ Pik3caH1047R cells were analysed independently using identical parameters. For each genotype, 2,000 highly variable genes were selected, and genotype-specific neighbourhood graphs and expression moments were calculated using 30 principal components and 15 neighbours. Transcriptional dynamics and velocities were estimated using the dynamical model. CellRank was subsequently used to construct a velocity-based transition matrix using the VelocityKernel and to identify macrostates using GPCCA. Velocity vectors were projected onto the shared integrated UMAP and visualized as streamlines and cell-level arrows.

It has been revealed that statistical analysis was performed using Prism 10 (GraphPad). Data are presented as the mean ± s.e.m. For in vivo experiments, each retina was considered an independent experimental unit. At least three mice from at least two independent litters were used per condition, except for in Extended Data Fig. 11i (n = 2). For the iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R model, only retinas containing identified recombined cells were included. Experiments using mouse endothelial cells included biological replicates, whereas those using human endothelial cells were performed as independent experimental repeats. Sample sizes are indicated in the figure legends. Statistical significance between two groups was assessed using either an unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-tests or the two-tailed Mann–Whitney U-tests. For comparisons involving more than two groups, one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s test or two-way ANOVA with Šídák’s test was used. No statistical method was used to predetermine sample sizes; sample sizes were based on previous experiments. Reproducibility was confirmed through multiple independent experiments. The experiments were not randomized, and the investigators were not blinded during the experiments or data analysis.

Sources indicate that a, Details of construct generation are provided in Methods. PGK-hygro-pA, resistance marker for selection; WPRE-pA, viral sequence that enhances transgene expression by promoting mRNA stability and nuclear export; CAG, strong and ubiquitous promoter; PGK-Neo-pA, resistance marker for ES cell selection; 2 A, viral peptide enabling equimolar expression of multiple proteins from a single open reading frame (ORF); HA, V5, and His, epitope tags for antibody detection; H2B, histone tag targeting proteins to chromatin; N-PhiM, non-fluorescent protein that is used as a reporter of promoter expression; INS, insulator sequence that prevents inappropriate enhancer-promoter interactions. b, Schematic illustrating the mouse strategy combining the pan-EC (pEC) tamoxifen-inducible Cre allele (Cdh5(PAC)-creERT2) with the iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R allele. c, Mouse lung ECs isolated from pEC-iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R mice were treated with 4-OHT for 6 h, expanded for 72 h and then replated. Samples were collected at 24, 48 and 72 h after replating, following 4 h of serum starvation immediately before each collection. d,e, Confocal images of primary mouse lung endothelial cells (ECs) isolated from pEC-iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R mice collected at 24, 48, and 72 h after seeding. Cells were stained with DAPI (blue, nuclei) and for eGFP (yellow, PIK3CAH1047R-expressing ECs), Cherry (cyan, wild-type ECs for Pik3ca), and Ki-67 (magenta, proliferating cells) (d) or and p-S6 (Ser235/236, grey) (e). f, Percentage of Cherry+ (cyan) and eGFP+ (yellow) cells among total Cherry+ and eGFP+ cells at 24, 48 and 72 h post-seeding (n = 6 biological replicates). g,h, Quantification of Ki-67+ cells (g) and p-S6 (Ser235/236) fluorescence intensity (h) within Cherry+ (cyan) and eGFP+ (yellow) cell populations at 24, 48, and 72 h after seeding (n = 6 biological replicates). Data are mean ± SEM. Two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple comparisons test (f–h). Scale bars, 200 μm (d,e).

According to recent reports, a, Experimental timeline for studies using the tEC-iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R model. b, Pie chart showing lesion categories, defined by the number of EGFP-PIK3CAH1047R-expressing endothelial cells per lesion in P8 tEC-iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R retinas (n = 14 retinas). c,d, Confocal images of P8 tEC-iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R retinas stained for IB4 (magenta), Cherry (cyan), eGFP (yellow), and Ki-67 (c, red/grey) or p-S6 (Ser235/236) (d, grey). e, Confocal images of an arterial lesion (top) and capillary regions (bottom) in P8 tEC-iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R retinas, stained for IB4 (magenta), Cherry (cyan), eGFP (yellow) and ERG (blue). Wrexham vs Portsmouth - prediction, team news, lineups

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (736 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Ben Sully | 26 Nov 2026 15:22.
  • Wrexham will look to extend their four-game unbeaten run when they welcome Portsmouth to the Racecourse Ground for Saturday’s Championship encounter.
  • Pompey, meanwhile, will be eyeing a second straight win after getting the better of West Ham United in midweek.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ben Sully | 26 Nov 2026 15:22.

Wrexham will look to extend their four-game unbeaten run when they welcome Portsmouth to the Racecourse Ground for Saturday’s Championship encounter.

Pompey, meanwhile, will be eyeing a second straight win after getting the better of West Ham United in midweek.

After overseeing just three wins in the first 13 league games, Wrexham boss Phil Parkinson has eased some of the pressure that was building on his shoulders with a four-game unbeaten run.

Wrexham went into the international window on the back of a 2-0 win over Middlesbrough and a 1-1 draw against Wolverhampton Wanderers, before they returned to action with a narrow 1-0 victory over Lincoln City at Sincil Bank.

They then took the lead in Tuesday’s away clash with Bristol City, but were ultimately forced to settle for a point after Joe Worrall saw his opener cancelled out by Cam Pring’s equaliser, leaving Wrexham in 14th spot in the Championship table and five points adrift of the top eight.

After playing back-to-back away games, Wrexham will be looking forward to returning to the familiar surroundings of the Racecourse Ground, where they have taken seven points from their last three outings since losing to West Bromwich Albion last month.

Wrexham are also one of six teams to score in every Championship home match this term, extending their overall run to at least one goal in each of their last 15 home league games since drawing a blank in a 2-0 loss to Millwall over seven months ago.

In fact, that scoring run includes a 2-1 victory in their recent meeting with Portsmouth in February, which came courtesy of first-half goals from Sam Smith and Max Cleworth.

Portsmouth, meanwhile, are just two points adrift of the playoffs after winning five, drawing three and losing just one of their last nine matches.

After losing to Stoke City before the international window, Pompey resumed their campaign with a hard-fought away draw against Bolton Wanderers before they claimed a 1-0 win in their first home meeting with West Ham United in 14 years.

Odin Bailey’s maiden Portsmouth goal proved enough to secure the club’s first head-to-head victory since a 1-0 success at Upton Park in April 2008, while also keeping their first home clean sheet since the start of September.

John Mousinho’s side will now head on their travels with hopes of extending their four-game unbeaten away run, which started with a 1-0 win over Norwich City and continued with three consecutive draws on the road.

No Championship team has conceded fewer away goals than Portsmouth, whose defence has been breached just six times in their eight road trips this season.

Given the fact they only took a point from their two meetings with Wrexham last term, Pompey will head into Saturday's fixture with hopes of claiming their first head-to-head league win since recording a 2-0 away victory in January 1983.

Wrexham forward Sam Smith will miss the remainder of the season after sustaining an anterior cruciate ligament injury earlier this month.

The hosts are also likely to be without the services of Liberato Cacace, Seb Revan, Josh Windass, Callum O’Hare and Nathan Broadhead.

Ollie Rathbone and Kieffer Moore are pushing for starting berths, the latter of whom is Wrexham’s top scorer with five Championship goals to his name this term.

Jayden Meghoma will be out for up to 10 weeks after sustaining an ankle ligament injury in last weekend’s draw against Bolton.

Meghoma is the latest addition to a lengthy injury list that features Keshi Anderson, Luke Brooke-Smith, Marko Milovanovic, Colby Bishop, John Swift, Mark Kosznovszky, Connor Ogilvie and Benjamin Arthur.

Marlon Pack, Josh Murphy and Adrian Segecic are options to start if Mousinho decides to freshen up his side for Saturday’s away trip.

Wrexham possible starting lineup:.

Patterson; Cleworth, Worrall, Doyle; Kabore, Dobson, Whiteman, Ekomie; O’Brien, Rathbone; Moore.

Portsmouth possible starting lineup:.

Schmid; Devlin, Poole, Dia, Swanson; Pack, Mohamed; Segecic, Bailey, Murphy; Shade.

Portsmouth have conceded more than one goal in just one of their eight away league games this term, and with that in mind, we think they will do enough to avoid defeat in Saturday's fixture.

However, we believe they will fall short of claiming maximum points against a Wrexham side that are unbeaten in four games.

Tech Report: Roma draw 2-2 at PSG as Malen’s late penalty adds to Juventus’ December challenge

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (493 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Juvefc

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Roma came from behind to draw 2-2 with holders Paris Saint-Germain, with substitute Donyell Malen scoring a 78th-minute penalty.
  • Roma left the Parc des Princes with a point and with their reputation enhanced.
  • It has been revealed that in Europe, Malen’s spot-kick was his fifth goal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Roma came from behind to draw 2-2 with holders Paris Saint-Germain, with substitute Donyell Malen scoring a 78th-minute penalty. The leaders' rivals above Juventus indicated the depth of their squad less than a month before they host Spalletti's side.

Roma left the Parc des Princes with a point and with their reputation enhanced. Mario Hermoso gave them the lead against the European champions. Paris Saint-Germain turned the game around through an Illia Zabarnyi header and an Ousmane Dembélé penalty.

It has been revealed that in Europe, Malen’s spot-kick was his fifth goal. Across all competitions, it marked his 17th strike of the campaign, from 16 appearances. It came days after he scored four times in Roma’s 5-1 win at Parma. Yet he did not start in Paris, and neither did Paulo Dybala. Gian Piero Gasperini mentioned he left Malen out because of the number of games he had played for Roma and the Netherlands.

According to recent reports, that a reshuffled Roma could take a point in Paris indicates plenty about their squad. Luis Enrique’s side had not dropped points since a home defeat to Monaco on 4 September.

The result does not fix Roma’s European position. The club lists the game as Matchday 5 of the league phase. Roma have one win, two draws and two defeats so far. Under the format, clubs finishing 9th to 24th enter the play-offs, while 25th to 36th are knocked out. The top eight go straight into the round of 16.

Recent findings suggest that that leaves Roma with work to do in a crowded December. Their next Champions League match is at home to Sporting CP on 8 December, kicking off at 21:00. They then travel to AEK Athens on 19 January and host Lille on 27 January 2027.

Domestically, Roma’s form has been strong. Their league record highlights nine wins and three draws, with 36 goals scored and 11 conceded, Corriere dello Sport reported.

In a recent development, for Spalletti’s side, the schedule offers some contrast. After that European fixture, Roma play the derby away to Lazio on Sunday 13 December at 12:30. That leaves them six days between the derby and the visit of Juventus. Before travelling to Rome, Juventus are away to Como on 29 November. Udinese and Monza then come to Turin in Serie A, on 6 December and 14 December respectively.

Recent findings suggest that whether Roma’s European commitments take a toll remains to be seen. The evidence from Paris suggests Gasperini can rotate without a sharp drop in quality. Malen’s form, from the bench or from the start, will be a central concern for Juventus.

The two sides meet in round 16 of Serie A on Saturday 19 December 2026, with kick-off at 20:45.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that as the Argentine coach approaches the Red Devils bench, a statement made a few months earlier resurfaces in England.
  • This discussion notably referred to previous missed opportunities between Mauricio Pochettino and Manchester United.
  • Manu Tournoux is a passionate and knowledgeable football enthusiast with a special focus on French football.

It has been revealed that as the Argentine coach approaches the Red Devils bench, a statement made a few months earlier resurfaces in England. According to The Standardthe current coach of the United States would have reached a verbal agreement with the Mancunian leaders to succeed Michael Carrick. A situation which today gives particular resonance to an exchange that occurred during the 2026 World Cup. Questioned by journalists, Pochettino had joked with his faithful deputy Jesús Pérez about a possible arrival at Old Trafford. “ One day, your dream team will come true! You will go to Manchester United », he told her. His colleague immediately replied: “ United should have signed you! » Amused by this response, the former PSG coach then concluded by repeating: “ in the future, in the future! » A joke which should therefore become reality a few months later, while Manchester United now seem decided to entrust him with control of their first team.

This discussion notably referred to previous missed opportunities between Mauricio Pochettino and Manchester United. The Argentine technician had already been a candidate for the position in 2018 then in 2022, without managing to convince Mancunian leaders to entrust him with the project. Since then, the former Tottenham and Chelsea manager has never completely closed the door on a return to the Premier League. Earlier this year, he told The Team that he remained open to this possibility, despite his responsibilities at the head of the American selection. Now, the negotiations appear to have progressed considerably, although several administrative obstacles remain. Manchester United must still reach an agreement with the American Federation to release Pochettino from his contract, the departure clause of which would be estimated at 9 million euros, not including possible compensation for his assistants. Furthermore, the English club formalized the departure of Michael Carrick this Thursday. With 294 games managed in the Premier League, Pochettino will return to the English championship for the first time since his departure from Chelsea in the summer of 2024.

Manu Tournoux is a passionate and knowledgeable football enthusiast with a special focus on French football. Born and raised in France, Manu discovered his love for the beautiful game at a young age and developed a deep understanding of the ins and outs of "Le Championnat." His French roots and extensive experience in football journalism have made him an invaluable asset to the French Football Weekly team. As an author for the website, his expertise includes not only in-depth analysis of Ligue 1 and Ligue 2 matches but also insightful profiles of up-and-coming talents, detailed transfer news, and engaging coverage of the French national team. His captivating writing style and undeniable passion for the game have earned him a loyal following among our readers. When he's not crafting engaging articles for French Football Weekly, Manu enjoys attending live matches whenever he can, exploring football culture in various French cities, and engaging in spirited debates with fellow fans.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Darren Plant | 26 Nov 2026 15:41.
  • Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso has revealed that Moises Caicedo is available for Friday's Premier League fixture against Nottingham Forest.
  • The Ecuador international has found himself in and out of the Blues starting lineup this season due to several fitness issues.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Darren Plant | 26 Nov 2026 15:41.

Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso has revealed that Moises Caicedo is available for Friday's Premier League fixture against Nottingham Forest.

The Ecuador international has found himself in and out of the Blues starting lineup this season due to several fitness issues.

Caicedo's latest injury came during the first half of last weekend's game versus Leeds United, the midfielder landing awkwardly on his back and needing to be withdrawn.

As a result, Caicedo has been an obvious injury doubt for what is a potentially-crucial game for Alonso after three defeats in four top-flight games.

However, speaking at his pre-match press conference, the Spaniard declared Caicedo available for selection.

He told reporters: "Yes, he's going to be OK for tomorrow.".

On a negative note, Alonso acknowledged that Joao Pedro would remain sidelined for the trip to the East Midlands.

Meanwhile, providing an update on Maxence Lacroix's hamstring injury, he added: "It's one less week than the last game so we are closer to recovery but not for this game.".

There have been reports which suggest that Lacroix could return earlier than the initial target return period of January.

With Lacroix still injured, Alonso may feel forced to start Wesley Fofana alongside Levi Colwill, despite being furious with the Frenchman's comments in an interview this week.

There is the possibility of Josh Acheampong starting in the centre with Colwill, with Marco Palestra potentially starting at right-back.

If Jorrel Hato remains sidelined with a back injury, Pep Chavarria is favourite to start at left-back.

Alonso also has the option of going with a back three featuring the aforementioned centre-backs, with Pedro Neto at right wing-back and Palestra on the left.

Is AIIB's complaint mechanism failing affected communities?

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1048 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For members of the Indigenous Sasak community on the Indonesian island of Lombok, the conflict over their land is not over.
  • For them, a tourism and infrastructure project co-financed by the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) is a source of frustration, as they believe it has led to the expropriation of their land and destruction of their livelihoods.
  • In late September, they officially filed a complaint with the bank.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For members of the Indigenous Sasak community on the Indonesian island of Lombok, the conflict over their land is not over.

For them, a tourism and infrastructure project co-financed by the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) is a source of frustration, as they believe it has led to the expropriation of their land and destruction of their livelihoods.

In late September, they officially filed a complaint with the bank. It remains unclear whether this complaint will lead to an independent investigation.

The AIIB, which finances major infrastructure projects across Asia, has a mechanism in place to deal with such complaints.

Individuals who suffer adverse effects from the bank-financed projects may, under certain conditions, file a complaint with the institution.

However, access to this process — known as the Project Complaints Mechanism (PPM) — remains controversial.

According to a report by The Diplomat, a magazine that covers political and economic developments in Asia, none of the 45 complaints listed on the AIIB's website had been deemed admissible as of mid-September.

The bank acknowledged that "no cases have passed the PPM's eligibility assessment," but it stressed that this is "only part of the story.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The AIIB emphasized that not every issue needs to be resolved through this mechanism.

The PPM is "only one part of AIIB's grievance redress ecosystem," the Beijing-based bank mentioned in response to a query from DW.

Those affected should first attempt to resolve concerns directly with the project team at the local level, it said.

According to the bank, "twelve complaints were in fact resolved at the project level — as a direct result of AIIB's follow-up and intervention — and one was resolved through domestic courts.".

But critics see this as a major weakness.

"The mechanism must be easily accessible," said Arntraud Hartmann, a development economist at the Johns Hopkins University School of Advanced International Studies (SAIS Europe) in Bologna, Italy.

Recent findings suggest that she argued that people affected by the projects, for instance, are required to document potential violations of environmental and social standards from the start. "How is the affected party supposed to know which standards might have been violated?" she questioned.

In a recent development, the AIIB disputes this claim. "In terms of accessibility, we have made the submission form simpler and translated it into 12 languages," it remarked, adding that complaints can be submitted online, by phone, or by email.

Sources indicate that urgewald, a German environmental NGO, cites another problem with AIIB-financed projects. For many of them, information on environmental impacts and resettlements is either missing or published late, it noted.

According to recent reports, for 2024, the NGO found that 11 of the 16 projects it examined lacked complete environmental and social impact assessments. In many cases, information on the potential number of displaced residents was also missing, it added.

In a recent development, "The information published on the bank's website is often insufficient and inconsistent. Particularly important documents, such as environmental impact assessments or resettlement plans, vary widely or are missing entirely," said Nora Sausmikat, a China expert at Urgewald.

The lack of information makes it difficult for those affected to respond promptly and report violations early on, she underscored, adding that the situation is particularly difficult for people without formal land titles.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Christoph Steinert, a political scientist at the University of Konstanz, remarked the mere existence of such grievance redressal mechanisms "is not enough.".

Particularly vulnerable groups often know little about their rights, he stated, adding that information should be available in local languages and targeted outreach directed at affected communities.

Criticism of the AIIB's procedures is not latest. A 2023 report by international aid organizations, including Recourse, Accountability Counsel, and Inclusive Development International, revealed that the AIIB's grievance mechanism had failed to accept a single complaint since its 2019 inception.

The study highlighted that 101 of the 219 AIIB-financed projects, or 46% of the total projects at the time, were ineligible for review due to co-financing exemptions.

Industry observers note that the AIIB typically provides funding without leading projects, a standard practice in development finance. When complaints arise, it directs complainants to the lead lender. As a result, nine of the 45 complaints fell outside its jurisdiction.

According to recent reports, for Sausmikat, this is part of the problem. "The AIIB, however, decided against revising this requirement and established a mechanism that is very difficult to access," she mentioned.

As of January 1, 2026, following two years of external consultations, the AIIB reformed its complaints mechanism. Under certain conditions, complaints can now be filed even while legal proceedings are ongoing.

In a recent development, but Sausmikat stressed that the changes are insufficient. Of the eight key recommendations made by an independent expert, only three were adopted, she underlined. "The revision did not remove the actual obstacles.".

The AIIB stated that the reforms are intended to make the mechanism "more accessible and responsive.".

The new rules have been in effect for only 10 months, and their implementation is being closely monitored, the bank stated.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Steinert said fear of reprisals poses another fundamental challenge to such procedures.

Documented cases from Latin America, for instance, show that complainants have faced administrative or legal problems, and in some cases even violence.

Such risks could deter others from filing complaints, Steinert noted. However, his research does not specifically address AIIB projects.

The bank noted that it "does not tolerate retaliation against anyone who raises concerns.".

"Requestors may ask for confidentiality, and the revised PPM policy strengthens protection against reprisals," it added.

Sausmikat remarked Germany — as a co-founder and the fourth-largest shareholder of the AIIB — could also play a role, working with other member states to push for changes.

Sources indicate that hartmann also stressed that the bank's shareholders bear responsibility and urged the AIIB's Board of Directors to amend the rules governing the grievance mechanism. "We need a policy based on good-practice standards.".

This article was originally written in German.

Recent findings suggest that for several gatherings, the corridors have been a real construction site for the French team. And it’s not this evening in Milan that’s going to fix things. At San Siro, the Blues started their meeting well, before gradually losing their footing and conceding their first defeat of the Zinedine Zidane era (3-1), on the occasion of this 5th day of the Nations League. In this debacle, Malo Gusto particularly suffered. Aligned in the right lane, the Chelsea full-back increased his attempts, struggling to contain the Italian offensives.

In a recent development, the former Lyonnais, however, had a great opportunity to get back on his feet, after a complicated start to the club season. Far from being an indisputable starter this season under Xabi Alonso, he was still called up by ZZ to compensate for Jules Koundé’s injury. “ He was the next player on my list. He knows the selection. He certainly has less playing time at the moment, but he already has experience at this level. This is therefore the opportunity to give him the opportunity to return to Blue », justified the French coach when questioned about his choice to select Gusto. A missed opportunity. Taken behind his back, overwhelmed in duels and unable to secure his side, the 23-year-old was undoubtedly the worst French player on the pitch.

According to recent reports, faulty on the first Italian goal signed Pio Esposito after being overwhelmed on his side (26th) by Cambiaghi, Malo Gusto then caused a penalty, certainly missed by Sebastiano Esposito. Two situations which weighed heavily on his performance, while the full-back was greatly expected. Unable to reassure defensively, he only won his first duel… in the 47th minute of play (2 out of 6). Enough to accentuate his completely upside-down match, in addition to his eight lost balls and his three fouls committed. In the 77th minute, his ordeal ended with the entry of last-minute call-up Saël Kumbedi, two minutes after the second Italian goal, coming from his side with this cross from Dimarco for Frattesi (63rd).

Recent findings suggest that destroyed on all sides, he was however spared by his coach who preferred to give a general assessment of the meeting: “ there were some good things, especially in the first half. Afterwards, we did less good things. Particularly in duels and in 1v1s, we were a little worse… The start of the second half was good too. It’s true that when we were in difficulty, we didn’t know how to react and stay within the framework set up. We did it in the first, and afterwards when they took the advantage, we dispersed a little, also on the defensive level. » While no player stands out for the moment on the right side, Malo Gusto seems to have burned his cards during this first match. Conversely, he is even going through a very difficult period in the selection, since France conceded eight goals in their last 166 minutes of play with him on the pitch. Not sure that he will be renewed on Sunday against Turkey.

Two teams at the bottom of the Scottish Premiership standings will do battle on Saturday, when St Mirren welcome Kilmarnock to the Marbill Coaches Stadium.

The hosts are 10th in the table with 14 points from 14 games, while the visitors are propping up the standings with just nine points from 14 fixtures.

St Mirren initially enjoyed a positive start to the 2026-27 Scottish Premiership season, winning three and drawing one of their opening four league fixtures.

However, Craig McLeish's side subsequently endured a miserable run of results, going on to record just one win in their next 10 league fixtures.

The Saints have suffered eight defeats during that run, alongside one draw, leading to St Mirren rapidly falling to 10th in the Scottish Premiership table with just 14 points.

St Mirren, now just one point above the drop zone, face a particularly vital match in the early relegation battle, as a win against Kilmarnock would extend their lead over the bottom-placed side to a healthy eight points.

On the other hand, a defeat, which would mark their fourth consecutive loss, would see St Mirren's current five-point lead slashed to just two points.

Despite their ongoing struggles, the Saints have been at their best at home, including winning one, drawing one and losing one of their last three home fixtures.

Kilmarnock, meanwhile, are enduring a dismal 2026-27 league campaign, sitting at the bottom of the standings with just nine points after 14 matchdays.

Neil McCann's side have recorded two wins, three draws and suffered nine defeats in their 14 league games, including remaining winless in their last five matches, with four losses and one draw.

Kilmarnock's biggest weakness has undeniably been their defensive vulnerability, having conceded 33 goals in 14 league matches - seven more than any other team in the division.

However, Killie are equally ineffective in offence, having scored just 15 goals in 14 games - only St Mirren (13) have scored fewer in the league.

Despite their disappointing campaign to date, Kilmarnock do boast a strong recent record against St Mirren, winning three of the last five encounters, although they did lose 1-0 earlier this term.

Meanwhile, Max Stryjek remains unavailable due to a knee injury, leaving Nico Mantl to continue in goal.

George Stanger and Michael John Kamara should provide protection in central defence, with Tom Lowery, Aaron Tshibola and Greg Kiltie featuring in midfield.

After the international break, Paris Saint-Germain will return to the Champions League with the reception of AS Roma at the Parc des Princes on November 25. A meeting placed at very high risk according to the French authorities, as indicated RMC Sport. If, usually, the visitor parking lot at the PSG grounds can accommodate between 2,000 and 2,300 supporters depending on the matches, the capacity of this area of ​​the Parc des Princes will be reduced to 1,500 spectators for the Italians, by order of the Paris Police Prefecture and the National Division for the Fight against Hooliganism (DNLH).

This measure is explained in particular by the close proximity between certain fervent supporters of Paris Saint-Germain and those of Napoli. This attachment could lead to a rise in tension around this meeting with the AS Roma ultras. UEFA must also rule on this situation, which requires 5% of the stadium to be reserved for visiting fans.
